reviews: Rating: 5 - North and South Ninepin Islands, October 8, 2021. Took bus 92 from Diamond Hill to Sai Kung at 9:30 AM. Quickly bought bread for the afternoon, met up with friends, and boarded the speedboat. Soon after setting sail, a sudden downpour and we were soaked to the bone! 😅 Arriving at the North Ninepin Island pier, we could already see the imposing hexagonal basalt rock formations. Following the path to Lighthouse No. 200, we admired the rugged cliffs. Returning to the pier, we found the world-famous Silver Neck Bridge on the opposite shore, offering views of Moon Cliff, Cannon Rock, and other unique Hong Kong landscapes. We had visited Moon Cliff and Cannon Rock last November, and this time we aimed to see them. Be aware that climbing across is dangerous; assess your abilities and don't force it.  At 12:30 PM, we boarded the boat to South Ninepin Island. After disembarking, we found a place to eat. We continued taking photos at the Stone Arch, also known as the "Tiger's Mouth Cave," and then went to find the smallest Tin Hau Temple, which was already closed. With over an hour to spare before boarding, I sat down to enjoy the sea breeze and relax.  I was very happy and lucky; the weather was sunny and beautiful after we disembarked, resulting in many lovely photos.

Rating: 5 - Located in Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon, Hong Kong, 1881 Heritage is a cultural and shopping landmark housed in the restored Former Marine Police Headquarters. Built in 1884, it is one of the oldest surviving government buildings in Hong Kong and was declared a monument in 1994. The site features Neoclassical and Victorian-style buildings, including the original Main Building and the Old Kowloon Fire Station. Historically used to signal time to ships in the harbor, the Time Ball tower has been fully restored and still performs a daily time-setting ceremony at 1:00 PM. FWD House 1881: The main building has been transformed into a luxury boutique hotel featuring upscale dining concepts. The complex is a hub for high-end brands, including a new BAPE flagship store (opened December 2025) featuring an in-store cafe concept. Heritage Hall: A dedicated space where visitors can learn about the site's history and view original artifacts like police holding cells and historical cannons. Entry to the complex is free. Free guided tours are conducted daily; reservations are recommended. To get there: Take the MTR to Tsim Sha Tsui Station (Exit L6) or the Star Ferry to the Tsim Sha Tsui pier.

reviews: Rating: 4 - Aberdeen Harbour has a rich history of fishing industry that dates back several centuries and still thrives in this area on the south of Hong Kong Island.  Today the harbour is lined with urban promenades on both sides and is the location of the important Aberdeen Wholesale Fish Market. It also a typhoon shelter meaning it is loaded with vessels of all manner, including expensive yachts, coastguard speedboats, passenger ferries, sampans and all manner of small vessels used to support and supply the local seafood wholesale market.  The harbour is teeming with boat traffic which is fun to see and experience. This is also where you also find the famous Jumbo (floating restaurant) which is presently closed but will likely reopen under a future tourism scheme after the pandemic is over.  Visitors can also arrange sampan joy rides around the harbour or take ferries from the promenade to/from outlying islands such as Lamma and Po Toi.

Besides the audio guide on board, the guide's explanations were detailed, with special introductions to Hung Shing Temple and Shui Yuet Temple, giving me a deeper understanding of Aberdeen's history and culture. reviews: Rating: 5 - Lunch at ' The Horizon '  Sure, Hong Kong has its fair share of good Michelin star Dim Sum restaurants, a few even garnered 3* status. However, the impressive and delightful Dim Sum luncheon at this prestigious, members only club, can easily rub shoulders with some of Hong Kong’s creme de la creme! The appealing, compact menu, featuring a mix of refined, traditional and innovative Cantonese Dim Sum plus a few added nostalgic creations from yester-years, made our selection process a challenging affair.  After a few iterations, our collaborative decision making effort resulted in creating a sumptuous Dim Sum lunch menu to remember!  We ordered a plate of perfectly seasoned and charred centre-cut Iberico Pork Char Siu. A rare find of classic Fried Wonton with Sweet and Sour sauce was added without hesitation. Next, an order of delightful and creative, freshly baked, Matcha infused, BBQ Pork buns. Traditional Har-Gow and Taro croquettes followed. The latter with diced roasted duck, chives and shitake mushrooms filling…..so juicy and good! A smoky, mildly spicy and savory XO sauce stir fried Cheung-fun with ample wok-hay plus an umami packed braised Chinese Mustard Greens with Chinese Ham in a Shan-Tong chicken broth rounded off our near perfect meal! The dessert of duo Mango and coconut jello pudding was lovely and refreshing, not overly sweet.  BTW, the view from our window table, overlooking the yacht club and harbour, was spectacular and breathtaking!

reviews: Rating: 3 - The Aberdeen Wholesale Fish Market is not a traditional sightseeing venue but is an interesting place to see the inner workings of the seafood industry at the wholesale stage of the supply chain. It is located just west of the Aberdeen Promenade and is really busy first thing in the morning. The market opens at 4am and is a hive of activity until later in the morning and early afternoon once the day is mostly done here.  If you visit mid-morning, prior to ferry trips or schedule sampan rides arranged along the promenade, you can get a glance at how the industry works. You'll find trucks being loaded with large containers and boxes of live fish and shellfish of many varieties. Peek into the staging areas and you'll find endless tanks with seafood ready to be sold, packaged and sent out to retailers throughout Hong Kong. Be mindful as the water is gushing here, some areas, the floor is running 2 inches deep in water spilling out of the tanks. Notice, the workers all wear high rain boots and for good reason.  Note: You can take pictures within the Aberdeen Wholesale Fish Market and if you pay attention to not get in the way, nobody will be bothered by your presence.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Amah Rock: Chinese: 望夫石, is a naturally shaped, 15-meter tall rock formation located on a hilltop in southwest Sha Tin District, Hong Kong. It is situated within Lion Rock Country Park and is a popular destination for hikers due to its unique appearance and panoramic views of the Sha Tin district. The rock’s name, which literally translates to "the stone gazing out for her husband," stems from a poignant folk legend: A fisherman’s wife would climb the hill every day with her baby on her back to watch for her husband's return from the sea. Unbeknownst to her, he had drowned. In recognition of her loyalty and faithfulness, the Goddess of the Sea turned her and her child into stone so their spirits could remain united. Today, it stands as a symbol of loyalty and is a place of worship for women. The rock is accessible via several hiking trails. The most popular trail is the Hung Mui Kuk Nature Trail which is the easiest route; it starts near the northern entrance of Lion Rock Country Park and takes approximately 30–45 minutes to reach the rock. Generally rated as easy to moderate. The path is a mix of stone steps and paved trails, though it can be steep in certain sections.

It is situated just next to the historic Tin Hau Temple (stop 5) and just past the walled village of Lo Wai (stop 4) if you are starting the trail from the south. What you see today is a well-preserved, three hall building which honours the memory of the founding ancestors of the Tang Chung-ling Clan who settled this area of Hong Kong as early as the late 13th century. The Ancestral Hall is open for visitation from 9am to 1pm (morning) and 2pm-5pm (afternoon) daily but is closed on Tuesdays.  Historically, the Tang Chung Ancestral Hall was built in the early 16th Century. The exterior is attractive with grey-brick construction, plaster, motifs, fascia boards, auspicious animal decorations and tiled roofing. It is similar to Chinese temple architecture and appearance you may have come across when sightseeing temples around Hong Kong.  The interior offers several interesting things to see including the large screen (dong chung) which separate the front and centre hall, the delicately carved wooden beams and a peculiar stone plaque of the Nam Him Study Hall which no longer exists. In the Rear hall, there are three bays with shrines dedicated to past members of the Tang Clan. The Centre Bay shrine includes the Soul Tablets including the Imperial relative, the Song Dynasty Princess and her husband Tang Wai-kap. The information panels will help you identify this particular Tablet amongst the others.  Of further interest and note, the Rear Hall serves as a default information centre for the entire Lung Yeuk Tau Heritage Trail and makes for an important source of information and details about the various attractions found along the trail. What you will find are large panels for the various respective heritage sight with historical accounts for each. It is very much worth spending some time here to read up and learn about the various places. I'd also recommend taking pictures of the panels as well. These come in handy later on, particularly when coming across the attractions which don't have posted information nearby.  In the end, a 10-15 minute visit to admire the architecture and craftsmanship work of the Tang Chung Ancestral Hall is warranted. Another 15 minutes reading up and reviewing the heritage sights information panels is advisable as well. Then continue onward to the somewhat isolated Tung Kok Wai (stop 7) which is the next call on the heritage trail.

Rating: 4 - Kat O (Crooked Island) is a zigzag-shaped island in the Double Haven of Plover Cove Country Park in the North Districtof Hong Kong. It is also part of the Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark and a place usually visited along with sister island, Ap Chau, by weekend day-trippers from the city.  Historically, the island for several centuries had a thriving fishing community. As late as the 1940s, around 6,000 people lived on Kat O, many of whom were Hakka people and Tanka fisherman. However, like most remote and small island based communities around Hong Kong, most residents left in recent decades in search of better living conditions and livelihoods in the city or abroad. Today, it is estimated that less than 50 people regularly reside on the island.  There are some interesting things to see and do along the Kat O Nature Trail which covers an 800 metre stretch of the island north and south of the main ferry pier. You can read about this trail on the HK Geopark website. It includes a nice viewpoint at Ko Tei Teng in the north, a stroll along the Kat O Main Street past small temples and properties mostly abandoned and a public square of sorts where you find a small cluster of attractions in the historic Tin Hau Temple, the Kat O Story Room (heritage centre), monumental archway structure, a couple of 19th-century cannons and the interesting Lover's Tree.  Note: There are a few less developed hiking trails that cover the island beyond the main Nature Trail but these are more recommended for those who plan to spend the entire day on Kat O and not combine visits with Ap Chau as you may need more time depending on how far from the main ferry pier you plan to venture.  There are no hotels or camping facilities on Kat O at present. However, you will find several casual eateries as well as snack & drink shops clustered around the ferry pier and there are public toilets on the beach in the north of the island past the old Fisherman's Village and south of Tin Hau Temple just next to a smaller temple dedicated to Guan Yim (Kun Iam) just past the south end of the trail.  How to Get to Kat O (and Ap Chau) You can arrange private and small group tours to Kat O. However, you can also take public ferries from Ma Liu Shui at Science Park on weekends and public holidays as well. The journey is 90 minutes each way and costs HK$90 (cash payment) per person for day return ticket.  There is one morning departure at 9am making call at Kat O, Ap Chau, Kat O and then departing back to Ma Liu Shui at 3.30pm. Note that many do combined visit with Ap Chau. This ferry, calls on Ap Chau as well, allowing nearly two hours to explore this sister island before returning to Kat O at 12.30pm. The ferry later departs Kat O at 3.30pm to return to Ma Liu Shui. Note: Do check the updated ferry departure times online before making way to Ma Liu Shui if you want to visit Kat O and Ap Chau.

reviews: Rating: 4 - Unique art center and event space on the site of a British arsenal. Rating: 5 - A serene escape in the city. I attended many events at Asia Society Texas when I lived in Houston, and this location did not disappoint. Rating: 4 - Wonderful heritage space for exhibitions and events, and just the venue itself is worth an hour or so of touring. I joined Asia Society's free public tour and learned a lot about the history and architecture of the center. Located in the former Victoria Barracks area, the Asia Society has taken over the former Explosive Magazines A and B as its venue of events and exhibition. The whole area comes with a holistic approach to historical preservation, art, ecology and architecture. Of the many heritage sites at the Asia Society, I found the explosives track to be the most interesting. Arsenal Street used to be where the raw materials for ammunition and explosives were transported to the Victoria Barracks by the coolies. The workers must wear lint-free garment to avoid causing sparks when they transported the explosives. The architects have preserved the transportation tracks as a way to celebrate the unique history of the former Victoria Barracks.

reviews: Rating: 2 - We booked the afternoon tea high tea set for 2 people. It cost us around 840HKD. We were given a comfy window seat with uninterrupted views of Victoria Harbour. The tea selection was excellent, the food however left much to be desired. According to their instagram they had recently hired a new executive pastry chef so we were excited to try the new menu. Well, I don't know where he got his training from, but the bakery section of the local grocery store would definitely rival whatever he makes, and that's being generous. The high tea itself was a selection of savoury sandwiches, scones, and desserts. The sandwiches were edible but the same can't be said for the desserts, which mostly had the texture of sugary cake batter that's been left in the fridge to chill. I would rather eat jelly made from the $2 jelly crystals that you dissolve in hot water than that awful citrus tartlet. The scones were better but on the drier side. Cannot recommend the high tea set at all. The toilets were nice and well maintained. Perfect for crying in after spending a fortune on the budget quality bakery items.

Rating: 5 - I’ve been here with completely zero expectations. My goal was just to enjoy the views and have a drink or a snack. However, plan changed as soon as we checked the menu and we realized how many good options are there. Everything went perfect, I think one of the best experience had so far. Thumbs up for the service, we felt welcomed and treated with kindness. Food was amazing and with generous portions! So curious to try their desserts, but it will be for our next time in HK. We were not guests of the hotel and we were coming from the M+ museum. This place is not super hard to find, but also not the easiest. Add an extra 10 minutes to your schedule just in case!

Rating: 1 - Food was disappointing and very very overpriced. I ordered a Caesar salad and it came only with the bitter part of the romaine including the ends of the stalks. The croutons and bacon bits were both from a packet and there wasn’t an anchovy in sight. Also, the menu said it included flatbread which was not served. The truffle burger was made from frozen as well. I expected better from a Ritz Carleton establishment.

Rating: 5 - The atmosphere was wonderful, and the location offered a stunning view of Hong Kong's skyline—a truly beautiful place. However, the phrase is also frequently used in negative or ironic contexts. For instance, one might say a dull party "wasn't exactly a barrel of fun," or a difficult job is "not a barrel of laughs". In such cases, the phrase highlights the absence of enjoyment through sarcasm. Essentially, "a barrel of fun" signifies an abundance of pleasure and entertainment, whether used literally to praise a wonderful experience or wryly to critique a boring one. Its meaning relies heavily on context and tone to determine if genuine amusement or a lack thereof is being communicated.

Rating: 5 - The Bishop’s House (會督府) is one of the most remarkable symbols of the development of the Anglican Church of Hong Kong (also known as Hong Kong Sheng Kung Hui 香港聖公會). The first building on the site appears to have been a boys’ school constructed in 1845-1848. Alterations and additions were made to the school building in 1851 in “collegiate style”. The building then housed St. Paul’s College (聖保羅書院) and also the Residence of the first appointed Bishop, George Smith, who was Warden of the College. Today the stone plague inscribed with 聖保羅書院 (St Paul’s College) is still visible near the main entrance of the Bishop’s House.  The style of the building, which is quite unusual for Hong Kong, is the Tudor Revival style. Tudor style elements include an oriel window, flat head and pointed windows, label mouldings over the windows, buttresses, and imitation cross-shaped loopholes to the top of the tower. Classical elements are also apparent in the use of quoins, rusticated granite stonework to the G/F storey on the north-east façade, the regularly spaced windows and the glazing bar patterns.

Rating: 5 - I recently visited Bishop's House, located at 1 Lower Albert Road, Central, Hong Kong. This historic building, constructed in 1848, now serves as the Hong Kong Anglican Church's provincial office and is listed as a Grade I historic building. Its unique Tudor Revival architectural style, combining a granite base with a three-story octagonal tower, showcases a simple yet elegant aesthetic.  Bishop's House was originally conceived in 1843 by Reverend Vincent John Stanton to provide education for Chinese boys. In 1851, St. Paul's College was founded here, becoming one of the oldest secondary schools in Hong Kong. With the establishment of the Diocese of Victoria, Bishop George Smith took over the college and used the building as his bishop's residence and office.  From 1851 to 1941, the south wing of Bishop's House also served as the school building for St. Paul's College, nurturing many distinguished alumni, including the first Chinese barrister and Legislative Council member, Ng Ting-fong.  Although the Governor's House is not open to the public today, its exterior still retains traces of history. The stone plaque on the exterior wall bearing the school motto "Reverence for God, Love your neighbor as yourself" bears witness to the long history of St. Paul's College.  Overall, the Governor's House is not only a testament to Hong Kong's history but also an important landmark in the development of religion and education. Its architectural style and historical background are well worth a visit for any tourist interested in Hong Kong's history.

The trail starts from the north side of the High Island Reservoir dam, it then negotiates stone steps for roughly 0.5 km, away from the reservoir dam, with views of the north rim of the reservoir. reviews: Rating: 5 - Quite a bit of history around this little parked tucked away between apartment buildings and construction sites behind the former Mariners Club in TST.  A quick hike up a steep little hill gets you to the main section of the park.  The Tower you can find there dates back to 1907 and was used to house a time ball that sailors used to set their chronometers with before radio-telegraphy became a thing.  There are also four concrete gun emplacements on the south side facing Victoria Harbour.  The Signal Tower is worth a walk through, but be warned it only opens twice a day at certain times. Rating: 4 - Tsim Sha Tsui may seem like a place with many commercial streets, shopping malls, fine restaurants, and upscale hotels, but it's actually home to many hidden parks and urban oases, one of which is Signal Hill Park.  Signal Hill, also known as Blackhead Point and Big Bag of Rice, was originally a promontory on the shore of Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon. It was established by the Hong Kong Observatory in 1907. From that year until 1933, due to the lack of radio technology, it was primarily used to report time to ships passing through or docked in Victoria Harbour and to residents. It was subsequently declared a monument in 2015 and is now home to Signal Hill Garden, a place for public relaxation. The entrance to Signal Hill Garden is located at Burma Terrace. From the park entrance, it's a short, somewhat strenuous, four-minute walk up the slope to the Signal Tower, which leads to the summit. The garden features two major attractions: the office and the Signal Tower. The office is not open to the public, but many young girls come to check in at the signal tower. The signal tower was originally two stories high, with an exterior wall made of red bricks. It is an Edwardian-style building. It is rare to find European-style buildings in the city.

Rating: 5 - Old Lei Yue Mun Barracks is one of the earliest British Army fortifications in Hong Kong. In1985 the Army relinquished the site to the Hong Kong Government. The site was subsequently converted into Lei Yue Mun Park and Holiday Village.  Block 25 dates back to the period 1884-1890 and is the oldest building of the former barracks. It used to be the Officers’ Mess. It is an elegant Colonial Classical Revival two-storey building with open colonnaded and balustraded verandahs on three sides.  Block 25 has built heritage value as it is the oldest of the former barrack buildings. It is a good representative example of early colonial military architecture contributing to the group value of the historic buildings in the camp.

Rating: 5 - Block 25, used as the officers mess, is believed to have been built in the late 1890s to early 1900s. It is one of the earliest buildings constructed in the first phase of the barracks development and is a good representative example of early colonial military architecture.  Block 25 is a 2-storey building with elegant simplified Classical design, featuring open colonnaded and balustraded verandas on 3 sides. The east facade retains much of its original appearance. The walls and columns are painted brickwork. The verandas are supported by square brick columns with simple bases and capitals. Nestled under the overpass near Causeway Bay, the wet market is bustling with fresh produce, meat, and seafood vendors catering to both neighbourhood residents and professional chefs. Upstairs, the cooked food centre transforms into a haven for local food lovers. Diners can expect traditional Cantonese dishes served hot and fast—stir-fried clams with black bean sauce, roast meats, seafood noodles, and wok-fried vegetables are popular staples. The place may not be air-conditioned or spotlessly clean, but that’s part of the experience. It’s loud, slightly chaotic, and filled with character. Prices are affordable compared to the trendier eateries in the city, making it a favourite among budget-conscious foodies and adventurous tourists. Some reviewers mention the environment can feel cramped during peak hours, and English may not be widely spoken, but the warm hospitality of the stall owners often bridges the gap. For those seeking a taste of traditional Hong Kong, Bowrington Cooked Food Centre is an unforgettable culinary stop that delivers flavour, atmosphere, and cultural immersion in one vibrant location.

The location is free to visit and observe, just be mindful and respectful as this is trusted by many Hong Kong people. If you want to participate, a small fee is listed on the board.

Rating: 4 - Hong Kongers are seizing on an ancient ritual to relieve their frustration turning to “villain hitting” to curse troublesome people just in time for Halloween 😅 to share this post.  Hong Kong is a modern metropolis that’s also home to countless time-honoured traditions, a folk ritual in Hong Kong and China, primarily Cantonese people - it is on the list of ‘Intangible Heritage'.  Also known as a “petty person beating,” is considered more effective on Jing Zhe the year’s first thunder according to the lunar calendar, for dispelling evil, people can pay older women who are professional beaters to place a curse on their enemies or rid of demons.  Usually, located under the Ngo Keng Kiu, or Canal Road Flyover, in Causeway Bay, Hong Kong 🇭🇰 you’ll find these old ladies sitting in front of miniature shrines adorned with idol statues and incense sticks from about noon.  The women wave incense sticks and murmur curses, while beating paper effigies - somewhat like a voodoo doll, which they’ll beat loudly and repeatedly with an old shoe. The practice is supposed to help dispel evil and is followed by a blessing to protect you from further harm. It’s a surprisingly cathartic experience even for those who aren’t superstitious.  The paper is then burnt and put symbolically in the mouth of a paper tiger. Together they are thrown into a tin can next to the shrine, then another yellow Paper is used to bless the person. Initially just like that then after lighting it with fire.  It could be your boss or a cranky relative or an envious neighbor or the demons 😈 👻 👽 🧛‍♂️ At the end of it, you are emotionally clear that someone has taken care of an enemy for you? They say it blesses you staying protected, while some of these ladies are also astrologers who can see your hand and suggest additional solutions.

Rating: 4 - 50 hkd for beating villain and another 50 hkd for peace/protection. The lady gives you two; don’t think you need two if you don’t want to buy both. Interesting event. Can watch for free. Loud slapping under bypass. Wait not bad 5 min. Easy to get to by Ding Ding.

Rating: 5 - Short walk from Causeway Bay station exiting F2. Was there on a weekday afternoon, saw just one customer patronizing one of the many stalls. There are probably around 10 stalls or fewer, each with an old lady manning it. Only when you walk near the old ladies or go near their stalls will they try to sell their service. Costs 50hkd to 打小人, but I think auntie was trying to upsell, said one was for peace/safety and another for luck, so 50x2. Told her I just wanted the peace package. If I had written names on both sets of "joss/praying papers", would probably have to pay 100hkd.. The prayers/chanting lasted maybe 3 mins or so? If it helps in any way, it's good, else just an experience. One can also just visit the place without buying or paying for anything.

Rating: 4 - Walking beneath the Canal Road flyover between Causeway Bay and Wanchai on the island side of Hong Kong, you may be startled to hear the repeating loud ‘thwack’ of a shoe over and over again. If you're curious enough to investigate, you will see a couple of old ladies repeatedly hitting their shoes against a brick. This spectacle of ‘villain hitting,’ known as da siu yan (打小人）in Cantonese, is an old ritual generally practised in Hong Kong and Guangdong. The tradition is believed to come from ancient agricultural traditions, where villagers used to hold an annual ceremony to scare away the ‘White Tiger’ who would destroy their crops and harm the village. As time went on, this tiger eventually morphed into the more general ‘villain.’  The ritual is believed to be a way to ‘curse’ your enemies, bringing them bad luck and misfortune after they have been ‘hit.’ If there is someone you want to ‘curse,’ all you need to do is get a photo of them or write their name on a piece of paper, then begin hitting it with a shoe whilst reciting chants such as “beat your little head (打你個小人頭), I'll beat you until you'll never get ahead for the rest of your life (打到你成世冇出頭),”  Hong Kong’s ‘villain hitters’ are a group of government licenced elderly women who squatted on stools in front of numerous incense laden shrines, with their slippers in hand. From workers who have an issue with their bosses, to scorned wives wanting to curse a husband’s mistress, to students wanting to perform well in exams - people from all walks of life come to visit these ‘villain hitters.’ It’s become so popular that Time Magazine’s “Best of Asia'' feature listed it as its “Best Way to Get It Off Your Chest” item.  For 50 HKD to start, you can have these old ladies beat away your enemies, whilst bringing you good luck. The process has a few steps to it, including presenting an offering to the deities, lighting incense and worshipping at the altars, writting the name of your enemy on a special piece of paper, or present a photograph, and using one of your own shoe if you like, then leave the rest to the lady that doing the beating. Even if you don’t have a sworn enemy, you can still experience villain hitting. All you have to do is head over to the Canal Road flyover (香港堅拿道天橋）—from there you can marvel at this ancient ritual for however long you like.

Rating: 5 - If you are spending some time in Hong Kong, this is a place you must visit. A great place to enjoy nature away from the city life. The waterfall was beautiful and we enjoyed it a lot. Once you reach to the bottom of waterfall the sceneries are fantastic and you can take beautiful pictures. But have to be careful when you reach to this place because some times rocks are slippery. Once you complete watching waterfall then you can came back to trail and continue towards that and complete the round trail which is not more that 3 kms. Overall well recommended this place if you are nature lover and visit Hong Kong for your vacation

Rating: 5 - Difficulty 2/5 stars; you’ll have to walk/climb up a stream to reach the pool.  The 15 meters high Bride’s Pool Waterfall is located in Shuen Wan Country Park. It is easily accessible from the main road, Bride’s Pool Road parking lot/gazebo. There are a few different ways to walk there but we went this way: descend from the main road via the staircase in the parking lot. As you walk down, you’ll pass by some picnic/BBQ areas. You’ll reach a split end. Take the left which will bring you to the Bride’s Pool (right, up the stairs to Mirror’s Pool with a 35 meter high waterfall). You’ll reach another split end, take the descend one and continue. You’ll reach an open space with a stream. If you want to reach the waterfall, you’ll have to walk/climb up the stones to reach to the upper stream. The stones are slippery at times covered with lichen. Reward yourself with a dip in the pool at the end of the walk. The water is quite clear, you can see some fishes and shrimps in the water.

Rating: 5 - Nice trail with a waterfall at the end. It's a very easy hike with just a few stairs and the path is clearly marked. There are public toilets on the way as well. You can't get super close to the waterfall though
Rating: 2 - Easy to access but the water fall is not attractive.

Rating: 3 - I was lucky with the weather and spent a short bit pleasant time at this place. It was a bit difficult to get there. From Tai Po Market railway station you need to catch the mini bus (20R on weekdays) which leaves once an hour. Some people weren’t lucky enough to get a seat so they had to wait for the next one. That happened to me on the way back so I almost waited 2 hours in the middle of nowhere… To the trail: it’s a short roundtrip with quite steep stairs. You can hear the waterfall but you can’t really see the whole beauty. I met less than 10 people on the whole trip. But there were 3 guys at the bottom of the waterfall to take pictures and I could here them talking the whole time because of the echoes. I imagine it to be very annoying with even more people. I was looking for a quiet place in the nature. You could spend more time in that area with other routes but it could take quite a long time to get there/back.

There are many short films related to the development of Cantonese opera and famous performers; those interested can watch them at their leisure, otherwise they might find them unremarkable. Compared to the Sha Tin Cultural Museum, the Ko Shan branch is more in-depth, while the Sha Tin branch is more general, clearly focusing on different aspects. I particularly enjoyed seeing many scripts, not physical copies, but displayed on electronic screens. The handwritten original scripts were truly captivating, some even bearing the handwritten notes and revisions of the performers.  The park surrounding the Ko Shan Theatre, though small, offers tranquility amidst the bustling city, and the trees surrounding the sports field are beautiful.

Rating: 5 - i hiked here coming from north along the coast which included a lot of climbing along the cliffs and rocks.  small little fisherman houses on the way. scenic and unspoiled.  i like sleeping in abandoned historical buildings so this battery was a must! a lot of mosquitos at night but veryyyy beautiful surroundings... highly recommended. but very windy at night due to the non existing windows. beautiful sunset as well

Rating: 4 - One of the interesting historic attractions to see at Cape D'Aguilar on Hong Kong Island is the war era battery at the western end of the cape known as the Cape D'Aguilar Battery. This is a Grade II Historical Building in Hong Kong.  This military installation was built in 1939 and fell under the Eastern Fire Command to protect the southern coastline. What you will find is an exposed battery on a flat rock point. You can walk around the entire battery. There is concrete staircase that allows you to enter the first floor of the structure, from within there are three windows facing the sea.  Just next to the staircase is a dated information panel, it is aged but can still be read fairly clearly for those interested in the history of the battery as well as other gun supplements and military installations mounted around the Cape.  To access the Cape D'Aguilar Battery, you will first see it from a distance as you walk down Cape D'Aguilar Road in the direction of the marine park. Near Hok Tsui Lower Village, there is a small, unmarked trail that leads nearly 500 metres through forested hillside that descends down to the coast where find the battery beautifully situated on the sea. It is helpful to have a map or installed mobile phone hiking app. which includes this informal trail. I recommend the Hiking Trail HK app.  Note: there are other WWII military installations around Cape D'Aguilar, the easiest to find and visit is the Bokhara Battery located on the eastern shore near the Cape D'Aguilar Lighthouse and above the famous Crab Cave. It is easy to spot and a short quick walk up a hillside to see this particular ruin.

Rating: 5 - Tough to spot the trail head to get to this place. The trailhead is right after the set of mailboxes that you would see as you make your way to the tip of the cape. The path is under maintained and often times you would have to pull on tree branches to help your balance. But the views are well worth it.

reviews: Rating: 1 - This is a membership only eatery consist of 2 restaurants at the location.  We met at the Lounge for lunch.  Location: Conveniently located in Tsim Sha Tsui within a 10 min walk from the TST MTR station.  The restaurants are at 55/F where you can have a spectacular view of the Victoria Harbour as well as the Kowloon and outlying islands.  Food: We ordered a Wagyu beef burger, a Char Siu rice and a vegetarian tofu dish.  The taste of all three are acceptable but nothing to write home about.  Certainly far from even Michelin recommendation.  Among the desserts, I like the chocolate cake the most.  The other 2 were mediocre.  Service: The Lounge service was pretty accommodating.  The manager offered to combine 2 small tables after seeing we were short on space (common issue in HK) after ordering a few drinks and waters.  The most troubling thing with this place was from the female hostess when we arrived.  After informing her our friend's name and membership number, we were told to sit at the sofa without any offer of even a glass of water.  And she was also firm on that we could not wait at the restaurant while waiting for our friend.  This could be fine if I was not with my disabled mother whom clearly has mobility issue and carries a cane in her daily life. But I found it hard to accept this kind of hospitality toward elders and disabled persons.  It seems to me the Carlyle group prioritizes exclusivity over compassion in the way they run business.  In contrast, I had dinner at a Japanese restaurant from the Town Club in the New World building at Central.  Yakuma was a lot more accommodating and seated us immediately when we arrived the restaurant as guests.  In conclusion, I have the following recommendations.  1. Come to Carlyle group for the view. 2. If you are not a member, then make sure you arrive after your friend with a membership or you and your friend arrive together.  Otherwise, you would get stuck waiting outside of the restaurants.

Rating: 5 - With an amazing 360-degree view of the iconic Hong Kong skyline, Central Harbourfront Event Space offers almost 36,000 square metres of outdoor, open-air space with easy accessibility to public transportation. Events on the Central Harbourfront Event Space can span across some – or all – of the site, providing a high level of flexibility. Its easily accessible location and impressive surrounding views make CHES the ideal location for public and private events of a variety of scales and natures. One of these events is the Hong Kong Wine and Dine Festival. Surrounded by Hong Kong’s iconic skyline, the annual Hong Kong Wine & Dine Festival offers an unparalleled opportunity to discover the finest wines from around the world - all at affordable prices. Explore renowned labels from Europe, Australia and beyond – including award-winning bottles and James Suckling picks. Venture beyond the mainstream too, with hidden gems from lesser-known regions, Chinese wines, natural wines and low-alcohol alternatives. Nowhere else can you savour such a diverse array of wines immersed in Hong Kong's vibrant energy and cosmopolitan flair. Feast on beloved local delicacies alongside innovative global dishes in one lively setting at the Hong Kong Wine & Dine Festival. With hundreds of booths offering an enticing mix of traditional and trendy fare, discover the city’s dynamic food landscape. Pair your wines with the spectacular harbour view and the very best of Hong Kong’s diverse culinary culture. How to Get to the Central Harbourfront Event Space? By BUS: Depending on the bus route, you can alight in Central, Admiralty or the Outlying Ferry Piers and walk to the site. MTR: Access the site from Central (exit A) or HK Station (exit A2). Approximately 10 minutes walking distance. From Admiralty Station head towards Tamar Park, walk through the park towards the Waterfront Promenade and turn left. Approximately 10 minutes walking distance. FERRY: Take the Star Ferry to Central and walk towards the left after disembarking. Approximately 1 minute walking distance. TAXI: Alight at the Star Ferry taxi drop off and walk straight ahead. Approximately 2 to 4 minutes walking distance.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Sha Tin Che Kung Temple is one of Hong Kong’s most well-known and spiritually significant temples, especially associated with blessings for good fortune, protection, and new beginnings. Dedicated to Che Kung, a historical general from the Southern Song Dynasty believed to have protected the region from plagues and disasters, the temple holds deep cultural and religious importance for locals.  Located in Sha Tin, the temple complex is spacious, well-organized, and easy to explore. One of its most iconic features is the large bronze statue of Che Kung inside the main hall, which immediately creates a powerful and solemn atmosphere. Visitors often come to pray for health, success, career progress, and safety, especially during Chinese New Year, when the temple becomes extremely busy with worshippers seeking good luck for the year ahead.  A unique and well-known ritual here is spinning the brass windmills, which are believed to bring good luck depending on how smoothly they turn. This practice adds an interactive and symbolic element to the visit, making it memorable even for first-time visitors. The scent of incense, the sound of prayers, and the movement of people performing rituals together create a calm yet spiritually charged environment.  Architecturally, the temple is traditional and dignified, featuring red pillars, decorative carvings, and classic Chinese design elements that reflect centuries-old religious traditions. Despite its popularity, the temple grounds are well-maintained and feel peaceful outside of peak festival periods. There is also an open courtyard area that allows visitors to walk around, observe rituals respectfully, and take photos of the surroundings.  Sha Tin Che Kung Temple is not only a place of worship but also a cultural landmark that offers insight into Hong Kong’s spiritual life and traditions. Whether you come to pray, learn about local beliefs, or simply experience a quieter side of the city, the temple provides a meaningful and reflective experience. It is a worthwhile stop for travelers interested in history, culture, and the everyday spiritual practices of Hong Kong.

reviews: Rating: 4 - Che Pau Teng is a natural landmark known as The Rhino Rock located near the hilltop found on the Stanley Peninsula. It can be visited by way of a couple of trail routes found at and near the end of Wong Ma Kok Road south of the Stanley Village.  The simplest route starts at the bus stop at the end of the road right next to the Stanley Fort. This is a paved walk up to the transmission station before turning into a natural trail through shrubs and winding over, around and even through boulder piles until you reach the iconic landmark. Unfortunately, when I passed by recently, I found this trailhead closed to the public and unavailable for access.  The second route starts around 500 metres back on Wong Ma Kok Road, north of the Regalia Bay Residences. You'll find two small buildings and a trail that begins just next to the lower building. You'll climb southward at first beside a pipeline for around 40 metres before beginning a fairly sharp ascend up the hillside to the southeast. The trail requires some minor navigation skills and good footwear. I recommend gloves as well as you have to do some scrambling at times. You'll go through some thick wooded stretches, low hanging bamboo and boulder outcrops before reaching the same transmission station where the two routes meet.  There are great viewpoints throughout on the second route, particularly looking back to the north at Stanley. Even if it is more challenging, it is worth taking for the views alone. You'll be rewarded with more fine views of the sea from the boulder piles near and at the Rhino Rock. Inherently, the Che Pau Teng landmark does clearly resemble the face of a rhinoceros.  Note: Neither trail route up to the Rhino Rock is well documented nor do they show up properly on Google Maps. However, if you upload Hiking Trail HK, you can see both routes fairly well on their more detailed maps of the Stanley Peninsula.  Note: The hike isn't particularly long but it is steep and route two is fairly requiring. Bring sufficient water and a hat for the areas that are exposed to the elements.  Note: To reach the trailheads, you can walk down Wong Ma Kok Road around 20-25 minutes south of the village. During stretches of the road, there are no pavement sidewalks so you have to walk directly on the street. If this makes you uncomfortable, just take bus routes 6X or light green minibus 14 from the village to the end of the road where you find the trailheads.

Rating: 4 - A nice activity to do on Cheung Chau is the Cheung Chau Family walk, which covers some nice outdoor grounds on the southeast of the island including a section referred to as the Mini Great Wall.  This trail section was constructed in 1997 and is 850 metres long. It starts from near the back of Kwan Yam Beach and ends at a pavilion structure looking at interesting rock structures and the sea.  What you find here is a long stretch of granite railing that has been given the unique name of the Mini Great Wall. It covers a particularly impressive area along the coast with impressive views of the sea as well as large oddly shaped boulders which have also been given unique names by the local residents of Cheung Chau over the years. Along the Mini Great Wall, you will find signs with pictures of the various rock structures so you know what to look for. There are a couple pavilion viewpoints along this short hike as well.  Overall, this is a fun and easy area to hike and a place that is child-friendly if you want to get out with the littles to enjoy a bit of hiking and spending time in the great outdoors of Hong Kong outlying island of Cheung Chau.

Rating: 4 - A nice activity to do on Cheung Chau is the Cheung Chau Family walk, which covers some nice outdoor grounds on the southeast of the island including a section referred to as the Mini Great Wall.  This trail section was constructed in 1997 and is 850 metres long. It starts from near the back of Kwan Yam Beach and ends at a pavilion structure looking at interesting rock structures and the sea.  What you find here is a long stretch of granite railing that has been given the unique name of the Mini Great Wall. It covers a particularly impressive area along the coast with impressive views of the sea as well as large oddly shaped boulders which have also been given unique names by the local residents of Cheung Chau over the years. Along the Mini Great Wall, you will find signs with pictures of the various rock structures so you know what to look for. There are a couple pavilion viewpoints along this short hike as well.  Overall, this is a fun and easy area to hike and a place that is child-friendly if you want to get out with the littles to enjoy a bit of hiking and spending time in the great outdoors of Hong Kong outlying island of Cheung Chau.

address: Cheung Sheung Country Trail, Sai Kung, Hong Kong
reviews: Rating: 3 - The Cheung Sheung Country Trail is a 4.1 km trail that transects the Sai Kung West Country Park from east to west between Hoi Ha Road through the old Cheung Sheung Village on onward to Yung Shue O on the western coast the Three Fathoms Cove. The trek is moderately challenging, requiring a fairly steep ascend and descend on both ends.  This country trail is well paved and includes stone steps at the eastern end until you reach Cheung Sheung Village. There are some exposed stretches but a fair amount through semi-mature trees providing shade here and there. At Cheung Sheung you will find a village shop (Hui Lam) that is open on weekends and public holidays. You can buy simple local dishes here and take a rest here if hiking on weekends. There is a public portable toilet and some camping grounds here as well.  Between Cheung Sheung and Yung Shue O the trail is a mix of paved and dirt trail and there are some stretches that are a bit overgrown and not as well maintained. It mostly makes way through mature forest with lots of shade. Of note, it is a steep downhill ascend to Yung Shue O much of the way or a tough uphill slog if going the other direction.  Lots of good vegetation on the Cheung Sheung Country Trail. There are some wild pigs in the area, good chances of seeing feral cows during your hike, especially around the old village and Hui Lam shop. Fair chance of seeing lizards, lots of butterflies and dragonflies as well. Very few viewpoints on this trail unlike what you will find on the nearby MacLehose Stage 3 trail to the south.  Note: The official trail is just 4.1 km but the trailheads are quite far from anywhere on both ends. The the Hoi Ha Rd trailhead is around 1 km walk from the Pak Sha Bus Stop to the north so best to just get a taxi from Sai Kung if you want to be dropped off at the actual trailhead.  At the western end of the trail at Yung Shue O, you are 3.5 km walk south until you reach Sai Sha Road where buses can be found to Sai Kung or back towards Ma On Shan, Sha Tin and the city. If you know the ferry schedules, you can hike around 3 km up the coast from Yung Shue O to Sham Chung. Ferries come by a few times a day in route to Ma Liu Shui (University MTR Station) and Wong Shek. Do check the ferry schedules online before trying this.  Overall, there is nothing wrong with the Cheung Sheung Country Trail but it is less convenient starting and stopping and can make a 4km hike into 9-10km with too much time walking along roads to/fro bus stops on both ends. Further, there are some amazing viewpoints from the MacLehose trail just to the south which you simply won't find on the Cheung Sheung trail. Thus, if you had to choose between these two, most will definitely go with the MacLehose and leave the Cheung Sheung trail to Hongkongers who are done the rounds and are just looking for other trails to hike.

To its left is the kitchen and meal preparation room. A stable is in front of the main entrance with separate entrance.  The building is constructed of green bricks with its walls and granite columns supporting its pitched roofs of timber rafters, beams, purlins and clay tiles. The entire venue is decorated in a color scheme of 80% white and 10% purple. The live music and instrumental accompaniment for the hymns are provided by the brothers and sisters.  If you have any religious affiliation, you are welcome to visit the central church to inquire, listen to sermons, and participate in activities!  One more thing worth mentioning: that side is the Christ Central Church. The church's mission is to heal the lost and misguided based on God's love. And in stark contrast is Yan Chai Hospital. Rating: 5 - Poem Title: Bamboo Grove Zen Temple  The verdant bamboos mingle with a cool breeze, a pavilion nestles beside a small fishing pond.  Flowers bloom beside the Chanling Bridge, and the Heart Sutra is chanted within the courtyard.  This poem describes Bamboo Grove Zen Temple, located at 28 Furong Shan Road, Lo Wai, Tsuen Wan, New Territories, Hong Kong, on the southern slope of Furong Shan. The temple was built in 1928, and the pagoda hall was completed in 1932, officially naming it Bamboo Grove Zen Temple. Construction of the Main Hall began in 1975 and was completed in 1982. The temple houses the Main Hall, the Skanda Hall, the Heavenly King Hall, the Ksitigarbha Hall, the pagoda hall, the Guanyin Hall, the Fude Temple, and the Sutra Library. The temple also houses statues of Sakyamuni Buddha, Amitabha Buddha, the Medicine Buddha, Maitreya Buddha, Guanyin Bodhisattva, and Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva. Zhulin Monastery attracts large crowds during holidays and festivals. Numerous temples are located around Furong Shan in Tsuen Wan District, including the Yuen Yuen Institute, Western Temple, Puguang Garden, Xianghai Cihang, Longmu Buddhist Hall, Donglin Buddhist Hall, and Nantianzhu Temple. Furong Shan may also have the highest concentration of Buddhist halls and temples in Tsuen Wan. To reach Zhulin Monastery, take the 85 minibus from Siu Wo Street in Tsuen Wan, or take a taxi or drive.

reviews: Rating: 5 - The Former Kowloon-Canton Railway Clock Tower is one of Hong Kong’s most important historical landmarks, standing proudly along the Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront. Built in 1915, this red-brick clock tower is all that remains of the original Kowloon-Canton Railway terminus and serves as a quiet reminder of Hong Kong’s colonial and transportation history.  The design is simple yet striking, with its tall structure and classic clock faces making it easy to spot from a distance. While you can’t go inside, the surrounding open space allows visitors to walk around, take photos, and enjoy views of Victoria Harbour. It’s especially beautiful at sunset and in the evening, when the tower is softly lit and the harbour breeze adds to the calm atmosphere.  Located right next to the Star Ferry Pier and close to the Avenue of Stars, the Clock Tower fits perfectly into a relaxed harbour walk. It’s not a place that takes long to visit, but it adds depth and historical context to the area. Overall, it’s a meaningful stop for those interested in Hong Kong’s past, photography lovers, or anyone looking to slow down and appreciate a quieter side of the city amid the busy surroundings.

Rating: 5 - The Former Kowloon-Canton Railway Clock Tower, officially named the Clock Tower, is located in Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon, Hong Kong. It is a prominent, iconic landmark near the Victoria Harbour waterfront and the Star Ferry Pier. The surrounding area is wheelchair accessible, and the site offers free admission as it is a public space. The 44-meter-tall red brick and granite tower is the only remaining structure of the original Kowloon Station terminus, which was a major transportation hub and was demolished in 1978. It served as a memorable landmark for many Chinese immigrants and travelers arriving in Hong Kong by rail in the early 20th century. The tower is a key point of interest located near the Hong Kong Cultural Centre, the Hong Kong Space Museum, and the Avenue of Stars, which offers stunning views of the Victoria Harbour skyline. It is easily accessible by public transport: MTR: East Tsim Sha Tsui Station, Exit L4 (short walk) or Tsim Sha Tsui Station, Exit Ferry: Star Ferry Pier in Tsim Sha Tsui, which is right next to the tower.

Rating: 4 - Had I come to see the clock tower on its own, I probably would have only given it 3 stars. It is essentially just one monument and other than seeing it, there isn't anything to do there. However I came to the clock as part of a visit to the area where I took in other sites and attractions. This made viewing the clock better and in doing this, I would recommend stopping by to see it. reviews: Rating: 5 - Built between 1875 and 1889 , In the earliest days of the colony, street lighting came in the form of oil lamps hanging in the doorways of houses. Convenient for homeowners and cheap for the government, but not great for nocturnal navigation. So in the 1850s the government erected public oil lamps between Central and Wan Chai, and in 1864 the Hong Kong and China Gas Company—better known as Towngas—introduced gas lighting to the territory. The gasworks on Whitty Street in Shek Tong Tsui was the first of its kind in Asia, making the city also the first in Asia to be lit by gas. Kowloon, naturally, had to wait another 28 years. When first introduced, the lamps had to be manually lit and extinguished every day. These days the process is automatic, and the Duddell Street lamps (still served by Towngas) flick on and off automatically at 6pm and 6am, respectively.

Rating: 5 - These granite steps and last four remaining gas powered street lamps represent rare historic gem, serving as a reminder of Bygone era and first lamps in East Asia and keeping the old-school Hong Kong charm. Named after George Duddel, declared as a monument since 1979.

Rating: 5 - These gas-lit lamps are a heritage-listed 'Declared Monument'.  Happy to announce that the lamps have been fully restored to working order as of 27 December 2019. I managed to catch the gas company fixing the lamps during the day, so I returned at night to see the full effect of the beautiful radiant lamps.  For those who complained that they are just lamps - you knew before you visited that they were lamps, so what the f*** did you expect? Maybe you need to get off your mobile phone and learn to appreciate and respect art, cultural heritage, and the historical value of such things.

Rating: 5 - Crown Diamond Art Museum, Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon  Walking into the afternoon in Tsim Sha Tsui, I strolled slowly along Canton Road, passing through crowds, buses, and trucks, until the golden facade of China Hong Kong City came into view. I've been here many times, but today's destination held a certain anticipation—the Crown Diamond Art Museum.  The entrance resembled a typical retail store, making it easy to miss the museum. Inside, the lighting was soft, and the diamonds in the display cases sparkled like stardust in the air. A guide greeted me with a friendly smile, and the light journey officially began.  The museum has two floors. The guide led me through a mysterious passage to the first floor. The first item I saw was a Coca-Cola diamond handbag. The red and white color scheme was reinterpreted by diamonds, both familiar and somewhat absurd. Further on were diamond golf clubs. The light shone on the shafts, reflecting a cool glow. I imagined someone actually using one to tee off—they'd probably be nervous. To avoid that nervousness, you can also try it out with a regular club.  Next came diamond sunglasses, diamond watches, diamond phone cases… each one made me stop in my tracks. They weren't the kind of items so expensive they were unapproachable, but rather they challenged the limits of everyday objects. What would it be like if everything in your life were replaced with diamonds?  At the end of the first floor, the most talked-about exhibit appeared—a diamond toilet. It sat quietly in its display case, its surface densely studded with diamonds. At that moment, I suddenly felt that the soul of this museum wasn't "luxury," but rather "daring to dream and daring to do."  The exhibits on the second floor were completely different in style and more story-driven. Walking up the stairs, historical photos of the Guanlinglong brand hung on the walls. Upon reaching the second floor, Dr. Shen Yunlong stood in the center of the exhibition area, his warm smile welcoming everyone. He stood next to a diamond guitar—the world's most valuable diamond guitar, the light shining on its body like a frozen starry sky.  Dr. Shen personally explained the guitar's design philosophy and inlay techniques, and shared his story of how he went from a small subdivided flat to where he is today. His tone was simple, yet every word carried power.  Next came another guitar, the one with the most gemstones in the world, showcasing the Michael Jackson family rings. At that moment, I suddenly felt very close to the history of popular culture. The brilliance of the diamonds shone on the rings, illuminating those stage memories that once shook the world. He walked to the diamond scepter, which from a distance looked like the center of attention. Dr. Shen explained that this scepter was not just a work of art; it was also the exclusive scepter of Miss Asia—symbolizing glory and stage brilliance.  Upon closer inspection, the diamonds and gemstones intertwined under the lights, creating an almost mythical luster. In that instant, images of Miss Asia's coronation on television flashed through my mind: lights, applause, smiles, tears… carrying the collective memory of Hong Kong. Further on was a diamond lipstick case. Small, but so exquisitely crafted that you couldn't help but look closer. That kind of delicacy could only be achieved by someone truly passionate about craftsmanship.  As I left the museum, the night in Tsim Sha Tsui was already lit up, creating a familiar scene before my eyes. In this bustling city, there was still such a dazzling place, so full of stories.  #BigJlovesTravel  #ilovetravel  #traveller  #enjoymylife  #foodies  #travelislife  #jasontai1106  #jason_tai1106  #HongKong  #TsimShaTsui  #Kowloon  #ShenYunLong  #aaronshum  #GuanLingLongDiamondArtMuseum  #ipshk

Rating: 5 - Hong Kong's own Diamond Art Museum.  It displays ten Guinness World Record-breaking diamond pieces. Two of these diamond guitars have been used by renowned artists such as Michael Jackson and the Wynners, adding a touch of sparkle to the stage. The value of the diamonds themselves, combined with their historical significance, elevates the guitar's value beyond the size and quantity of the diamonds.  Other items include diamond tiaras, ceremonial items, watches, sunglasses, a Coke bottle, and golf clubs, all worth a look.

Rating: 5 - You can see ten Guinness World Records jewels on the upper and lower floors at once. The place is spacious and comfortable, and there are guides to give detailed introductions. It feels very worthwhile 👍🏼

Rating: 5 - This is a museum that requires reservations. I booked through Klook. I got 25% off the HK$200 admission fee. After checking in, a staff member was assigned to me and provided a full guide. They spoke very basic English, so even though I only have a junior high school level English, I was able to understand 80% of it. Inside, you can see diamond-adorned artworks registered in the Guinness Book of World Records. I believe this is the only museum in Hong Kong or Japan where you can see masterpieces created by such skilled modern artisans. Although the number of pieces is small, each piece is of such high quality that you'll want to examine them closely, and the total price is impressive. At the end of the museum is the Coronet showroom, where you can purchase diamond jewelry at a discount from the listed price. From simple to elaborate pieces, diamond lovers will enjoy buying one as a souvenir from Hong Kong. It's definitely cheaper than buying it in Japan. The diamonds seemed of very high quality. If you find something you like, I recommend buying it. There were only a few colored stones. Don't worry, there's no pressure to buy anything. The atmosphere was more like, "If you see something you like, let me know." I think your opinion will change depending on how you view the $200 admission fee, but personally I was very satisfied. I was attracted by the fact that there is no other museum where you can see these things, and by the hospitality provided by the attentive guide. I went alone, but I think it would be more comfortable to go with a group. You'll get a glimpse into Hong Kong, the city where gems gather.  Finally, the female staff member who guided us was incredibly kind. Thank you!

Take the mtr to university station, then walk to the ferry pier from there.

Rating: 4 - Kat O (Crooked Island) is a zigzag-shaped island in the Double Haven of Plover Cove Country Park in the North Districtof Hong Kong. It is also part of the Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark and a place usually visited along with sister island, Ap Chau, by weekend day-trippers from the city.  Historically, the island for several centuries had a thriving fishing community. As late as the 1940s, around 6,000 people lived on Kat O, many of whom were Hakka people and Tanka fisherman. However, like most remote and small island based communities around Hong Kong, most residents left in recent decades in search of better living conditions and livelihoods in the city or abroad. Today, it is estimated that less than 50 people regularly reside on the island.  There are some interesting things to see and do along the Kat O Nature Trail which covers an 800 metre stretch of the island north and south of the main ferry pier. You can read about this trail on the HK Geopark website. It includes a nice viewpoint at Ko Tei Teng in the north, a stroll along the Kat O Main Street past small temples and properties mostly abandoned and a public square of sorts where you find a small cluster of attractions in the historic Tin Hau Temple, the Kat O Story Room (heritage centre), monumental archway structure, a couple of 19th-century cannons and the interesting Lover's Tree.  Note: There are a few less developed hiking trails that cover the island beyond the main Nature Trail but these are more recommended for those who plan to spend the entire day on Kat O and not combine visits with Ap Chau as you may need more time depending on how far from the main ferry pier you plan to venture.  There are no hotels or camping facilities on Kat O at present. However, you will find several casual eateries as well as snack & drink shops clustered around the ferry pier and there are public toilets on the beach in the north of the island past the old Fisherman's Village and south of Tin Hau Temple just next to a smaller temple dedicated to Guan Yim (Kun Iam) just past the south end of the trail.  How to Get to Kat O (and Ap Chau) You can arrange private and small group tours to Kat O. However, you can also take public ferries from Ma Liu Shui at Science Park on weekends and public holidays as well. The journey is 90 minutes each way and costs HK$90 (cash payment) per person for day return ticket.  There is one morning departure at 9am making call at Kat O, Ap Chau, Kat O and then departing back to Ma Liu Shui at 3.30pm. Note that many do combined visit with Ap Chau. This ferry, calls on Ap Chau as well, allowing nearly two hours to explore this sister island before returning to Kat O at 12.30pm. The ferry later departs Kat O at 3.30pm to return to Ma Liu Shui. Note: Do check the updated ferry departure times online before making way to Ma Liu Shui if you want to visit Kat O and Ap Chau.

address: D'Aguilar Peak, Shek O, Hong Kong
reviews: Rating: 4 - Many hikers know to visit the Cape D'Aguilar Coastal Reserve to see crab caves and whale bones. However, many may not know where the Cape D'Aguilar landmark is located.  Take bus number 9 to the Cape D'Aguilar Road roundabout bus stop. Behind the water tank next to the bus stop, there's a hidden entrance to the mountain path (red section) leading to the summit. The path's slope is moderate and relatively easy, but the directional ribbons are not very clear. From a distance, the mountain doesn't appear to have dense vegetation, but there are still many trails through the woods (no need to rush, the paths are clearly marked). The view from the summit isn't expansive; the path at the highest point is shaded by trees. The landmark is located on a section of large rocks to the left of the path at the summit; be careful going up and down to take photos. After descending, return to the roundabout on Cape D'Aguilar Road via the launch site to complete the trip.

Rating: 4 - As spring arrives, the temperature is moderate, there is no rain, and the sunshine is abundant. It is a good time to go hiking. I would like to introduce a route with beautiful scenery, strange rocks, large specimens, sea caves, lighthouses, many check-in spots, and a beautiful ocean view to you~Hok Tsui Mountain.  Transportation: Take bus No. 9 from Shau Kei Wan Bus Terminal and get off at Shek O Terminal. On the way back, take bus No. 9 from Hok Tsui Station on Hok Tsui Road back to Shau Kei Wan.  Route: Shek O> Tai Shek Po> Hok Tsui Mountain> High Frequency Radio Transmitter Station> Hok Tsui Undersea Cable Station> Hok Tsui Lighthouse> Lei Yin Cave> Whale Skeleton> Crab Cave> Hok Tsui Coastal Reserve> Hok Tsui Road> Tai Fung Au> Hok Tsui Bus Station The entire journey is about 8 kilometers  Notes:  ~ Some sections of Hok Tsui Mountain are rugged and must be climbed with hands and feet  ~ If you do not choose to climb to the top of Hok Tsui Mountain, you can go from Tai Fung Au along Hok Tsui Road and pass through Hok Tsui Village to reach the coastal reserve  ~ Some areas of the Hok Tsui Coastal Reserve are not allowed to enter, please pay attention to the road signs  ~ Everyone has the responsibility to keep the countryside clean, take your own garbage away  Take bus No. 9 at Shau Kei Wan Bus Station Get off at Shek O Terminus, pass by Shek O Beach, run to the far right, and see a BBQ restaurant with a mountain trail next to it. This is the starting point of Hok Tsui Mountain. First, go through a section of stone steps and pass through a small forest. If you look to the right, you will see some large rocks. One of them looks like a wild boar pointing towards the sky. It is the pig nose stone. After checking in, continue walking along the mountain path and enter a small jungle. When you look up, you will see a large rock slope, which is the size of a small golf course. The slope is about 40 degrees. The surface is smooth, but it is not easy to bare your feet. It is called a stone slope.  Walking to the mountainside of Hok Tsui Mountain, you can overlook the entire Shek O Beach. There are two small islands next to it, named Wu Fen Chau and Tai Tau Chau, with beautiful scenery.  Continue walking along the trail and you will see a warning sign with a red skull as a mark. After passing through the jungle, you will reach the top of Hok Tsui Mountain. Walk to the upper column and look down from the column to see a large group of rocks. In the distance, you will see two giant satellite antennas.  Going down the mountain along the trail, you will return to the concrete road. You can go down the concrete road directly to the coastal reserve. Visitors can also choose to go down the mountain from the trail next to the launch station, but the slope is very high and the road is relatively rugged.  Continue to check GPS, and you will easily find the Hok Tsui Mountain Lighthouse. The all-white building is a statutory historical monument with a very beautiful appearance. You can walk to another old building next to the lighthouse. The lighthouse is even more beautiful when viewed from here. It is also a holy place for photography enthusiasts to take pictures of the sunset. After checking in, continue to descend along the mountain trail and you will arrive at Leiyin Cave. Before you reach the entrance of the cave, you can hear a rumbling sound in the distance. After walking a section of gravel road, you will find it. Every time a big wave comes, it will make a rumbling sound, which is very shocking.  Go straight along the concrete road and you will find a whale skeleton when you reach the coastal protection area. It is said that a sperm whale was stranded in Victoria Harbor and was made into a specimen and placed here. Going back across a large rocky beach, there is a huge stone cave named Crab Cave, which is another landmark of Hok Tsui Shan.  After a short break, you can return to Tai Fung Au along Hok Tsui Road and take bus No. 9 back to Shau Kei Wan to complete the journey.
Rating: 3 - If you come in from the concrete road, the path is even shorter... the scenery is superb... most importantly, don't lock yourself in!

Rating: 5 - August 22nd. From the hillside ridge of Cape D'Aguilar to Shek O Beach.  The weather was clear that day. We got off the bus on Cape D'Aguilar Road and found the right entrance; it only took about half an hour of hiking to reach the summit. Next to the marker pillar is a satellite communication station. If we had gotten off from the station, we would have quickly reached the coastal protection zone. However, that day we took a different route, crossing the hillside ridge to reach Shek O Beach. The hillside ridge is a discontinuous stone path. We enjoyed the blue sky and sea along the way. In the distance, what looked like two warships in front of Shek O Beach were Tai Tau Chau and Ngau Fen Chau. Finally, we descended along the stream to reach the beach.

Rating: 4 - From Cape D'Aguilar, you can enjoy panoramic views of the Shek O coastline. Climbing to the summit from the beach requires traversing a steep, rocky ridge – a challenging yet fun climb. It takes just over an hour to reach the 325-meter peak. Further along the path is the Cape D'Aguilar Satellite Communications Station, and descending further leads to the Cape D'Aguilar Marine Reserve.

Rating: 5 - Man Mo Temple is a truly beautiful and serene place tucked away in the heart of Hong Kong. From the moment you step inside, you’re greeted with a calm and peaceful atmosphere that feels like a welcome escape from the busy city outside. The temple is very well maintained, clean, and thoughtfully preserved, which makes the entire experience even more pleasant.  The traditional architecture, intricate details, and hanging incense coils create a spiritual and tranquil vibe that allows you to slow down and really take in the surroundings. Despite being a popular spot for visitors, it never felt overcrowded or rushed, and there was a strong sense of respect and quiet throughout the temple.  It’s a wonderful place to pause, reflect, and appreciate Hong Kong’s cultural and spiritual heritage. Whether you’re visiting for prayer, cultural interest, or simply to experience a moment of peace, Man Mo Temple is definitely worth a visit. A calm, grounding, and memorable experience overall.

Rating: 4 - A Spiritual Oasis Right Off the Bus – A Must on the Red Route  ​If you are riding the Hop-on Hop-off bus (specifically the Red Route), the stop at Hollywood Road is arguably the most convenient cultural detour on the entire loop. The Man Mo Temple is located literally steps away from where the bus drops you off, making it the perfect place to "hop off" without worrying about navigating steep hills or getting lost in the winding streets. ​What makes this spot so special is the immediate contrast. One moment you are surrounded by the roar of traffic and towering skyscrapers; the next, you step over the high wooden threshold into a different world. The interior is dark, mystical, and surprisingly quiet. The city noise seems to bounce off the thick walls, replaced by a hushed, reverent silence. ​The atmosphere feels incredibly authentic. The ceiling is dominated by hundreds of large, spiral incense coils that burn for weeks, creating a hazy, cinematic lighting. It is also clearly a living site of worship—you will see many locals praying and making offerings, so it doesn't feel like a staged tourist trap. ​So, why 4 stars instead of 5? The temple is quite intimate and small. You can essentially see the entire complex in about 15 to 20 minutes, so it is a brief stop rather than a long excursion. Also, the incense smoke can be quite intense; if you have sensitive eyes or asthma, you might find the air a bit heavy after a few minutes inside. ​Verdict: A beautiful, soulful pause in a busy day. It is the ideal spot to catch your breath and soak in some culture before hopping back on the bus to rejoin the chaos of Central.
