reviews: Rating: 5 - This hotel is a calm and comfortable stay option in Hong Kong, especially for travellers planning a visit to Disneyland immediatly after landing at airport. The rooms are spacious with a pleasant sea-facing atmosphere, and the hotel offers a convenient shuttle service to Disneyland starting around 10 AM, which makes commuting easy if booked in advance. The dining experience is also enjoyable, with a good variety of menu options and excellent Hong Kong–style tea. Overall, it is a peaceful location away from the city rush, making it ideal for families and leisure travellers.

Rating: 5 - Auberge Hotel is one of my favorite hotels in Hong Kong. It’s located away from the bustling city. A great getaway place if you want to reset and relax. Location is far from everything else, so only go if you’re looking for an escape and a retreat. There are convenient stores and restaurants close to the hotel, where you can buy whatever you need and plenty restaurants to choose from.  My room is the ocean view, with a large sofa lounge area which is super spacious, a huge bathtub with waterfall shower head and a king bed. It’s definitely worth every penny. I’m definitely going back!

Rating: 5 - My husband and I had a wonderful stay at Auberge Discovery Bay. The staff were professional, friendly, and very accommodating. They were easy to talk to and always ready to help. The café at the lobby served refreshing and delicious dishes, which we really enjoyed.  We loved the free shuttle service to Disneyland, which made our trip extra convenient. The hotel is just a few meters away from Discovery Bay North Plaza, where you can explore more restaurants and the marketplace.If you want to relax, visit D’Deck.  I fell in love with this place! It is perfect for chilling out, enjoying the sea breeze, and taking in the beautiful view.

Rating: 3 - I stayed at Discovery Bay for almost three months. Overall, my stay was very enjoyable, although there were a few drawbacks which I will mention at the end of this review.  Pros: The hotel is very clean and well-designed: you can tell there is an effort to make it feel like a brand. Its location in Discovery Bay by the sea is truly extraordinary: it’s also very close to Disneyland. The northern part of Discovery Bay is very beautiful, recently built, and well-planned: it’s aesthetically pleasing, very safe, and has everything you need nearby, from grocery stores to restaurants. It’s also conveniently close to the airport.  The breakfast team was excellent: the selection was very comprehensive. The housekeeping staff was great as well: even when I left my room after 3 PM, they still cleaned it, which was very appreciated (although there was often an unpleasant smell from the toilet after housekeeping cleaned the room, possibly due to the use of the same cleaning cloth on the floor). For long stays, the hotel also offers a free laundry service: it was very convenient and of high quality.  The hotel really has an island and resort vibe: it gives a genuine holiday feeling. The shuttle services were very convenient: they allow easy access to Hong Kong, Disneyland, and Sunny Bay, which is especially handy for day trips to Disneyland. Among the shuttle staff, the lady and the blond-haired driver were particularly friendly and professional: making a real difference. The rest of the hotel staff was sometimes not pleasant: some staff didn’t smile or even say “Hello” or “Goodbye.”  The rooms are spacious and offer beautiful views. There’s a lovely rooftop pool and a well-equipped gym facing the sea.  Cons: There isn’t a proper beach next to the hotel: there is a small one, but it’s quite damaged and littered. While Disneyland is nearby, it’s not within walking distance: this is a shame and could easily be improved. The shuttle schedules to and from Disneyland are not very convenient: there are only morning departures, and the return shuttle in the evening often comes before the show ends.  A major issue I experienced was cigarette smoke: every morning around 7 AM, my room was filled with cigarette smell, clearly coming from the air conditioning. Since there are no windows, it was impossible to ventilate. I reported this multiple times, but nothing was done. I was offered a room change, but the other floors smelled even worse. The smoke seems to come from both hotel guests and staff: I personally saw some employees smoking on the second floor. For a family hotel with children, this is a significant problem.  The smell of cigarette smoke affected my sleep: I would wake up multiple times during the night, sometimes as early as 5 AM. The odor was so strong that it caused nightmares. Even on floors where there was no smoke, it occasionally came through the air conditioning. This issue greatly affected my stay and was the main negative aspect.

Rating: 2 - The Mountain View room is ok, but with some issues. 1. The bathroom has a glass window to the bedroom, and the privacy blind was totally covered in black mould. 2. The bed was not level, and had a significant angle toward one side. The pillows were cheap quality and not comfortable or supportive. 3. Check in was very smooth and the staff member was very polite. However, check out was not the same, and the staff named Leo was quite unfriendly and impolite. He did not return my greeting, and after checking our room details simply said “ok”. Not another word spoken.  Overall, if these issues were sorted the hotel would be comfortable and quiet, and suitable for short stays.  Definitely not a 5 star hotel. 3 at best.

reviews: Rating: 5 - I happened to unintentionally walk to seafood street on my way to somewhere else. I count myself lucky that I got the chance to see it! The street isn't overly long but has a lot of shops selling dried seafood, dried meat and some Chinese medicines and tonics. I was fascinated by all the displays, products sold and what they are used for. I ended up spending a fair bit of time wondering through and exploring.

Rating: 5 - If you happen to be in hk , go here for an authentic local experience. Yes, set yourself apart from the crowd and come to browse through the thousands of articles for sale . Impossible to find what you are looking for but fun to attempt 😉

Rating: 4 - A fun place to visit for those who enjoy markets is the stretch of Des Voeux Road West found in Sheung Wan/Western District that is known as the Dried Seafood Street.  Here you can find a cluster of shops dealing in various dried seafood and other exotic items that are commonly used as ingredients for traditional Chinese tonics as well as for cooking.  A stroll down Dried Seafood Street can be a real eye-opening experience for those who have not seen many traditional Chinese seafood shops before. Here these shops line up one after another, making for a very interesting street market environment and experience for visitors.  In addition to visiting the Dried Seafood Street, you are very near to Ko Shing (Medicinal Street) where shops have even more exotic items commonly found in Chinese herbal and traditional medicines. This is another neat place to poke around and see in this area of Hong Kong Island.  Overall, we find the market scene in Sheung Wan/Western districts to be interesting to visit. They offer a look into Hong Kong's past that has managed to live on while being engulfed by the modern world of vast skyscrapers, fast transportation, technology and the ultra fast pace of life in Hong Kong.  Note: While some shopkeepers are happy to let you take a photo or two, others are not so keen on you to photograph them or their shops. Best to just show that you have a camera and point to it if you want to take a picture. They will nod either way if its ok or not. Of course they are happy for you to look at and investigate the interesting items they have in store.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Built between 1875 and 1889 , In the earliest days of the colony, street lighting came in the form of oil lamps hanging in the doorways of houses. Convenient for homeowners and cheap for the government, but not great for nocturnal navigation. So in the 1850s the government erected public oil lamps between Central and Wan Chai, and in 1864 the Hong Kong and China Gas Company—better known as Towngas—introduced gas lighting to the territory. The gasworks on Whitty Street in Shek Tong Tsui was the first of its kind in Asia, making the city also the first in Asia to be lit by gas. Kowloon, naturally, had to wait another 28 years. When first introduced, the lamps had to be manually lit and extinguished every day. These days the process is automatic, and the Duddell Street lamps (still served by Towngas) flick on and off automatically at 6pm and 6am, respectively.

Rating: 5 - These granite steps and last four remaining gas powered street lamps represent rare historic gem, serving as a reminder of Bygone era and first lamps in East Asia and keeping the old-school Hong Kong charm. Named after George Duddel, declared as a monument since 1979.

Rating: 5 - These gas-lit lamps are a heritage-listed 'Declared Monument'.  Happy to announce that the lamps have been fully restored to working order as of 27 December 2019. I managed to catch the gas company fixing the lamps during the day, so I returned at night to see the full effect of the beautiful radiant lamps.  For those who complained that they are just lamps - you knew before you visited that they were lamps, so what the f*** did you expect? Maybe you need to get off your mobile phone and learn to appreciate and respect art, cultural heritage, and the historical value of such things.

reviews: Rating: 4 - Our experience with the Dukling Antique Boat Tour was very positive overall. We arrived late for our original departure, and the customer service team handled the situation exceptionally well. They kindly rebooked us on the next available tour, charging only the price difference, which we truly appreciated.  The treatment onboard was excellent. The crew was friendly, attentive, and professional throughout the journey. The tour itself was enjoyable and well organized, and we were even offered complimentary beers, which was a nice and unexpected touch.  The only area I would suggest improving is the sound system. The explanations were difficult to hear, especially during the tour. I would recommend considering a system similar to those used in silent discos, allowing guests to listen through headphones. This could also help synchronize the commentary and music with A Symphony of Lights, enhancing the overall experience.  Despite this minor point, it was a very pleasant tour, and I would gladly recommend it to visitors looking for a unique perspective of Victoria Harbour.

Rating: 4 - Do you have to go on a boat tour to get harbour views in Hong Kong? Not really, as you can see the skyline just fine from either shore. Does it provide a different perspective and experience away from the crowds? Yes, it sure does.  The Dukling is a unique ship that has been rescued, renovated and repurposed across decades. They do not overcrowd the ship, and the ticket came with a free drink. Definitely a fun 45 minutes spent bobbing around the harbor. You get a little history lesson about the boat and then it's just free time to enjoy the ride. They basically just make a little circle and drop you back off where you started. Fun little activity to burn some time.

Rating: 5 - The Dukling Tour in the evening was a truly impressive experience. The traditional boat combined with the sparkling skyline creates a unique atmosphere that stays with you. The ride was smooth and enjoyable, and the crew on board was very friendly and shared interesting insights.  A wonderful way to experience Hong Kong at its most beautiful.

Rating: 5 - Taking a sunset harbor tour on the Dukling, Hong Kong’s oldest Chinese junk boat, is a truly memorable experience. As the boat sails slowly around Victoria Harbour, you can admire breathtaking panoramic views of Hong Kong’s skyline bathed in the warm hues of sunset. The changing colors reflecting on the water and the city’s iconic skyscrapers create a magical and serene setting that is perfect for photography. Onboard, you are welcomed with a complimentary drink. What makes the Dukling tour special is the rich historical commentary provided during the cruise. You learn about Hong Kong’s maritime heritage and the traditional fishermen culture that shaped the city’s past. It’s highly recommended for visitors seeking an authentic and peaceful harbor experience during the golden hour.

Rating: 5 - We booked tickets with GetYourGuide app and it was nice and smooth. The journey was lovely and included a beer for each of us. Really loved the antique boat and seating at the back to appreciate the sails and all the city skyline. Such a lovely experience for our first day in Hong Kong!

reviews: Rating: 4 - Interesting background info on former mine near Ma On Shan situated in the former Lutheran church in the village. The staff are friendly and willing to answer questions. Entrance is free open Fridays, Saturday and Sunday only. There is a small cafe next door serving drinks and snacks.

Rating: 4 - Discovered this place during hiking. Nice place to visit to understand more about HK History. Friendly curator introduced us the history of the mining industry and also shown us the camping site and hostel. Eco tour can also be orgsnized upon request. A very good attempt to revitalize historical place.  The cafe here offers refreshments. The coffee and cookies we ordered are both very nice!  tips : worth visit the real entrance of mine 240M.L. which is located near to the center. Walk down to the parking lot, turn right on the road after the lot. Not much distance up the road, on the left hand side, there is a trail blocked by a concrete bar on the ground. The entrance is about two hundred meter inside.

Rating: 5 - A renovated school and church converted into education centre and local cafe.  The education centre briefs the visitors with the mining history of Ma On Shan Area and the livings of the miners. It also provides geotechnic information on Ma On Shan rocks and offers samples of rock collected in the area. Visitors can learn how to distinguish iron ores in the exhibition. Air conditioning is provided in the exhibition hall, making it an excellent place for resting.  The cafe offers local herbal drinks, freshly brewed coffee and local food like tofu puddings. A great place to talk with the locals and rest after hiking.

Rating: 4 - After a short hike from the Ma An Shan BBQ site, you will reach Grace Youth Camp. This place used to be a church and school for the village of the mine, and it's a great place to visit and have a cup of coffee before continuing the hike.  The Mining Cafe looks like a cabin in the ski resort, and the coffee and snacks are great!

Rating: 4 - The Grace Youth Camp (Mining Heritage Centre) is located within the Ma On Shan Country Park at the far end of the Ma On Shan Country Trail road. It is located within the small village up a few flights of stairs. The Centre is open on weekends and public holidays from 10am to 5pm.  Essentially what you find here is a collection of historic buildings and an informal museum (free entry) which aims to preserve the mining history of the Ma On Shan mountain range. The Ma On Shan iron mines started around 1906. During the heyday of the 1950's and 1960's, there were 2-3K miners working the mines and an estimated community of around 10K residents living in the area. The mines closed in 1976 which saw the miners and residents move out to find livelihoods elsewhere.  While the mining days are long past, some community preservation efforts have persisted over the decades resulted in this Grace Youth Camp initiative. Within the camp grounds, you will find the old Lutheran Yan Kwong Church building which is now repurposed and used as the Mining Heritage Centre exhibition hall. Inside what was once the main hall of the church, you will find two walls with information (Cantonese & English) displays regarding the old mines as well as the people that lived and worked here during those days. There are some exhibition items that complement the information displays and a video program being played (Cantonese language only). A few panels are also setup to provide historic account of the church and mission efforts which served the religious needs of the people and village in the past.  Within the camp grounds there is an old Kindergarten, Primary School, Teacher dormitory and article storage building which collectively has Grade III historical building classification in Hong Kong. Next to the church is a small eatery called I cafe. This is a neat little place and good stop for a quick drink or snack before/after your hike through the Country Park.  Note: To find the Grace Youth Camp Mining Heritage Centre and I Cafe, just make your way through the small village in direction of the church you will see from the end of the street, car park and mini-bus NR84 drop off & pick up point. There are a few signs pointing the way from within the village, which is really small so you can't miss it unless it is closed.  In the end, this is a genuinely good endeavour to preserve local history and well worth the 20-30 minutes of your time to visit the Heritage Centre and have a coffee and snack at the I cafe if you are visiting the Ma On Shan Country Park on weekends and public holidays when they are open.

The well-maintained greenery, sandy beaches, and the gentle sound of waves create a tranquil environment that allows visitors to unwind. Skating, rollerblading, and scootering are also popular activities along the smooth, well-paved paths.  Water sports enthusiasts can try activities such as kayaking, windsurfing, and stand-up paddleboarding, taking full advantage of the beautiful coastline. Fishing is another relaxing pastime enjoyed by visitors, with designated fishing zones available. The variety of activities ensures that people of all ages can find something they love to do.  East Coast Park is a fantastic spot for families with children. The Marine Cove playground is a highlight, featuring interactive play structures suitable for kids of different age groups. Parents can relax while their children enjoy the safe and engaging play areas. Additionally, there are open spaces for kite flying, picnicking, or even playing frisbee.  The BBQ pits and picnic areas make it easy for families and friends to gather for outdoor meals. Many visitors bring their own food, but there are also food outlets and vending machines around the park for added convenience. The entire precinct is designed with accessibility in mind, ensuring that everyone, including those with mobility challenges, can enjoy the space comfortably.  Food lovers will appreciate the variety of dining options available within the precinct. From casual beachside cafes to famous seafood restaurants like East Coast Lagoon Food Village, the park offers something to satisfy every palate. Indulging in Singapore’s famous chili crab, satay, and grilled seafood while enjoying the sea breeze is a memorable experience that shouldn’t be missed.  East Coast Park Precinct is a gem in Singapore, offering a perfect mix of relaxation, adventure, and social activities. Whether you're a solo traveler, a fitness enthusiast, a nature lover, or a family looking for a fun day out, this park caters to all. With its well-maintained facilities, beautiful coastal scenery, and endless recreational options, East Coast Park is undoubtedly a must-visit destination.

reviews: Rating: 3 - The F11 Foto Museum is a specialist attraction, making use of a Grade 3 historical building from the 1930s. The property is of subtle Art Deco architecture and a nice venue for rare photography exhibitions which are held here throughout the year.  Within the museum, you will see rare cameras, phones, books and Art Deco furniture. At present, there is an exhibition of photos of Hong Kong in 1959-60 by influential Dutch photographer, Ed van der Elsken (1925-90). The exhibition includes around 150 images and an entry of HK$100 per person. The exhibition is curated well and offers a wonderful opportunity to view life on the streets of Hong Kong during a time long past and much different to what you see in the modern era.  The information brochure provided with your ticket is generic information about the exhibition only. If you have a mobile with data plan you can scan a barcode in the museum. This gives you access to an online guide with information about the various photographs. Unfortunately, information is mostly in Chinese with limited English text. There are a few audio stops in English describing a handful of the images. These were nice to listen to.  Overall, the exhibition is visually rewarding and we were glad to have attended. At the high price of HK$100, a better job was expected for providing English language details for the pieces on display. This is something for them to think about for future exhibitions.

Rating: 5 - The Hong Kong Golf Club is a private golf club. It is home to the Hong Kong Open, a tournament co-sanctioned by the European and Asian Tours.  Then, the "Royal Hong Kong Golf Club" was started in 1889 by "thirteen golfing enthusiasts" in a shared location in Happy Valley. According to "History of the Royal Hongkong Golf Club", which was written by T.F.R. Waters, of these thirteen, with the exception of Robert Murray Rumsey R.N. (then Hong Kong Harbour Master and the Rumsey Street was named after his name.) and Gershom Stewart (afterwards Knighted and a member of parliament for Hoylake) very few had much notion of the game but readily agreed to do what they could to established a foothold for it in the Colony. Although Captain Rumsey and Stewart had clubs and balls and had in fact been driving these balls within the race track at Happy Valley before 1889, the opinion of the Meeting was that attempts should be made to acquire land then in possession of the military in Kowloon. Rumsey had been elected captain of the new club and had secured the consent of the Governor – Sir William Des Voeux – to accept the presidency. Despite this influence at Court the military authorities could not be persuaded to become cooperative, and after some months the proposition had to be dropped. However, on 30 September 1889 permission was eventually obtained from Hong Kong Government to use ground at Happy Valley. Money was raised and work was started making the greens and tees. The architect of the course at Happy Valley was Captain (afterwards Colonel) H. N. Dumbleton R.E. The work progressed rapidly, and it is recorded that in May 1890 a match of six a side was played between the club and the 91st Regiment of the Argyle and Sutherland Highlanders, which the Club won easily.

Rating: 1 - The Fanling Magistrates' Courts Building is a magistrates' court located at 1 Pik Fung Road, Fanling, New Territories, Hong Kong. The 11-story building has a floor area of ​​18,720 square meters and is the most advanced criminal court in the Tai Po District, Northeast New Territories, and Border District. It opened on July 2, 2002, replacing the inadequate Fanling Magistrates' Courts building. It was another modern court building constructed by the judiciary after the Kowloon City Magistrates' Courts and is also the second court building in the New Territories East. The court has nine courtrooms, including an adult court, a juvenile court, and a court specifically for handling protection orders. Ancillary facilities include eight related magistrates' chambers, eight public consultation rooms, 16 witness waiting rooms, one protected witness room, detention rooms, and two waiting rooms in the juvenile court. There are also meeting rooms, a library, a general affairs office, a records storage room, and other ancillary facilities. The construction cost was approximately HK$491.6 million.

Rating: 3 - Finger Hill is the highest peak on Peng Chau Island at 95 metres. You reach it as part of the Peng Chau Family Walk in the southern section of the island. Just follow the signs. It is no more than 5 minutes from the main village. Do expect a steady and steep climb up a long set of paved steps before reaching the peak.  At the Finger Hill peak you will find a pavilion with shaded seating where you can have a rest. Unfortunately the vegetation is thick and tall obscuring views pretty much in all directions from Finger Hill. If you stand on top of the concrete block at the peak you can see some very nice views of the village and as far as Lantau Island to the north as well as the open sea to the south.  In the end, you'll enjoy better views on the trail up to Finger Hill and from various lookout points throughout the Family Walk Trail than you will from the peak itself. If you want the exercise and don't mind the climb, its fine to include the walk up to Finger Hill. However, if it is really hot outside and you are feeling tired at this stage of your hike around Peng Chau, this is something you may want to skip.

Rating: 3 - This is a recreational area located on three sides of Central Plaza, along Fleming Road and Gloucester Road. This garden provides a resting area for foreign domestic workers on weekdays and weekends, and complements the covered area of ​​Central Plaza, creating a popular recreational spot. Besides weekends, it also provides space for residents interested in exercise and fitness, as well as private exercise classes. Facing Fleming Road, the garden features a large three-tiered pond surrounded by a vibrant triangular flowerbed. On the other side, facing Gloucester Road, there's another large triangular flowerbed. The garden offers seating and restrooms, with tall trees planted between the seats, providing shade during the morning sun. One thing worth mentioning is the restroom. Due to the pandemic, only one stall in the women's restroom is open. The floor is constantly wet, the flush tank fills slowly, preventing continuous flushing, and the soap dispenser is often insufficient. Upon inspection, it was discovered that the restroom has been handed over to Central Plaza by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department for management. To comply with the government's clean restroom policy, it seems the Central Plaza Management Office needs to take action. The public restroom, which received poor reviews, was closed for renovations in March of this year and reopened on July 1st. The renovations truly lived up to expectations. The women's restroom, originally a single stall, was expanded to three, one of which features a baby seat built into the wall for caregivers' convenience. The restroom is bright and fresh. Perhaps due to the good ventilation or the frequent cleaning, I haven't noticed any odors since its reopening. Toilet paper and soap are also plentiful. After the renovations, the management of this restroom, previously managed by Central Plaza, was transferred back to the Leisure and Cultural Services Department, and the results are truly remarkable.

Rating: 5 - The former Central Magistracy is located at 1, Arbuthnot Road, Central, Victoria, Hong Kong. It was constructed from 1913 to 1914.  The site where the building is standing was originally occupied by the first Hong Kong Magistracy. The former building was probably erected in 1847 but was later demolished to make way for the present building. Difficulty and delay in the construction work was caused because of the provision of an extensive basement in the new magistracy. The building's majestic appearance, with the imposing pillars of the façade and other features in the Greek-revival style, are lost to its poor exposure fronting onto a steep, narrow road. The massive retaining walls were constructed with granite blocks. The Central Magistracy was closed in 1979 and had been used by different associations affiliated to the Hong Kong Police Force.  The buildings of the Former Central Magistracy, together with the adjacent Central Police Station and the Victoria Prison are declared monuments of Hong Kong. These buildings are collectively known as the Central Police Station Compound.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Tai Kwun, officially known as Tai Kwun – Centre for Heritage and Arts, is one of Hong Kong’s most impressive cultural spaces, where history meets contemporary creativity. Located in Central, this revitalized complex was once the Central Police Station, Magistracy, and Victoria Prison. Today, it has been transformed into a vibrant hub for art, culture, dining, and community life—without losing its historical soul.  The architecture is the highlight. Restored colonial-era buildings stand alongside modern structures designed by Herzog & de Meuron, creating a striking balance between old and new. Walking through the open courtyards and stone corridors, you can still feel the weight of history, while modern art installations and exhibitions bring fresh energy into the space.  Tai Kwun hosts rotating contemporary art exhibitions, cultural events, and performances, making every visit slightly different. Even if you’re not entering a gallery, the atmosphere alone is worth it. The space feels calm, thoughtful, and surprisingly open, especially compared to the surrounding skyscrapers of Central.  There are also stylish cafés, bars, and restaurants tucked into the complex—perfect for taking a break or enjoying the view as the sun sets. At night, the lighting adds a dramatic, cinematic mood.  Tai Kwun is not just a place to visit; it’s a place to experience Hong Kong’s past, present, and creative future all in one walk.

The government decided to build the first New Territories Magistracy and it opened in 1861. As time progressed, more of other magistracies were established in the New Territories.  This first one then became the Fanling Magistracy.  As a heritage site, the Former Fanling Magistracy now hosts a small exhibition on its own history. It is also home for the Hong Kong Federation Youth Groups Leadership Institute.  The Fanling Magistracy has retained its classic appearance even after it no longer served its judiciary purpose. During the time that it was closed between 2003-2010, it became the setting for a number of movies and TV dramas. The most well-known one is Internal Affairs II.

While not a conventional tourist attraction, it does remain an interesting and attractive building to see and is a constant reminder of Hong Kong's early 20th century past.  It is interesting to imagine this building at this elevated position, overlooking the Central district below all the way to Victoria Harbour - views that would have existed during the first half of the 20th century. Those days are long gone and those views long since blocked by the skyscrapers which dominate the Hong Kong Skyline today.  If you stop by The Former French Mission Building in the Central District for a look around, it is also worth making way to St. John's Cathedral just a minute or two away. This is another declared monument worth seeing if you enjoy architecture and seeing historic buildings.

Built in 1915, this red-brick clock tower is all that remains of the original Kowloon-Canton Railway terminus and serves as a quiet reminder of Hong Kong’s colonial and transportation history. It’s not a place that takes long to visit, but it adds depth and historical context to the area. Overall, it’s a meaningful stop for those interested in Hong Kong’s past, photography lovers, or anyone looking to slow down and appreciate a quieter side of the city amid the busy surroundings.

Rating: 5 - The Old Stanley Police Station (Chinese: 舊赤柱警署) was a police station constructed in 1859 in Stanley, Hong Kong Island. It is now the oldest remaining police station building in Hong Kong, and was declared a monument on 15 January 1984.  The British Army, during the early years of the colonial era, used the station from time to time in conjunction with the police because of its strategic position as the most southerly outpost on Hong Kong Island. During the Japanese Occupation, the Japanese Gendarmerie used the police station as a local headquarters and a mortuary was built onto the building. After the war, the building reverted to its original use and served as a police station until 1974. Since then, it has had a number of unrelated uses including a sub-office of the Southern District Office, a restaurant, and currently it is used as a Wellcome supermarket  There have been various attempts to have the government discontinue its commercial use, and to use it for some official function. One recent suggestion was to use it as a branch of the Hong Kong Police Museum.

Nestled inside the serene Kowloon Walled City Park, the Yamen is the only remaining original structure from the old Walled City, and stepping inside feels like entering a different era.  The building itself is elegant and understated, with traditional Qing-style architecture, timber beams, courtyards, and stone details that reflect its past roles as an administrative office, magistrate’s court, and later as a police station. The restoration work is excellent, keeping the original character while making the site easy to explore.  Inside you’ll find well-curated exhibits showcasing the Walled City’s complex history — from its early days as a Qing military outpost to its transformation into a legendary labyrinth of life, shops, and homes. The displays include maps, old photos, artifacts, and stories from former residents, giving a vivid picture of how vibrant and chaotic the Walled City once was.  What makes the visit especially memorable is the contrast: the peaceful garden surrounding the Yamen and the knowledge that this tranquil space once bordered one of the most crowded places on earth. It’s a perfect blend of history, culture, and reflection.

Rating: 5 - Kowloon Walled City: 📽️A Cinematic Journey – A Must for History Buffs & Curious Minds!  My husband and I have long been fascinated by the history of the Kowloon Walled City—what was once a densely packed, lawless urban enclave right in the heart of Hong Kong. Despite the heat and humidity on the day 🥵we visited, the whole experience was smooth and well-organized.  As this is a relatively new exhibition, there were a few ‘group tours’ the day we visited. Whether it was at the ticket counter or inside the exhibition itself, they were kind and welcoming throughout.  This temporary exhibition will be up for the next three years, so whether you're a tourist, a history lover, or just curious about one of Hong Kong’s most mysterious and misunderstood neighborhoods, I highly recommend checking it out.  The Kowloon Walled City was once dubbed the “Forbidden City” of Hong Kong—a chaotic maze of gangs, drugs, illegal dentistry, prostitution, and unspeakable crimes… and somehow, that’s exactly what makes it so fascinating. 😅  🗺️ Discover it while you can!

Rating: 5 - Fuk Tak Temple, commonly known as the Land God Temple, is located in Ngau Tau Kok. It was built by Teochew people who moved to Ngau Tau Kok Lower Estate in 1967. Since the establishment of the Ngau Tau Kok District Teochew Association, five different ceremonies have been held annually at the temple to thank the gods. The Jade Emperor's Birthday (also known as the Birthday of Heaven and Earth Parents by Teochew people) on the ninth day of the first lunar month is particularly lively due to its timing during the Lunar New Year. The small temple is packed with worshippers offering incense, and the inside and outside are filled with offerings commonly used by Teochew people. A plaque and flags adorn the top of the temple.   According to District Council documents, Fuk Tak Temple is an illegal and provisionally permitted building. Under current land policy, the temple and its ancestral tablets have no right to be relocated and must be demolished to make way for the redevelopment of Ngau Tau Kok Lower Estate. Although the relevant departments had explored the feasibility of preserving Fuk Tak Temple on its original site, it could not be preserved on its original site because the temple is located directly above the Drainage Services Reserve. Therefore, the temple's manager repeatedly requested that it be preserved on its original site, but these requests were not approved. However, the government has reserved a plot of land at the southern end of Ngau Tau Kok Lower Estate for the Fire Services Department to redevelop the temple.

Rating: 5 - The Government House in Hong Kong is the official residence of the Chief Executive of Hong Kong. The history of the building dates back to 1851 when it was originally built as a mansion for the first Governor of Hong Kong, Sir John Bowring. It was designed in the neoclassical style by Charles St. George Cleverly, an English architect.  The building was subsequently renovated and expanded over the years, with the addition of a ballroom and a banquet hall in the early 20th century. During the Japanese occupation of Hong Kong in World War II, the Government House was used as the residence of the Japanese Governor.  After the war, the building was returned to the British colonial government and was used as the residence of the Governor of Hong Kong until the handover of Hong Kong to China in 1997. Since then, it has been the official residence of the Chief Executive of Hong Kong.  The Government House is located on a hill in the Central district of Hong Kong Island and is surrounded by a beautiful garden. The building is now a declared monument and is open to the public for guided tours on designated days. It remains a symbol of Hong Kong's colonial past and its evolution into a modern metropolis.

Rating: 4 - Tap Mun (Grass Island) is an island located just north of the Sai Kung West Country Park that makes for a popular day trip and overnight wild camping location for Hongkongers. It is relatively small at 1.7 square kilometres and is known for its grassy hilltop (hence the name) and numerous ferrel cows that share the island with visitors and those who reside here.  Historically, the island has been habited since at least the mid 16th century. At its height there were likely 2000 residents, mostly tanka fisherfolks. Like most remote villages on the outlying islands of Hong Kong, those numbers dwindled to a spartan few towards the end of the 20th century, as youth opted to move to the city or abroad in search of better living conditions. Today it is estimated that around 100 people continue to reside here at Tap Mun.  To visit Tap Mun, most take daily ferries from the Ma Liu Shui ferry terminus at Science Park (1.5 hour one way) or the nearby Wong Shek Pier (15 minutes one way). Check the schedule online for exact sailing times before setting off to visit Tap Mun.  Upon arrival at the main ferry pier at Tap Mun, visitors will find public toilets and a few casual eateries and restaurants at the Old Fisherman's Village. Just to the south is a New Fisherman's Village where there are a few more places to eat. Otherwise, few options for food and drink provisions on Tap Mun so best to pack what you need prior to making your trip to the island.  Sightseeing around Tap Mun includes a roughly 1 hour long loop trail which circles the southern tip of the island. It passes by the 400 year old Tin Hau Temple at the Old Fisherman's Village, the grassy hilltops and gentle sloops that overlook the the western and southern coast. This is a very popular area for wild camping, particularly on weekends and public holidays.  There are a few pavilion rest stops along or near the main trail as well as a few interesting geological features for visitors to enjoy. These include the Balanced Rock and the Tap Mun Cave both accessible along the boulder and pebble beach just below the main trail.  Another popular geological land formation to find is Long Keng Kan (Neck of the Dragon) found at the end of the informal trail north of the Hilltop Pavilion. This beautiful natural landmark is accessible by way of rope repelling down the step wooded hillside. There are rewarding views of the sea and other outlying islands to the north and east from this location and along the trail. They rival the very good views found along the main loop trail to the south.  Overall, Tap Mun is a neat place to visit if you've done the rounds of island trips around Hong Kong and are looking for somewhere different to spend half a day. There is a nice mix of heritage, history, geology and natural beauty to enjoy and while time consuming to visit from the city, everything is pretty straightforward and easy to experience once you are there.

reviews: Rating: 3 - One of the interesting things to see at the Hong Kong Zoological and Botanical Garden is the bronze statue of King George (George VI) which is found just southwest of the Fountain Terrace Garden and large water fountain.  This is a nearly two metre tall bronze of King George that was created by British sculptor Gilbert Ledward and erected at this location in 1958 as a late commemoration of Hong Kong's 100th anniversary (1941). What you see is a middle-aged George IV, standing in regal attire and crowned. His left hand grips a sword in scabbard. The statue stands upon a simple pedestal. There is a small information panel near the monument.  Interestingly, this monument is placed upon the location of an earlier statue of Sir Arthur Kennedy who served at Hong Kong's seventh governor (1872-1877). This monument was confiscated, sent to Japan and melted down during the Japanese occupation.  You can convenient view the King George statue in between viewing birdlife enclosures at the Zoological Garden. Its worth a few minutes to see if you enjoy statue and monument viewing during your travels.

reviews: Rating: 4 - A highly convenient method to access Hong Kong International Airport (HKIA) from Macau is by utilizing the hotel shuttle bus service. The shuttle departs from the hotel in Macau and proceeds to the HZMB port (bridge). Upon arrival at the port, passengers should proceed to the upper floor towards the Departure hall, as the hotel shuttle stops at the Arrival hall.  At the Departure hall, there are two bus counters. The regular bus requires passengers to carry their luggage, while the HKIA bus offers more privileges to those flying with specific airlines, including Cathay Pacific, JAL, HK Express, China Airlines, and others. Please note that this information may be subject to change over time, so it is advisable to recheck before traveling.  As I was flying with Cathay Pacific, I opted for the HKIA bus. The fare was 280 MOP or HKD (please note that HKD coins are not accepted, only notes). After purchasing the ticket, I was able to load my luggage and receive a boarding pass, similar to the process at an airport.  Following this, I proceeded downstairs and followed the green line marked "To Hong Kong." This led me to the immigration area, where there was a waiting area (without food and beverage options) for passengers to gather before boarding time.  The bus journey from the port to HKIA, SkyPier, takes approximately 40-45 minutes. Upon arrival at SkyPier, passengers are required to present their passport and boarding pass for immigration clearance once again. It is important to note that any bottled water in possession must be consumed or discarded before proceeding, as it is not permitted through security.  Finally, a shuttle train is available to transport passengers to all gates within the airport. This makes the overall travel experience from Macau to HKIA very convenient and straightforward.  Nevertheless, it would have been more helpful if they had provided clearer and more detailed information about this on the website. Although I visited the website multiple times, I only learned about it when I inquired at the counter at the HZMB port.

Rating: 5 - Very seamless way to travel from Shenzhen Shekou to HongKong airport in 30 mins . Appreciate the convenient and stress free way of crossing between the 2 countries. Luggages can be checked in at Shenzhen Shekou Pier. Pls checked ur airlines to determine if they offer such services. After alighting the ferry , walked up to the departure hall and clear custom into HKG airport. Remember to claim back the $120HKG airport tax with the paper receipt. Still can’t believe how easy it is to get fm Shenzhen to HKG airport transit area under 1 hour. Remember to check in ur luggage at least 3.5 hours before your Flight at Shenzhen Shekou Pier to avoid any possible problems.

Rating: 4 - SkyPier at Hong Kong International Airport (HKIA).  The SkyPier is a unique and convenient ferry terminal located airside (within the restricted area) of HKIA. It allows transit passengers to transfer directly to and from destinations in the Pearl River Delta and Macau without passing through Hong Kong immigration or collecting their luggage. Who Can Use the SkyPier?  · Arriving Passengers: You must have a through ticket (air and ferry) issued by your airline or a confirmed ferry ticket, and you must be heading directly to a ferry destination. · Departing Passengers: You are coming from a ferry and connecting to a flight at HKIA.  You CANNOT use the SkyPier if:  · You have already cleared Hong Kong immigration and collected your baggage. You are a member of the public trying to buy a ferry ticket.  · Location: The SkyPier is at the west end of the HKIA terminal, near the North Satellite Concourse. · Getting There: The only way for eligible passengers to reach it is via the automated people mover (APM) from the main terminal's transfer area.  If You Cannot Use the SkyPier (The Public Option)  If you have already entered Hong Kong (cleared immigration and collected baggage), you need to use the public ferry services.  · SkyPier is for Transfers Only: It's an airside facility for passengers connecting directly between a flight and a ferry. · Luggage is Transferred Automatically: This is the biggest benefit. · Check with Your Airline: Confirm if your airline participates in the through-check-in service for ferries. · Verify Ferry Schedule: Schedules can be reduced, especially outside of peak times. Always confirm before you travel.

There is an improvised trail to the left and going up at this point, it is quite "developed" initially, it leads to some illegal graves. Once you get to them just go up the mountain, there are a loose collection of paths to follow. At the top, one way back is another social trail just north of the flag poles that heads down northeast to intersect with the aforementioned trail blocked by squatters. By going straight at this intersection you will rejoin the road (not shown as connecting on Google Maps, but it does) at a rather large illegal grave collection. This route is "rustic" and not developed for the most part. There probably is an easier way from the Yuen Tsuen Ancient Trail. reviews: Rating: 5 - To our surprise entry for tourists is free, so in we went smiling as tourists usually get ripped off. Although we were there early the razzamatazz of race night was already in full swing, music, bright lights, but no obvious signs of bookies or the tic tac men. We felt our way around and found a very helpful attendant who showed us how to bet using one of the large touch screens, similar to those in McDonald’s. So we were now in our element.  I got Gemini AI to forecast the winners from the programme we got from the self vending machine. With bets placed and a beer in hand we found a couple of seats high up in the terraces with a reasonable view of the finish line. We had an hour to kill before the race but like these things it was interesting just watching the antics of the crowd.  Soon the horses were being paraded up and down and our horse, number four Savvy Twinkle, appeared on the big screen looking rather grand, a winner in the making. Ten minutes later the gates opened and they were off. The race was only over a thousand metres so no sooner had they started than we were on our feet egging Savvy Twinkle on. As the pack surged past us Twinky was ahead by a nostril. My goodness, he was going to win. And yeah, he did. First race and we were already up. Not sure what the odds were I decided to go and collect our winnings. To my surprise I got $480.00 including my $100.00 stake, a profit of £38.00. Well done Gemini AI.  Sad to say that’s where our luck ended as the next five races went without a place. Halfway through we consoled ourselves with another large beer, a huge hotdog and a bucket of fries.  We left two races before the end as they didn’t finish before eleven o’clock and we had a bus and train to catch back home. We actually caught a tram which rattled us to the MTR where we caught the train back. Unfortunately we left the station from the wrong exit and even with the help of Google Maps live, which doesn’t seem to work very well in the dark, we got completely lost. Fortunately this is an extremely safe city and even the dark corners feel safe. By luck we came across a street that Ros recognised so we were back on the straight and narrow back on the route home.

Rating: 5 - I’m a big sports fan but honestly never thought horse racing could be this thrilling and fun. Happy Wednesday at Happy Valley? Live music pumping, Food Street smells amazing, crowd going wild, drinks in hand – it’s an experience. Super cool vibe, super accessible, super addictive. If you’re in HK, don’t sleep on this. Best night out I’ve had here!

Rating: 4 - At Happy Valley Racecourse, the city gathers under floodlights. Opened in 1846, this historic track sits improbably in the middle of Hong Kong Island, ringed by high-rise towers that glow long after sunset. Here, sport, spectacle, and civic life run on the same track. #跑馬地馬場 #HongKong

Rating: 5 - First time at Happy Wednesday and… wow. Everyone told me ‘if you don’t go to the races, you don’t really know Hong Kong’. Now I get it. Horse racing is literally the favourite pastime of Hong Kongers. The energy, the crowd, the whole atmosphere – it’s pure HK. If you skip Happy Valley, you’re missing the soul of the city.

Rating: 5 - Free entry for tourists if we showed our non-HK passports when we went on Wednesday night in February. Fun atmosphere, great way to see HK horse betting culture. Efficient, friendly staff at entry/exit and memorabilia shop.

reviews: Rating: 4 - You'll find one of Hong Kong's oldest temples dedicated to Tin Hau, Goddess of the Sea, at the Tin Hau Temple Plaza on the west side of the Tuen Mun River. This temple is over 600 years old and was originally built by local fisherman at what was the seashore long before reclamations and the building up of Tuen Mun. Today it is situated noticeably inland, along the river and across from Tuen Mun Park.  The temple was greatly restored in 1990 given it the appearance that you see today. The exterior is grey brick but with a yellow creme colour coat of paint. You'll see a decorative facade and entrance and traditional two hall, three bay architectural layout. Within, there are shrines in the back of each of the three bays. The centre shrine is must interesting, holding a statue of the deity, Tin Hau along with other traditional items of worship. Look for the large scale model of a wooden sampan in the left bay and the ancient drum and bell which dates back to 1697 in the right side bay.  Interestingly, the Hau Kok Tin Hau Temple is the site of important Tin Hau Festival Parade and Fa Pau (Floral Shrine) celebrations held in the plaza in front of the temple on the 23rd day of the 3rd month on the Lunar calendar. You can learn much more about this important these festivities and see examples of the floral shrines at the Fa Pau Exhibition Hall located in a separate building next to the Tin Hau Temple. The exhibition hall is open from 10am to 6pm daily (closed on Mondays and during Chinese New Year).

reviews: Rating: 5 - The Hau Mei Fung Ancestral Hall celebrates Hau Mei-fung, who was a student of the Imperial Academy. The Hau Mei Fung Ancestral Hall was built in the late 18th century, in around the late reign of the Yongzheng and early reign of Qianlong emperors of the Qing dynasty. Like so many other ancestral halls in the New Territories villages, the Hau Mei Fung Ancestral Hall served chiefly the purpose of providing a place for family conferences (besides ancestral worship) for the descendants of Hau Mei-fung in the village.  It is said that Sir Robert Hotung had once lived in this ancestral hall. Over its long history, the Hau Mei Fung Ancestral Hall was once a private study, a mill, a candle and rattan workshop. In 2000, its roof collapsed after years of disrepairs, and with money from the Hong Kong Government, the villagers restored the Ancestral Hall to its former glory.  The Hau Mei Fung Ancestral Hall is a Declared Monument since 2019.

Rating: 5 - An old ancestral hall to commemorate Hau Jui-fei who was a student of the Imperial Academy in the Qing Dynasty. It is a typical two-hall-three-bay building with an internal courtyard flanked by two side chambers. It was declared as a monument on 25 October 2019 and it does not have much decoration or display inside.

Rating: 2 - Hau Mei Fung Ancestral Hall in Kam Tsin Tsuen, Sheung Shui, was built by Hau Cheuk-wan (侯倬雲) to commemorate his great grandfather Hau Jui-fei (侯聚裴), alias Hau Mei-fung (侯味峰), who was a student of the Chinese national literature (國學生) in the Qing dynasty.  The ancestral hall was built together with other village houses having the entrances facing east. It is a Qing vernacular building with a two-hall-one-courtyard layout. Structurally the greenbrick walls and the granite columns support the pitched roofs. Two red sandstone columns at the inner part of the entrance are used which symbolize the wealth of the families. At the far end of the main hall is the altar housing the soul tablets of the ancestors.  (AMO)

Rating: 4 - The Wei Fung Hou Ancestral Hall, located in Kam Kam, Sheung Shui, was built around the late 18th century to commemorate Hou Ju Pei (1634-1688), a scholar who was also known as Hou Wei Fung. The hall was constructed by Hou Zhuo Yun, Hou Ju Pei's great-grandson and a successful candidate in the imperial examinations in 1788 (the 53rd year of the Qianlong Emperor's reign). The hall's construction reflects the social and economic status of the Hou family's Wei Fung ancestor at that time. After its completion, the hall served as a family shrine for ancestor worship and a place for handling Wei Fung ancestral affairs.  The hall is a typical Qing Dynasty folk building with two courtyards, three bays, and a central courtyard. Side rooms are built on both sides of the courtyard. A pavilion with a curved roof is built at the front of the rear courtyard, a rare example of traditional Chinese architecture in the area. The stucco decorations on the ridge and walls, as well as the wooden components and ancestral niches decorated with auspicious beasts, flowers, geometric patterns, and Chinese folk tales, are all exquisitely crafted.  The Wei Fung Hou Ancestral Hall was listed as a historical site in 2019.

reviews: Rating: 5 - The High Court of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region is a part of the legal system of Hong Kong. It consists of the Court of Appeal and the Court of First Instance; it deals with criminal and civil cases which have risen beyond the lower courts. It is a superior court of record of unlimited civil and criminal jurisdiction. It was named the Supreme Court before 1997. Though previously named the Supreme Court, this Court has long been the local equivalent to the Senior Courts of England and Wales and has never been vested with the power of final adjudication.  The High Court Building is located at 38 Queensway, Admiralty. The 20-storey building was built in 1985 as the home of the then Supreme Court of Hong Kong, which was renamed in 1997. It was named the Supreme Court Building, and the road leading to its main entrance is still named Supreme Court Road. The High Court Building was designed by architect K. M. Tseng.

reviews: Rating: 5 - High Island Reservoir and the surrounding Sai Kung East Country Park area are absolutely stunning and a must-visit for nature lovers. The reservoir itself is massive and offers breathtaking views of the turquoise water, rugged coastline, and unique hexagonal rock columns formed by ancient volcanic activity. It’s one of those places that makes you forget you’re still in Hong Kong!  The area is great for hiking, with well-maintained trails that take you through lush greenery and along the coastline. One of the best routes is the MacLehose Trail (Stage 1 and 2), which offers scenic viewpoints overlooking the reservoir and the ocean. If you’re into photography, this place is a goldmine, especially during sunrise or sunset.  The best part? It’s peaceful and not as crowded as other popular spots in Hong Kong. Just keep in mind that there aren’t many facilities, so bring enough water and snacks if you plan to spend a few hours exploring. If you’re up for an adventure, you can also visit nearby hidden gems like Long Ke Wan Beach, which is just a short hike away.  Overall, High Island Reservoir and its surroundings are a perfect escape from city life, offering breathtaking scenery, fresh air, and a bit of adventure. Highly recommend visiting if you love nature, hiking, or just want to experience a different side of Hong Kong!

In any case, there is no short of scenic spots. Would be good if there is public transportation to get there on weekdays !

Rating: 5 - Must visit. A truly amazing part of Hong Kong.  Great views over the South China Sea, the marvel of engineering of the dam wall, and off course the famous hexagonal columns.  Everything is well sign posted. It's easy to walk around. There's some toilets too, but not any fresh water/food. So bring your own.

Rating: 3 - One of the interesting things to see in Po Fu Lam Country Park is the former Watchman's Cottage stationed at the reservoir in the lower section of the park. This is a Declared Monument building of important historical value in Hong Kong.  Constructed between 1860-63, the cottage is a single story building constructed in Neo-classical architecture, with white exterior, triangular pediments as well as Chinese tiled rooftop. This was an important property during the construction of the important reservoir here in the 1860s, when obtaining fresh and clean water source was an important issue of the times during the early colonial days.  Today the former Watchman's Cottage serves as the Country Park Management Centre, making it one of the oldest surviving buildings still in use in Hong Kong. You can see it from up close when visiting the country park and reservoir at Po Fu Lam.

reviews: Rating: 4 - This old pier structure was part of an important transportation hub along with the old Tai Po Kau Rail Station (1910-83) along the western shore of the Tolo Harbour just south of Tai Po.  The pier was an important method of transport for those living in remote villages around the Tolo Harbour, Northeast New Territories and what is now the Sai Kung Country Park until the second half of the 20th century.  With the advancement of area network of roads and rail, the rapid depopulation of the outlying villages, the need for ferry transport from the Tai Po Kau Pier greatly declined. Its fate as being used as a public ferry pier was then sealed with the opening of the Ma Liu Shui Ferry Pier at University and Science Park.  Afterwards, the Tai Po Kau Pier was used as a Marine Police pier. Today, it is still used as a tide monitoring station of Hong Kong Observatory, a recreation spot for fisherman and stop for photographs and to enjoy views of the harbour by cyclists on designated Tai Wan to Tai Mei Tuk bike trail that passes by this location these days.

Rating: 4 - The Upper Aberdeen Reservoir Main Dam is a notable historical landmark to visit when hiking in Aberdeen Country Park. The larger of the two Aberdeen reservoirs was built after the government bought and expanded the lower reservoir that was originally owned by Tai Shing Paper Factory. Both reservoirs were officially opened in 1931 by the then Governor William Peel to become the fourth and last reservoir group built on Hong Kong Island. Surrounded by nice forests, the whole area is a great place for hiking and enjoying nature.

Rating: 4 - The Aberdeen Upper and Lower Reservoirs were constructed in the 1930s and include a handful of building structures that are now designated as Declared Monuments of historical value in Hong Kong. There is signage on both sides of the two lake dams providing location and details regarding the various Declared Monuments including the two Dams, the Value Houses Pump and Chemical Houses and most impressive the Aberdeen Upper Reservoir Dam Bridge which you will see just below the dam. At first, I was like maybe it’ll get better in time, but it didn’t. The room also felt slightly dated and dingier.  That night I went to the reception and the staff member here were amazing. Super accommodating & wanted to help make it better. They let me check out another room, but it was the same. They said we had to wait until the next day to change to a more newer room that has been renovated.  The next day, we got moved to the 15th floor, and it was night & day! The room was so much more modern and updated. Most importantly, zero smell. If this was my original room, it would’ve been a great experience & no complaints. All that to be said, make sure you don’t get the outdated room if possible.

Rating: 1 - My recent stay at Holiday Inn Golden Mile Hong Kong was extremely disappointing, particularly in how elite members are treated. As an IHG One Rewards Diamond Elite member, my reservation was Loyalty Eligible under the 2026 IHG/Chase partnership. Despite this, front desk staff publicly denied my status and benefits during check-in. The situation escalated when I attempted to resolve the issue professionally by offering to pay the hotel directly if they would assist with canceling the Chase booking. Instead of constructive assistance, I was laughed at and dismissively told to “reach out to Chase.” Being mocked by service staff while they provide incorrect information is unacceptable. This reflects poor training and a breakdown in basic hospitality standards. To compound the issue: •	I was assigned a standard room overlooking Mody Road rather than being considered for Best Available Room as required for Diamond members. •	The “recovery” offered was breakfast — which is a standard Diamond benefit, not compensation for unprofessional conduct. This property needs significant retraining at the front desk level. Status recognition is not optional under published program terms. Professionalism should be baseline, not negotiable.  Very disappointing experience will not returned and Elite members beware.

The Bar- I had a welcome drink coupons so headed up to the bar and walked in. I waited for abit, and the lady just stood there at the far end looking at me expectedly. I walked towards her and asked if I could get the welcome drink here, she handed me a menu and told me that only for the drinks listed.  Ok, then after standing for a few minutes, I had to ask her if I could sit down somewhere. She looked surprised and shared that she expected me to take away my drink? Odd. Customer. Service. Because we had a great experience with a triple room in 2024 (booked via agoda), room was at a high floor, refurbished with new carpets and beds were wonderful. I thought booking directly with the hotel would be the same experience but we really had such a disappointing experience.  I booked my rooms this time direct with the hotel, 9 months in advance (messaged the hotel at booking and again before arrival for close by rooms), knowing that there are side by side triples on certain floors, but I suppose it could not be helped. My point is- I was hoping for a good experience with family who flew down to holiday in Hong Kong together. reviews: Rating: 5 - Hong Kong Cemetery is located on the west side of Happy Valley Race Cource and was previously known as the Protestant Cemetery or the Colonial Cemetery. Founded in 1845, It is the oldest Christian cemetery in Hong Kong. It is one of several other cemeteries located side by side along Wong Nai Chung Road, namely:  the Muslim Cemetery, Roman Catholic Cemetery, Hindu Temple, Parsee Cemetery, and the Jewish Cemetery.  Over 12,000 people have been interred here over the years; however, numerous burials have been lost or relocated over the decades. There are approximately 7,800 names carved onto the gravestones, ossuary tablets, and memorial monuments. There are also a number of illegible gravestones, ossuary tablets marked "Unknown," unmarked burials, and graves marked only by a number. Notable interments include business magnates Sir Robert Ho Tung and Sir Catchick Paul Chater as well as missionaries such as Karl Gutzlaff, Henrietta Hall Shuck, and Theodosia Dean. The cemetery opens daily 7 am to 6 pm. It is a peaceful place, and you will find solace there.

reviews: Rating: 5 - The Hong Kong Cultural Centre is one of the city’s most important cultural landmarks, located prominently along the Tsim Sha Tsui waterfront with stunning views of Victoria Harbour. Serving as a major venue for performing arts, the centre plays a vital role in Hong Kong’s cultural life while also acting as a public space where people gather, relax, and enjoy the surroundings.  Architecturally, the building is striking and recognizable, with its bold curves, geometric forms, and expansive open plaza. The design feels both monumental and approachable, blending modernist elements with a strong sense of openness. The large outdoor forecourt is especially lively, often filled with street performers, musicians, photographers, and visitors taking in the harbour views.  Inside, the Cultural Centre houses several world-class performance venues, including concert halls and theatres that host a wide range of events — from classical music and opera to ballet, drama, and contemporary performances. The interior spaces are well-designed, functional, and acoustically impressive, making it a respected destination for both local and international artists.  Beyond performances, the Cultural Centre is also a pleasant place to visit even without attending a show. Its location next to the Star Ferry Pier, the Clock Tower, and the Avenue of Stars makes it a natural stop while exploring Tsim Sha Tsui. Many people come here simply to sit, walk around, or enjoy the sea breeze, especially in the late afternoon and evening when the skyline begins to glow.  At night, the atmosphere becomes especially cinematic. The lights of Hong Kong Island reflect across the harbour, and the Cultural Centre’s open spaces offer unobstructed views of the city’s iconic skyline. It’s also a popular spot to watch the Symphony of Lights, adding to its appeal as both a cultural and scenic destination.  Overall, the Hong Kong Cultural Centre represents the creative and artistic side of the city while remaining deeply connected to everyday public life. Rating: 5 - Hong Kong Disneyland is the smallest of Disney’s 12 theme parks worldwide, and that scale works in its favor if you plan well. You can comfortably see the park in one day, but crowd levels matter—weekday visits are strongly recommended.  Purchase your tickets in advance and download the official park app as Disney has gone digital and printed guides are no longer available. Even with tickets preloaded, entry took us over an hour. The queue began well before official opening time and was extremely congested, with guests funneled through multiple holding lines. Expect shoulder-to-shoulder crowds, pushing, and slow movement until you finally clear the gates.  Once inside, the park is manageable and easy to navigate compared to other Disney parks. Attractions are compactly laid out, and with lighter crowds, it’s an efficient experience overall.  The absolute highlight is the 20th anniversary–only prelude to the closing fireworks. This special presentation features new storytelling elements, mesmerizing projections that sweep down the entire length of Main Street, U.S.A., and beautifully coordinated drone choreography that fills the sky with light. Be aware that guests begin staking out spots in front of the castle up to three hours before showtime, which speaks to how popular—and worthwhile—the show is.  Despite the rough entry process, the nighttime spectacular alone makes the visit memorable. With advance planning and a weekday visit, Hong Kong Disneyland delivers a solid, visually impressive Disney experience.

Mystic Minor includes many surprising jump-scares and has really nice air conditioning. My favourite part of the park is Tomorrowland. Tomorrowland includes a 4D cinema about Iron Man in Hong Kong. Ant Man and the Wisp is an interactive target shooting game where you get to compete with other visitor or friends and family in a competition for points. My favourite ride is the infamous dark rollercoaster ride, Star Wars themed, called Space Mountain. The speedy ride allows thrill and excitement. Another ride taht is also really fast is the Big Grizzly Mountain Runaway Mine Cars, it is a rollercoaster that includes a backwards drop and is outdoors, allowing you to feel all the elements. At night there was a cool parade, but it was replaced by a firework show and the caste acts as a screen. As they say “Disney is the happiest place on earth”.

Rating: 5 - Around 180 million years ago, during the Middle Jurassic period, multiple volcanic eruptions occurred. Lava mixed with volcanic ash solidified on the surface, covering previously formed sedimentary rocks. This volcanic rock layer, approximately 2000 meters thick, includes the coarse volcanic ash tuff found in the present-day Lai Chi Wo and Sha Tau Kok areas, and also formed the islands of Wan Chau, Ngo Mei Chau, and Kat O. Following the period of volcanic activity, a long period of erosion and weathering lasted approximately 20 million years. Rivers flowed down the mountains, carrying sand and gravel to the near-shore lowlands, forming a sedimentary rock layer approximately 500 meters thick, which includes the gravel, sandstone, siltstone, and shale found in the areas of Yin Chau Tong, Pat Sin Leng, and Chek Chau.

Rating: 3 - This is a small speciality museum for those with an interest in local correctional services and prison history in Hong Kong. It is located along Tung Tau Wan Road in Stanley, suitably near the Stanley Prison grounds. Opening hours are 10-1pm & 2-5pm daily (closed on Mondays) and is free to visit.  The Museum features 10 small galleries spaced out over two floors. Exhibitions represent over 170 years of history dating from the late Qing Dynasty through the colonial period all the way to the present era of National Security Law. The rooms are curated with photos and images from the past, various artefacts and information related to dealing with pirates in the early days, to prison internments during the Japanese occupation, the Vietnamese refugee situation as well as general prison life at the old Victoria prison. There are mock gallows and prison cells as well.  Overall, the museum isn't bad if you are in Stanley and have interest. However, for tourists, with Tai Kwan having opened up in Central over the past few years, a fair amount of what you see here is redundant to the various exhibitions available. If you are limited in time, you'll do fine enough visiting there instead.

Rating: 5 - A Magical Cultural Journey: From the Forbidden City to Ancient Egypt ​Rating: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ ​The Hong Kong Palace Museum is truly a world-class destination. It offers a unique atmosphere where Chinese imperial tradition meets modern architectural brilliance. If you are looking for a deep dive into history with a "magical" touch, this is the place to be. ​Why this visit is a must: ​Imperial Treasures: The exhibits from the Forbidden City in Beijing are breathtaking. Seeing the intricate craftsmanship and royal artifacts up close provides a profound connection to China’s dynastic past. ​The Egyptian Special Exhibition: A current highlight is the stunning special exhibition on Ancient Egypt. It is curated beautifully, offering a fascinating contrast between the two ancient civilizations. ​The Perfect Arrival: I highly recommend taking the ferry from Central Pier. It drops you off almost directly at the museum’s doorstep. It’s not just convenient; the scenic trip across the harbor sets the perfect mood for a day of culture. ​A Wonderful Cafe: Don't miss the museum's cafe. It is the perfect spot to take a break, enjoy great food, and soak in the incredible views of the Victoria Harbour. ​Pro Tip: Take Your Time ​You should definitely plan for a full afternoon. To truly appreciate both the permanent galleries and the special exhibitions without rushing, you will need at least 3 to 4 hours. It is an experience meant to be savored.  This is more than just a museum; it is a majestic experience. Between the world-class exhibits and the beautiful location, it is a 5-star highlight of Hong Kong.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Hong Kong Park is one of the nicest green spaces on Hong Kong Island and a great place to escape the city for a while. Sitting right in the middle of Central and Admiralty, it’s surrounded by tall buildings, but once you step inside the park it feels surprisingly calm. A lot of the park has been updated over the years, and it looks very different from what it used to be in the past. The paths, gardens, and water features are well maintained and the whole area feels clean and refreshed. It’s a great place to walk around, sit for a bit, or just slow down after being in the busy city. One of the highlights is the small zoo area, which is free and fun to walk through. You’ll see birds, turtles, and other animals, and it adds something extra to the park that many people don’t expect. Another great stop inside the park is the Flagstaff House Museum of Tea Ware, a historic building that now serves as a tea museum. It’s interesting to walk through and learn about the history of tea culture, and the tea house nearby is a nice place to relax after exploring the park. Overall Hong Kong Park is a must visit if you’re on the island. It’s a great balance of nature, history, and quiet space right in the middle of the city.

Rating: 5 - ​⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ A stunning green oasis amidst the skyscrapers! ​Hong Kong Park is an absolute highlight and the perfect place to escape the city's hustle and bustle for a while. The location is incredibly central and super easy to reach. ​I particularly enjoyed the Flagstaff House Museum of Tea Ware. It is a beautiful historic building with a wonderful atmosphere and very interesting exhibitions regarding tea culture. ​The contrast between the lush nature inside the park and the modern skyline in the background is simply impressive. Whether for a relaxing walk or a visit to the tea museum—this park is definitely worth a visit. Highly recommended!

We were staying at The Murray Hotel and was very fortunate to have this wonderful park within a 60 second walk of our hotel.  So much to see, so much nature, so much peace…. What more could you want.  Go to this park and spend time away from the wild side of the world.

reviews: Rating: 3 - The Hong Kong Police Museum is located on Coombe Road in the Wan Chai Gap area of the Peak. This is a focused speciality museum, which suitably makes use of the old Wan Chai Gap Police Station. Opening hours are 9am to 5pm (Tues to Sun), the museum is closed on Mondays. Entrance is free to the public.  Not the easiest museum to access but an interesting place to spend half an hour if you have hiked to this location by way of the Wan Chai Gap (Green Trail) from the north or up the Aberdeen Country Park trails from the south.  What you will find are 5 exhibition galleries with over 1200 items and photographs on display. The museum is curated pretty well, display items are a nice range and include English text for explanation. The galleries cover the storied history of the Hong Kong Police Force well and provide a good half an hour of learning opportunity for those with interest.

Rating: 3 - At the Happy Valley Racetrack you will find the specialty attraction called the Hong Kong Racing Museum. This is a decent (free) museum to visit and something that horse and horse racing enthusiasts will enjoy.  The museum was opened in 1996 and provides a history of horse racing in Hong Kong as well as the founding of the HK Jockey Club, Happy Valley and Sha Tin Racecourses.  One of the things we enjoy seeing at the HK Racing Museum are the historic images of the Happy Valley Race grounds as they where developed since being founded in 1846. It is always interesting to see an early Hong Kong during the colonial era, the 20th century Hong Kong prior to the arrival of our skyscrapers and then present day views of our modern metropolitan city with a horse track in the middle of the city. The transformation of the city and the tracks is incredible!  At the museum, you will find other highlights including; historic horses, jockeys and historic races (trophies). There is also considerable text information in regard to the HK Jockey Clubs long history of charitable contribution and role played in helping to develop a better Hong Kong.  Overall, this is a decent museum that is worth visiting if you plan to attend the races at Happy Valley or if you have done the rounds of major attractions in Hong Kong and are looking for other interesting things to do or see.

reviews: Rating: 4 - Really beautiful church in Central, a stone's throw away from Lan Kwai Fong. The church belongs to a group of heritage buildings that stand on an area named Tit Kong, the Iron Mound.  If placed in a historical context, this area’s hodge podge of heritage buildings exemplify the varied, colorful and eclectic character that forms the very core of Hong Kong’s heterogeneity.  The Anglican cluster of buildings then add to this unlikely mix of heritage the call for atonement and the pursuit of holiness. And surely, St. Paul’s Church’s architecture appeals to the soulful yearnings for peace and hope.  The main architectural style of the St. Paul’s Church is Neo-Gothic, with elements of Classical Revival, Dutch and Tudor.  On non worship days, the church is not open. You will have to visit a sermon in order to see the beautiful interior, including five painted glass panes featuring Jesus and his four disciples.

Rating: 3 - St. Paul's Church is located on Glenealy just south of the Fringe Club and the LKF district.  This is an early 20th-century church with several architectural influences ranging from the neo-gothic spire and tower at the front to the Dutch style gable at the back. The building is cream coloured with light blue trim and roof.  The facade of the church is a bit difficult to see as a later period building was constructed just few meters in front of it. However, you can make a side view of the church front from across Glenealy Road.  St. Paul's is an active Anglican Church with regular services. Check their website for details. It also functions as a local kindergarten as well.
