Rating: 5 - This church was built by the sons of the family, the latter which where killed in the boxer rebellion in China when they where missionaries from uk. The sons where in the Uk,  at school during the massacre, but decided to continue their parents work, hence the church and adjacent school. There is a brass plaque commentating their achievement in the church. Despite Hong Kong now being under Chinese control there are some wonderful examples of British built buildings, many I’m pleased to say have been historically preserved and well maintained by this regime, including the building that was once the resident of the military governor and now a museum of the history of tea making, situated in Hong Kong park, once Victoria Barracks of the British army, in which I served, but alas now gone and turned into a beautiful park with fantastic aviary. No fee for entry to either the Tea museum, park or aviary.

Rating: 5 - St. Paul’s Church (聖保羅堂) in Hong Kong was built in 1911 to serve the spiritual needs of expatriate residents and visitors of the Anglican faith. Its founding emanated from the joint efforts of four individuals: Lam Woo (林護), Huang Mou-lin (黃茂林), Li Wei-zhen (李維楨) and the Rev. A.D. Stewart (史超域牧師). It has evolved from a small church for the expatriates living in Hong Kong since those early days into one that accommodates a wide range of churchgoers. In 1938, St. Paul’s Church Parish was put under the direct control of the Anglican Church of Hong Kong.  Architecturally the church is an interesting mix of styles, predominantly Neo-Gothic with features and motifs drawn from Tudor, Dutch and Classical Revival styles. The colour scheme externally consists of crisp white stuccoed walls accentuated by the blue-painted roof and mouldings. A Dutch gable and canted bay adorn one end of the Church and a Gothic tower dominates the other end. A variety of different  window shapes contribute to the interesting architectural composition.

Rating: 5 - The Hong Kong Space Museum 香港太空館is an iconic, egg-shaped museum and planetarium located in Tsim Sha Tsui, Hong Kong, dedicated to the popularization of astronomy and space science. It features interactive exhibits and a state-of-the-art Space Theatre. The museum is divided into two main wings, each offering unique experiences: Stanley Ho Space Theatre: Located within the iconic egg-shaped dome, this theatre features a 23-meter hemispherical screen and advanced digital projection systems for immersive Sky Shows and 3D dome films. Hall of the Cosmos: This permanent exhibition on the ground floor focuses on the origins and evolution of the universe, with interactive displays on topics like black holes, the Big Bang, and galaxy formation. Hall of Space Exploration: Located on the first floor, this hall takes visitors through humanity's space travel history, with exhibits including replicas of spacecraft like the Shenzhou, models of Mars rovers, and a VR experience of walking on the Moon and Mars. The museum is very kid-friendly, with many interactive exhibits and activities designed for children. The museum is located at 10 Salisbury Road, Tsim Sha Tsui, Kowloon, Hong Kong. MTR: It is within walking distance of both the Tsim Sha Tsui and East Tsim Sha Tsui MTR stations. Ferry: It is also near the Star Ferry Pier.

Rating: 5 - I see lots of reviews saying to buy tickets online,  buy in advance, don't go on the weekend, and avoid the long lines. We arrived at 9:40am on a Sunday, waited a minute in line, bought our tickets with a credit card in person, and walked right through the turnstile with no issues.  When we boarded the tram, an aggressive woman tried pushing her way past me, and her attack was repulsed. Otherwise, the ride up the mountain was glorious, and a must do for visitors to this beautiful city. There are so many intricate views between buildings built into the mountainside. We did not pay anything additional for the highest viewing area, as all the other viewing areas provided more than enough vistas for us. There are several eateries, souvenir shops, bathrooms, and sitting areas for you to spend hours up here. And we went when the fog prevented us from seeing much past the initial mile or so of Kowloon's waterfront. It was still worth it.

Rating: 5 - The Peak Tram is one of those “classic” Hong Kong things that is actually worth doing. Rating: 5 - Riding the 6th-generation Peak Tram remains an essential Hong Kong experience, blending 130 years of history with a sleek, modern upgrade that features massive panoramic windows and increased capacity. Rating: 4 - Hong Kong Wetland Park in Tin Shui Wai is a unique ecological attraction that combines conservation, education, and recreation. Spanning over 60 hectares, the park allows visitors to explore diverse wetland ecosystems, including mangroves, marshes, and ponds. It features well-maintained walking trails, bird hides, and observation decks, making it an ideal destination for birdwatchers, nature enthusiasts, and families.  The park is home to a variety of wildlife, such as birds, amphibians, and butterflies, offering a peaceful retreat from the city’s hustle and bustle. While the visitor center, which normally provides educational exhibits on wetland biodiversity and conservation, is currently under construction to offer an enhanced experience in the future, visitors can still enjoy the outdoor trails and wildlife observation. Facilities such as a café and gift shop add convenience to the visit.  Easily accessible by public transport, Hong Kong Wetland Park remains a tranquil and educational destination for all ages.

Many migrating birds come here for retreating from their winter. Hence there are small huts for bird watching equipped with binoculars. The area is not too big only 60 hectare but have landscapes, sugar gum trees, pools for various vegetations like lotus roots and walkways made of wood panels with swamp at the side to see small creatures like crabs and jumping fish. A noticeable guest here is the Crocodile Pui Pui which was caught in the new Territories’ river several years back and now became a big one and long term guest. This place is an exhibition centre for wildlife conservation and education centre. One can easily spend 3 hours here. Canteen is available for food and drinks. Written on Apr 19, 2025

reviews: Rating: 5 - It’s honestly crazy how fast and massive this bridge was built. The Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macau Bridge feels like something out of the future — water everywhere, open sky, and then this long, elegant line cutting across the sea like it’s floating. This isn’t just a bridge — it’s a 55-kilometer (about 34 miles) mega sea-crossing system connecting Hong Kong, Zhuhai, and Macau. It includes: 🌉 22.9 km main bridge 🌊 A 6.7 km undersea tunnel 🏝️ Two artificial islands 🚗 Opened in 2018 💰 Cost around USD $20+ billion What makes it impressive isn’t just the size — it’s the engineering. Building across open water in the Pearl River Delta, with typhoons, heavy shipping traffic, and deep seabed conditions, is not easy. The bridge is designed to withstand: 8-magnitude earthquakes Super typhoons Ship collisions Driving across it feels surreal. Water stretches in every direction, and at certain points you almost forget you’re on solid structure. The transition from bridge into the underwater tunnel is smooth and futuristic. At sunset, the lighting and reflection on the water make it look almost unreal. It also drastically cuts travel time — what used to take 3–4 hours between Hong Kong and Zhuhai/Macau now takes around 30–45 minutes by car or shuttle bus. Whether you’re into infrastructure, photography, or just want to experience one of the largest sea-crossing projects in the world, this bridge is worth seeing at least once. It’s one of those projects that shows what modern engineering can actually do when scale and ambition come together.

Rating: 5 - Visiting the Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macao Bridge has been an absolutely stunning experience. This mega engineering and construction project is a remarkable testament to humanity’s ability to overcome technical and geographic challenges. Its 55+ km length, combining bridges, tunnels, and offshore viaducts, makes it one of the most iconic structures in the world.  As a professional specializing in engineering and construction, this landmark has been on my bucket list for years, and seeing it in person exceeded every expectation. Its scale, innovative design, and flawless execution are truly inspiring. I was deeply impressed and grateful for the opportunity to witness such a masterful achievement.  Definitely a 5-star experience ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ for anyone passionate about engineering and modern infrastructure.

Rating: 5 - From the HKIA, we proceeded terminal where we boarded a bus bound for Macao. We took a short bus ride from the airport to Hong Kong -Zhuhai- Macao bus terminal. It's a huge terminal that just feels like an airport. Very modern and impressive.  It didn't take much time for us to purchase our tickets to Macao. After a few minutes, we were already traveling to Macao by bus. A new experience for me since we took the ferry on our previous trips to Macao.

Rating: 5 - HZMB is an Engineering Marvel on this planet, The Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macau Bridge (HZMB) is a 55-kilometre  bridge–tunnel system consisting of a series of three cable-stayed bridges, an undersea tunnel, and four artificial islands. It is both the longest sea crossing and the longest open-sea fixed link in the world. The HZMB spans the Lingding and Jiuzhou channels, connecting Hong Kong and Macau with Zhuhai—a major city on the Pearl River Delta in China. It's simply stunning!!!

Rating: 3 - There are several Hau Wong Temples to be found in Hong Kong but this one is probably the most famous. The Hau Wong Temple in Kowloon City was built in 1730 and rests on Junction Road half way between the Lok Yu MTR station and the Kowloon Walled City Park. It is a Grade 1 historical building and makes a nice quick stop for those planning to visit the Kowloon Walled City.  There is disagreement as to the origins of this temple. However, the prevailing belief is that the temple commemorates a Chinese general, 'Hau Wong' Yeung Leung-jit, who helped the last emperor of the Song Dynasty by providing him refuge in Kowloon, averting invading forces in search of him.  Hau Wong Temple has cultural artefacts including attractive wall reliefs and Chinese calligraphy. Also, the main hall contains images of Hau Wong as well as chambers which are well decorated. The temple is quite small and can be comfortably visited in 10-15 minutes, making it convenient to see before or after your visit to the nearby Kowloon Walled City Park.  Overall, this Hau Wong decent temple visit but there are better temple visits in the area. These include Wong Tai Sin (Wong Tai Sin - MTR) and the Chi Lin Nunnery (Diamond Hill - MTR). In the end, this Hau Wong Temple is a good stop on the way to the Kowloon Walled City Park.

reviews: Rating: 5 - To our surprise entry for tourists is free, so in we went smiling as tourists usually get ripped off. Although we were there early the razzamatazz of race night was already in full swing, music, bright lights, but no obvious signs of bookies or the tic tac men. We felt our way around and found a very helpful attendant who showed us how to bet using one of the large touch screens, similar to those in McDonald’s. So we were now in our element.  I got Gemini AI to forecast the winners from the programme we got from the self vending machine. With bets placed and a beer in hand we found a couple of seats high up in the terraces with a reasonable view of the finish line. We had an hour to kill before the race but like these things it was interesting just watching the antics of the crowd.  Soon the horses were being paraded up and down and our horse, number four Savvy Twinkle, appeared on the big screen looking rather grand, a winner in the making. Ten minutes later the gates opened and they were off. The race was only over a thousand metres so no sooner had they started than we were on our feet egging Savvy Twinkle on. As the pack surged past us Twinky was ahead by a nostril. My goodness, he was going to win. And yeah, he did. First race and we were already up. Not sure what the odds were I decided to go and collect our winnings. To my surprise I got $480.00 including my $100.00 stake, a profit of £38.00. Well done Gemini AI.  Sad to say that’s where our luck ended as the next five races went without a place. Halfway through we consoled ourselves with another large beer, a huge hotdog and a bucket of fries.  We left two races before the end as they didn’t finish before eleven o’clock and we had a bus and train to catch back home. We actually caught a tram which rattled us to the MTR where we caught the train back. Unfortunately we left the station from the wrong exit and even with the help of Google Maps live, which doesn’t seem to work very well in the dark, we got completely lost. Fortunately this is an extremely safe city and even the dark corners feel safe. By luck we came across a street that Ros recognised so we were back on the straight and narrow back on the route home.

Best night out I’ve had here!

reviews: Rating: 5 - Hung Hom Kwun Yum Temple is a quiet and spiritually meaningful temple located in the Hung Hom area of Kowloon, offering a peaceful retreat from the surrounding urban environment. Dedicated to Kwun Yum, the Goddess of Mercy, the temple is deeply respected by locals who visit to pray for compassion, protection, health, and emotional well-being. Compared to larger and more famous temples in Hong Kong, this temple feels more intimate and grounded in everyday local life.  The temple’s architecture is traditional and modest, featuring classic Chinese design elements such as red pillars, decorative roof details, and carved stone ornaments. Inside, the atmosphere is calm and reverent, filled with the soft glow of incense smoke and the quiet rhythm of worshippers offering prayers. Many visitors come alone or in small groups, creating a reflective and respectful environment that encourages slow, mindful observation.  Hung Hom Kwun Yum Temple is especially known among locals as a place to seek inner peace and guidance during difficult times. The presence of Kwun Yum symbolizes mercy and unconditional compassion, and this sense of spiritual comfort is strongly felt throughout the temple grounds. On special days of the lunar calendar and during festivals, the temple becomes livelier, yet it still maintains a sincere and humble character rather than a festive or commercial atmosphere.  The temple is well-maintained and easy to visit, making it accessible even for those who are not familiar with religious customs. Visitors are welcome to observe rituals respectfully, light incense, or simply take a moment of quiet reflection. Its location within a residential district gives it an authentic, local feel, offering insight into how spiritual practices are woven into daily life in Hong Kong.  Overall, Hung Hom Kwun Yum Temple is not just a place of worship but a gentle sanctuary of compassion and calm. It is an ideal stop for travelers interested in local culture, spiritual traditions, or those seeking a quieter, more personal temple experience away from the crowds. The temple leaves a lasting impression through its simplicity, sincerity, and sense of inner peace.

reviews: Rating: 5 - I recently had the pleasure of joining an island hopping tour in Yan Chau Tong Marine Park, and one of the highlights of the trip was getting to see Hung Shek Mun. The scenery was absolutely breathtaking, and I would highly recommend a visit to anyone traveling to Hong Kong.  The area is nestled between lush green mountains and crystal-clear blue waters, creating a stunning backdrop for any photo. As we explored the area, I was struck by the natural beauty of the landscape and the peacefulness of the surroundings.  One of the things that I loved about Hung Shek Mun is the sense of tranquility that permeates the area. It's a great place to escape and relax, and I found myself feeling completely at peace as I wandered through the quiet streets.

Rating: 5 - Hung Shek Mun is a unique stretch of coastline on the east end of Plover Cove Country Park at Double Haven (Yan Chau Tong Marine Park). It is noted for the high presence of iron rich, deep red coloured sedimentary rock bed that lines the shores here, making for the most unusual and peculiar scenery and photograph opportunities.  This is a really neat place to visit but it is a bit of a challenge. You can hike there by way of 15.5 km out-and-back trail from Wu Kau Tang village that takes a full day to complete. Originally, you follow the main Double Haven Country Trail and then taking one of two splinter trails through the bush until you reach Hung Shek Mun. These two splinter trails loop back together shortly before arriving at the destination so you can go one way there and the other way back to Wu Kau Tang if you like. You can find this trail details on Hiking Trail Hong Kong mobile app. I very much recommend using this app as well to make your way in and out of Hung Shek Mun as well.  Note that the hiking trail is easy to follow for the first couple of kilometres of the Double Haven Country Trail. However, once you break off to the informal splinter trails to the coast, things change. The trail is easy to follow but is narrow, much overgrown and requires some fitness to complete. You will definitely need long trousers, long-sleeve shirt and hat to protect yourself from being shredded by the brush and vegetation that you will pass along the way. You will also want to make sure you have sufficient food, drink and sunscreen for a long day out. There are no public facilities of any sort after starting the hike at Wu Kau Tang.  Scenery is nice along the way, there are some viewpoints of Double Haven and the country park peaks to enjoy along the way. The hike is long and tiring but it is rewarding to finally make it and walk the shores of Hung Shek Mun to see the rich red coloured sedimentary rocks found for a couple kilometres along the shore.  Worth note, it is important to also research and be familiar with the tide schedule as this will impact how far you can walk along the coast and can affect a dam crossing, you make on the coast. Timing means the difference of keeping your shoes dry or not, not something to mess around with prior to a long hike back to Wu Kau Tang.  In the end, do plan on a long day if planning to hike out to Hung Shek Mun. Normal spend hiking will take you around 6-7 hours, potentially longer if you make regular stops to rest and take pictures. Allow another 1-2 hours minimum at the coast. Lastly, allow two 30-45 minute journeys from the Tai Po Market Station MTR Station to/from Wu Kau Tang village where the trail starts.

Rating: 4 - An interesting attraction to see in Wan Chai is the Hung Shing Temple. This is a Grade I historical building situated along the busy Queen's Road East. Opening hours 9am to 5pm daily.  This temple started off as a simple shrine on top of shoreline rocks directly on the harbour. Later the first temple was constructed here around 1850. Massive land reclamations since that time have resulted in the temple now being in the busy urban and commercial area of Wan Chai while the harbour is now only found much further north.  The temple is dedicated to Hung Shing, the protector of fisherman and sea traders. It is of typical 19h-century Chinese temple architecture, featuring grey brick walls, a simple entrance with a decorative porch and roof. The interior is a simple two hall structure with numerous deity figures, items of worship.  Overall, the Hung Shing Temple is smaller and less impressive than others you may plan to visit around the city. However, it remains interesting and worth a quick look inside if you plan to spend time in the Wanchai area and enjoy seeing buildings of historical value during your travels.

reviews: Rating: 3 - There are a handful of temples scattered around Hong Kong that are dedicated to Hung Shing, the protector of fisherman and sea traders, including this one in the village of Shui Tau Tsuen, which is believed to have been that is believed to have been originally constructed several centuries ago.  This Hung Shing Temple is a Grade III Historic Building in Hong Kong and is situated amidst a handful of heritage sites including ancestral halls, study halls and other temples. It was rebuilt in 1984 but seems to be kept closed most of the time by way of a large iron gate. Unfortunately, the obscures photo taking of the facade but it at least allows you to see the temple mostly clearly from the outside.  What you will be able to see on the outside is fairly typical of temples from the Qing Dynasty with two hall structure and open courtyard in the middle, the roof has classic green tiling while the brick facade has a creme yellow colour these days. You can peer through the iron gate into the temple and see open wooden panels and the altar in the back bay but that is about it as far as viewing the interior.  Have a brief look and then make your way to the other heritage attractions nearby which you can enter and have a look around.

Rating: 5 - Hung Shing Temple, Kam Tin, Yuen Long. The couplet on the gate reads: "Knowledgeable and discerning, thus holy and divine."  According to the inscription on the temple's reconstruction stele (erected in 1984), the temple was built in the late Ming and early Qing dynasties, over 300 years ago. Having endured considerable weathering, it has undergone several renovations to maintain its appearance, including three documented renovations in the tenth year of the Xianfeng Emperor's reign (1850), the sixteenth year of the Guangxu Emperor's reign (1891), and the twenty-sixth year of the Republic of China (1937). Later, the temple was acquired through a bidding process by the Deng family of Shui Tou Village. They formed a committee to rebuild the Hung Shing Temple, and the temple is now under the influence of the Deng family of Shui Tou Village.

Rating: 5 - Hung Shing Temple, located in Hang Mei Village, was built by the Tang clan of Ping Shan. According to the inscription on the temple plaque, it was likely built in the Dinghai year of the Qianlong Emperor's reign (1767). The existing structure was rebuilt in the fifth year of the Tongzhi Emperor's reign (1866), and underwent major repairs in 1963. Hung Shing is widely revered and worshipped, especially by fishermen and those who make their living from the sea. His birthday is celebrated on the 13th day of the second lunar month each year.  Hung Shing Temple is a two-courtyard building constructed of blue bricks, with a central courtyard. Its structure is simple. While other temples in Hong Kong often add roofs to their courtyards to create incense pavilions, Hung Shing Temple retains its original open design, resulting in better lighting and ventilation, which is the temple's most distinctive feature.  Hung Shing Temple was designated a Grade II historic building in Hong Kong in 1994, and its final rating was confirmed on May 17, 2010.  Hung Shing Temple  According to the inscriptions on the temple plaques, the temple was built in the Dinghai year of the Qianlong reign (1767), although some sources suggest it dates back to the mid-Ming Dynasty. The current structure was rebuilt in the fifth year of the Tongzhi reign (1866), and underwent another major renovation in 1963.  Hung Shing Temple is a two-courtyard building, with the Fu De Shrine and Tai Sui Hall on the left and right, respectively, and a central courtyard. The structure is simple and unpretentious. While most other temples in Hong Kong have covered their courtyards and converted them into incense pavilions, Hung Shing Temple retains its original design, providing better lighting and ventilation—a unique feature of the temple. Inside Hung Shing Temple are cast wooden clappers from the 29th year of the Qianlong reign (1764) and an inscription from the fifth year of the Tongzhi reign (1866) commemorating the reconstruction of Hung Shing Temple.  Hung Shing Temple enshrines Hong Xi, the Tang Dynasty governor of Guangli. (For the background, please refer to the Hung Shing Temple.)  The couplet at the gate of Hong Sheng Palace reads: "The majestic virtue of Hong Sheng Palace is awe-inspiring, its spirit responding to the well; The holy countenance shines radiantly over the Shajiang River."

Rating: 5 - First built in the mid-Ming Dynasty, the temple has undergone numerous renovations. Inside the temple are a castanets from the 29th year of the Qianlong Emperor's reign (1764) and an inscription inscribed with the title of the "Renovation of Hung Shing Temple" from the 5th year of the Tongzhi Emperor's reign (1866). Thirteen pairs of wooden couplets hang on either side, the largest number of any temple in Hong Kong.  The couplet on the temple gate reads: "Great virtue, majestic and spiritual, responds to the wells; "The holy face, radiant and glorious, illuminates the Shajiang River."  The deity enshrined: Hongsheng Guangli King of the South Sea.

Rating: 3 - Hung Shing Temple in Hang Mei Village, Ping Shan, was built by the Tang family in 1767 during the reign of Emperor Qianlong of the Qing Dynasty. The current structure was rebuilt in 1866, the fifth year of the reign of Emperor Tongzhi of the Qing Dynasty, and underwent extensive renovations in 1963. Legend has it that Hung Shing Ye, originally named Hong Xi, was a virtuous and upright official during the Tang Dynasty (618-907). He was posthumously honored by the reigning emperor as "Kuang Li Hong Sheng Da Wang." Many fishermen and those who make their living from the sea offer sacrifices to Hung Shing Ye.

reviews: Rating: 5 - I recently had the pleasure of hiking the Tung Chung to Mui Wo Olympic Trail, and I can confidently say it’s an excellent choice for beginner hikers! This trail offers a perfect blend of scenery, manageable terrain, and a welcoming atmosphere that makes it an ideal introduction to hiking.  Starting at Tung Chung, the trail kicks off with a gentle incline that allows newcomers to acclimatize without feeling overwhelmed. The well-marked path is easy to follow, and the gradual elevation gain means you can take your time and enjoy the views of Lantau Island and the surrounding waters.  The trail is approximately 10 kilometers long, which is manageable for most beginners, and there are plenty of rest areas along the way. Reaching Mui Wo is a rewarding experience, with its quaint village charm and beautiful beach providing a lovely place to unwind after your hike. Whether you choose to grab a bite to eat or simply relax by the shore, it’s the perfect way to celebrate your accomplishment.

Rating: 5 - JC Contemporary (also known as Tai Kwan Contemporary) is a new art gallery in Hong Kong located in the recently opened cultural heritage attraction area of Tai Kwan. This is a architecturally delightful building which includes over 15000 square feet of contemporary art exhibition space. Entry is free to the public and opening hours are 11am to 7pm with extended hours until 9pm on Fridays.  We visited the JC Contemporary art gallery for the first time recently and were very impressed with the building and the first round of exhibitions presently on display. The building exterior is of excellent design, a refreshing change from the many towering skyscrapers on Hong Kong Island. The interior is also nice, three floors of good art space. We particularly like the elegantly designed spiral staircase which winds up the three floors in a funnel like fashion.  The current 'Hollow in the world too full" exhibition by Chinese artist Cao Fei is spaced out over the three floors. Open displays are interesting to view. However, what we most enjoyed was the intriguing feature film called 'La Town' (approx. 45 minute) on the third floor. Another film about the prison life on the first floor was interesting as well but we ran out of time and were unable to watch in its entirety.  Note: There is a restaurant, the Old Bailey Restaurant, on the second floor for those interested in a meal at the JC Contemporary art gallery. Toilet facility can be found on the ground floor.  Overall, this is a very nice addition to the Tai Kwan project and the art museum and gallery scene here in Hong Kong. We are pleased with its opening and look forward to our future visits.

reviews: Rating: 4 - It was extremely loud and punctual. Try to be there 10 minutes before noon. The directions given by Google Maps today was misleading, the underground passage is actually an unlabelled door at the side of the building across the main road from the gun. Rating: 4 - Next to the Causeway Bay fire station is this harbour promenade. Along here ,is a great view of  "the old habour in Business" boats preforming the functions of entertaining theatres and eateries, in the late 50's . The  Jardine Noon gun is here also. It can be accessible by a secret route from the car park under the World Trade Centre. Beautiful views at any time.  The above was written and relating to the state and views at that time.  Jardine Noonday Gun  It is located on the harbour promenade  at the Causeway Bay Typhoon Shelter just across the World Trade Centre. It is owned by the Jardine Matheson Corp . Every noon the gun will be fired to signify the Time. The tradition started at 1830. So this is favourable spot for HK visitors.  From here fantastic views of Typhoon shelter, The Royal HK Yacht Club (HKRYC) can be enjoyed. Across the Victoria Harbour, at the Kowloon Peninsula City Water Front  from Tsim Sha Tsui East to Kowloon Bay the views are great.  This place was revisited again in March 27,2025.  Written on April 21st, 2025.

Rating: 4 - A quirky little stop if you're in the area. Fired daily at midday, and then the gates open for you to walk around and take pictures. Easiest way to access is via the underpass.  No tickets or payment required.
Rating: 5 - The ceremonial gun is fired at noon 12pm daily, and visitors can enter to see up close from 12-1230pm. Great view of the harbour!

Rating: 5 - The famous noon day gun. Made famous by Noël Coward's song "Mad Dogs and Englishmen" in which it's claimed "in Hong Kong, they strike a gong, and fire off a noonday gun; To reprimand each inmate who's in late". And it's still kind of true as the gun is fired daily at noon. The gun itself is in the historic and easily accessible east point now causeway bay that was sold by public auction in 1841 to Jardine. Over the years the tradition of firing the gun to greet the arrival of jardines ships built up. However this practiced annoyed a newly arrived naval officer who believed such a practise should be reserved for government officials only. The penalty handed down to Jardine was to fire the gun daily at noon in perpetuity, which save during WW2 was exactly what was done. The original gun was lost during the Japanese occupation but a new gun was installed in 1947 and the current gun in 1961.

reviews: Rating: 4 - The Kai Tak Sports Park finally opened earlier this year transforming the old Kai Tak Airport Grounds into an open sports park, stadiums, recreation and leisure area along with residential towers, restaurants and malls.  The Sports Park takes up a large area between the Sung Wong Toi and Kai Tak MTR Stations all the way to the harbour. It includes the new Kai Tak Mall Phases 1 to 3, the large and impressive Airside Mall, an open 10K capacity sports ground and the 50K Kai Tak Stadium where major events are starting to be held. It seems more sports activity areas continue to be developed that will open in the future as well as an opening dining area along the harbour just next to Kai Tak Stadium. reviews: Rating: 4 - This place has many hikers, runners and others…. Lots of people come here just to see monkeys included myself. It is not legal to feed monkeys anymore , but they get used to get food from humans and there is nothing to eat in the mountains. I wonder how are they going to survive!

Rating: 4 - We tried to follow the Google instructions on how to get there which took us in a loop. All you need to do is get the 81 bus from Shatin. When you get off the bus, carry on walking in the direction of the bus and you will come to the entrance on the left. If you are there for the monkeys then you need not go too far past the lower reservoir. If you are there for walking or jogging then walk as high as you like. There are several trails you can follow but they are all uphill. We got as far as M119 marker which was equivalent to 39 floors. There are rules for the monkeys, please follow them as they are wild animals and can attack. It was a mild 24°C when we went but still got a sweat on so take plenty of water. There are picnic stops along the way but be careful as the monkeys will attack you or snatch to get at the food. We witnessed monkeys raiding a car when the driver left his door open. He chased them but never got his things back. There are viewpoints along the way but not enough to make me want to climb to the top. I think you can see mainland China in the distance. The 2nd reservoir was underwhelming, I think that is why it is signposted as a jogging trail. Steep climb up too. Once was enough for me.

Rating: 3 - The park feels pretty far from civilization, but it’s actually easy to reach by bus. Just a heads-up—I didn’t notice any public restrooms around.  Watch out for the monkeys. Seriously. There are a lot of them, especially along the path, so stay alert both going up and down.  There aren’t any spots to refill water or really even sit down, so come prepared. It’s a long route, and the walk itself isn’t exactly the most comfortable.

Rating: 5 - Some say the original house was a Tin Hau Temple.  Some others say that it used to be a study hall.  Whatever it used to be, time has done its wonders on the structure.  The banyan tree next to the house slowly grew, over a few hundred years.  During the early Qing Dynasty, the Qing Government issued an imperial edict for coastal evacuation in order to quell the resistance by remnant supporters of Ming Dynasty, as they were known to be exceptional seafarers with naval power.  As such, the owner of this brick house abandoned it and has never returned since.  The banyan tree grew its aerial roots and effectively “devoured” the house.  Besides the tree house, the villages there (Shui Mei Tsuen and Shui Tau Tsuen) offer many, many wonderful historic sites as well. You can easily spend a whole afternoon there touring.

Rating: 3 - An interesting WWII era attraction to see on Lamma Island is the location of the Kamikaze Grottos (Kamikaze Caves) located along the shore between Lo So Shing and Sok Kwu Wan. There are several manmade tunnels (caves), one of which is marked with signs and a large opening which you can enter and look around. Use a torch if you want to walk all the way to the back, around perhaps 30 metres or so.  These caves were actually tunnels created by the Japanese during the four year occupation of Hong Kong. At that time the harbour around Lo So Shing was a naval position by the Japanese who dug out the Kamikaze Caves in order conceal speedboats which would have been launched as suicide missions against allied warships if they came near. It seems that the Kamikaze Caves were not completed or at least never used before the end of the war.  Note: In addition to the open Kamikaze Cave, there is another 20-30 metres away along the main footpath that is mostly concealed and covered with vegetation. There is a No Entry sign at the cave entrance but you can see into it pretty well if you have a torch with you.

Rating: 4 - Tung Ping Chau Marine Park was designated in 2001 and includes around 270 hectares of sea area that surrounds the small outlying island of Tung Ping Chau near mainland China's Mirs Bay. Additionally, you can see marine life in the rock pools and shallow waters that surround Tung Ping Chau. You'll find crabs, sea urchins, sea hares (slugs) and lots of small fish. The goby fish that hand out in the rock pools near Kang Lau Shek are really neat.  Another reason for visiting the Tung Ping Chau Marine Park is to view the outstanding geological features around the island, namely the sedimentary rock formations that offer splendid scenery and coastal areas to explore on foot. There are nice beachfronts and pebble beaches around the island as well. These contribute to the experience of visiting the Tung Ping Chau Marine Park. Rating: 5 - Kang Yung Study Hall is one of the few examples of study halls built purely for teaching purposes. Situated in the Hakka village of Sheung Wo Hang in Sha Tau Kok, it was built by the Li clan in the early Qing Dynasty. It began as a small private school for 20 to 30 pupils and was rebuilt in the Qianlong reign (1736-1795) and renamed Kang Yung Study Hall. As it was constructed purely for teaching purposes, the architecture is simple but functional. It is a two-hall building with cocklofts, providing classrooms and living quarters and comprises a rectangular structure of green brick walls, with unfired mud-bricks and rammed earth for internal partitions. It was declared a monument in 1991 followed by a full restoration undertaken by the government. It is now open to the public. (By AMO)

Rating: 3 - Tourists are generally not welcome here. There's an old man at the gate watching over everyone coming and going, so only authorized personnel are allowed inside. The walls, towers, and the temple visible inside are registered as Hong Kong's Grade 1 Historic Sites. (So why aren't you allowed inside?!) You're free to look around the perimeter as much as you like, but you can't go inside. It's essentially a fortress, and in fact, the surrounding land is privately owned. Its history is surprisingly long, dating back to the Northern Song Dynasty (about 1,000 years ago), but it took on its current form around the 18th century, when the walls and towers were built to protect against bandits. As you can see from the photo, almost all of the houses inside have been renovated, and there are almost no Taira-style houses left (although they may just be invisible). It's now in a modern style. Many of the residents inside are descendants or related to the Tang clan, and the entire property is privately owned, so it's pointless to go sightseeing. (If you're an official, you might be allowed in together.) At the very back of the gate, you can see what looks like a shrine, but unfortunately, you can't enter, so I don't know the details. Again, tourists are not welcome, so you can't enter.

Rating: 5 - Situated on Kau Sai Chau (Island), Sai Kung, Hung Shing Temple is a typical example of traditional temple architecture. Hung Shing is a deity who provides protection at sea, and the construction of the temple was funded by donations from local residents whose livelihood relied mainly on fishing. According to local history and the stone tablet at the temple, the building was built before 1889. Serving the district of Kau Sai Chau, the temple has long been a place in which to pray for the safety of fishermen, but it also fulfils the social function of strengthening community cohesion. Large-scale celebrations are held every year by the locals to mark the birthday of Hung Shing.  Hung Shing Temple is a two-hall, three-bay structure with a dong-chung door in the front hall. Altars are placed in the main hall where the deities Hung Shing, Choi Pak Shing Kwan and Shui Sin Yeuh are worshipped. (By AMO)

Located in the southern part of Kau Sai Chau in Sai Kung, it is a declared monument and a recipient of the 2000 UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Award for its exemplary restoration.  A typical Qing Dynasty two-hall, three-bay structure featuring grey brick walls, a timber roof frame, and intricate carvings. The most vibrant time to visit is during the Hung Shing Festival (13th day of the second lunar month), which features Cantonese opera, lion dances, and religious rituals.

It was rated as a Grade 3 historic building in 1990, and was later recognized as a Grade 1 historic building in Hong Kong on 2 September 2011.

Rating: 4 - Tsung Tsin Mission of Hong Kong Kau Yan Church was previously a church for Hakka people from China during the time of the Taiping Rebellion in the mid-19th century. A church known as Sai Kwok Lau (四角樓) was established in 1861 by the Society of Basel Mission (巴色傳道會) whose missionaries first came to Hong Kong from Switzerland in 1847.  After various moves and changes of name a permanent home was found and the present church was built in 1931-1932. In December 1941, when Hong Kong came under Japanese invasion, the Church became a refugee shelter for the residents nearby.  The Church was believed to have been designed by the well known local architectural firm of Palmer and Turner. The architectural style is Neo-Gothic with some Tudor features externally, but internally Romanesque arches, and Neo-Classical columns and beams are found. This mixture of styles gives the church a transitional feel of moving from one architectural style to another which is not uncommon in early churches.

Rating: 4 - Small but cool beach area with views and access to the rock columns. Ground is all round, biggish rocks, so it’s a little hard to walk around. Some trash on the water line though.

Rating: 3 - Kim Chu Wan is a hidden gem in the Sai Kung East Country Park and place to spend time up-close with giant stacks of hexagonal volcanic columns, famously situated in this area of the UNESCO Global Geopark area in Hong Kong.  You'll find Kim Chu Wan, a short enclosed pebble beach along the Po Pin Chau trail and Pak Lap Loop Trail, shortly past the uphill ascend to the famous Po Pin Chau viewpoint. You can view down the cliffs of Kim Chu Wan as you approach Po Pin Chau. However, the idea is to get down to the beach so you can see them up close. To do this, you have to make the rather steep descent down to the pebble beach area. The path down is easy to spot and there is a rope to assist if the ground is wet or if you have trouble with your footing going up or down the first section. Then it flattens out a bit until you reach the pebble beach area.  Once you are down near sea level, you will be treated to a spectacular experience of walking right up to the towering stacks of hexagonal volcanic columns that make up the sea cliffs here. It is a remarkable spot and real treasure for those with interest in geology. Depending on the time of day, you may find some shade along some of the cliffs, making for a nice picnic location before climbing back up to the main trail to continue onward with your hike in the area.  In the end, the little known Kim Chu Wan beach is one of my favourite spots to spend time in the UNESCO Global Geopark. Not an easy place to get to but definitely worth the trouble for the special views and access to rare and beautiful geology.
Rating: 5 - Love the track and challenging but in fun way!!!  Hidden gem with breathtaking view.  Bring gloves when you want to hike here

Rating: 5 - Very steep terrain, basically a rocky beach surrounded by steep sea cliffs and loose rocks. The main attraction is the vertical hexagonal rock columns, a kind of extrusive igneous rock formed by slow cooling. Rock columns elsewhere are usually made of dark grey basalt with low silica content. By contrast, the rock columns in Hong Kong are light-coloured, silica-rich, rhyolitic volcanic rock. The columnar joints are mainly pentagonal or hexagonal.

And yet, ever since King Yin Lei was saved from demolition in 2007, it has remained a mystery to the public - except for a few precious days a year when its green metal gates are thrown open to visitors.  The house is divided into 3 wings surrounding a central courtyard. reviews: Rating: 5 - Alhamdulillah, Visited the Kowloon Masjid and Islamic Centre, Hong Kong  A historic symbol of faith, unity, and heritage in Hong Kong.  The Kowloon Masjid and Islamic Centre, located in Tsim Sha Tsui, is the largest mosque in Hong Kong and a central hub for the Muslim community.  The mosque was originally established in 1896 to serve Muslim soldiers of the British Indian Army stationed in Kowloon. Over time, as the Muslim population grew, the mosque was rebuilt and expanded, and the present structure was completed in 1984 with the support of the local Muslim community and Islamic organizations.  The mosque can accommodate approximately 3,500–4,000 worshippers,  Offers separate prayer areas for men and women,  Hosts daily prayers, Jumu’ah, Eid prayers, and Islamic activities,  Serves as an important religious, educational, and community center.  The Mosque is surrounded by halal restaurants and easily accessible from Tsim Sha Tsui MTR.  The mosque offers comfort, spirituality, and a strong sense of belonging for Muslims from all over the world.  It is the place where history, faith, and community come together.

Rating: 5 - Hong Kong is a special place, and it can be difficult to put into words what makes it feel so special.  One of its great aspects is the pristine and varied nature on offer.  The most recent adventure was ‘suicide cliff’ at Kowloon Peak.  Now this is not a very nice name for an area, but when you get there you will see that although unpleasant, its most certainly an apt name.  Walking on mud trails, and through the fog made me feel like I was back in my home country of Wales, a real treat! It was a bit slippery and wet, but that added to the fun, and at time the grass was up to my shoulders or higher.  Of course with such great views on offer, and with the cliff dangling so close to your feet, pictures are an absolute must!  And boy did we take some pictures.  Group ones, individual ones, serious ones, funny ones, pretty much all types.   And as you’re standing above the panorama, clouds whirling around, gazing at the urban jungle below you, you really do feel a rush of exhilaration and adrenaline that makes you feel alive.  It was truly a marvel that will always be remembered.  The night time views especially are quite extraordinary.  Never seen anything like it to be honest.  Words can't describe. If you're in Hong Kong it's an absolute must

address: Kowloon Reservoir, Kam Shan, Hong Kong
reviews: Rating: 3 - This is a cluster of four small reservoirs found in the southern section of the Kam Shan Country Park north of the Kowloon Peninsula. Collectively they have a capacity of 2.9 million cubic metres of fresh water. You can visit the reservoirs and their respective dam structures while hiking and sightseeing in the country park.  Historically, the Kowloon Reservoir was constructed in 1910, making it the fourth man made lake in Hong Kong and the first in the New Territories. The Shek Lei Pui Reservoir was completed in 1925, followed by the Kowloon Reception Reservoir (1926) and Kowloon Byewash Reservoir (1931).  Interestingly, there are 5 historic structures at the Kowloon Reservoir that are Declared Monument buildings in Hong Kong. These include the Main Dam, Main Dam Valve House, Spillway Dam, Spillway Dam Recorder House and the Recorder House all of which were completed in 1910 and designated as declared monuments in Hong Kong in 2009.  It is easy to visit the Kowloon Reservoir Group. The main Kowloon Reservoir is at the start of the MacLehose Trail Section #6 and entry into the Kam Shan Country Park just north of the Tai Po Road. You will see it and the dam structures immediately upon entering the park.

reviews: Rating: 4 - "Kowloon Union Church, one of the earliest inter-denominational churches in Hong Kong, was built by the London Missionary Society with financial support from Sir Paul Chater. The foundation stone was laid on 27 May 1930 by the then Colonial Secretary, The Hon. W.T. Southorn C.M.G., and the church was officially opened on 10 April 1931 by the then Governor Sir William Peel. During the Japanese Occupation, the church ceased to function and the building was converted into a horse stable by the Japanese army and suffered severe looting and damage. The church was opened again for public worship with a rededication service held on 19 October 1947 and continues to serve the community until now.  The church possesses "Perpendicular Gothic" architectural features, with pitched Chinese-tiled roof, red load-bearing brick walls and contrasting grey granite steps and window surrounds. A semi-circular apse and an attached three-storey battlemented tower are built at the two ends of the church respectively. The double hammer-beam timber roof trusses in the sanctuary are rare in Hong Kong.  Kowloon Union Church was declared a monument on 13 October 2017 and is protected under the Antiquities and Monuments Ordinance."

Rating: 3 - In 1936, Master Baojing, the 44th patriarch of the Tiantai school of Buddhism, resided in Hong Kong, establishing a hermitage in Fanling, New Territories, for quiet practice and propagation of the Dharma. This laid a profound foundation for the Tiantai school of Buddhism in Hong Kong and established the basis for the founding of the Hong Kong Kwan Tsung Temple. Shortly after its completion, the hermitage was ravaged by war. While propagating the Dharma in Shanghai, Master Baojing contracted a serious illness and tragically passed away at the Jade Buddha Temple. In 1945, after Japan's defeat and surrender, Hong Kong was liberated. Master Jueguang, the 46th patriarch of the Tiantai school and a grandson of Master Baojing, returned to Hong Kong to continue the family tradition, raising funds to rebuild the hermitage and converting it into the Baojing Memorial Hall. Later, to meet the needs of the times, the memorial hall was expanded in 1981 and officially named the Hong Kong Kwan Tsung Temple.

Rating: 4 - Hong Kong 🇭🇰 The park was formerly the site of the Whitfield Barracks of the British Army, with a former battery (Kowloon West II Battery) in the northwestern part of the Park.  The Urban Council redeveloped the site into the Kowloon Park in 1970.[2] More than 70 buildings were demolished to make way for the park.[3] The first stage of the park was officially opened on 24 June 1970 by the then Governor of Hong Kong, Sir David Trench.[1] The opening was celebrated by a lion dance as well as a folk dance by students of the Tai Hang Tung Primary School PM Session. Music was provided by the band of the First Battalion, the Royal Welsh Fusiliers.[4] Sir David unveiled a commemorative plaque and declared Kowloon Park open.[4] The first phase comprised 18 acres out of a planned 26 acres.[3] It featured a floral clock as well as a Chinese garden set within an English landscape, which a government spokesman called "a reminder of Hongkong's cosmopolitan cultural heritage."[3]  However, part of the site was occupied in the construction of an MTR rapid transit line—originally the Kwun Tong line, now the Tsuen Wan line—from 1975 to 1978, and this was cited as a reason for the slow progress in developing the remaining three stages of the park for recreational use.[5][6] The Urban Council also placed some of the blame on the construction of Kowloon Park Drive, which cut through a corner of the park at the insistence of the government.[5]  The Government was criticised when the Executive Council approved plans in 1982 for a strip of retail premises fronting Nathan Road to be carved into the hill of Kowloon Park. The move was first proposed when the Barracks were converted into public open space in 1970, and ignited some controversy. It was opposed by the Urban Council, as well as the Muslim community, whose mosque was close by.[7] The rights for the development of the 5,410 square metre strip were sold in February 1983 to a subsidiary of New World Development for $218 million.[8] The commercial development is called "Park Lane Shopper's Boulevard". Owing to the grade change, the roofs of the shops are level with the ground of Kowloon Park, and so the gardens extend onto the building rooftops. Rating: 4 - Mo Tai Temple (武帝廟) in Hai Tan Street (海壇街) of Sham Shui Po (深水埗) was constructed before the 17th year of Guangxu (光緒, 1891) reign of the Qing (清) dynasty as a stone renovation tablet in the temple has the dating inscribed on it. The temple was established for the worship of Kwan Tai (關帝) by inhabitants of the area especially the traders of different businesses, workers of the police and forces, those with martial arts and others.  The temple is a Qing vernacular building of a two-hall-one-courtyard plan of three bays. The courtyard between the entrance and main halls has been covered. The building is constructed of green bricks with its walls and granite columns to support its pitched roofs of timber rafters. Its entrance is with a side platform on either side supported by two granite columns and a wooden bracket system with carvings. The roofs are covered with green ceramic tiles and its ridges with geometric mouldings and flowers and rocks paintings. A pair of ceramic aoyus (鰲魚) is on its ridges. A pearl is in the middle of the ridge of the entrance hall.  The name of the temple is engraved on the lintel above the entrance doorway flanked with a pair of couplets. The altar at the end wall of the main hall houses the statue of Kwan Tai in the middle with Man Cheong (文昌) to its right and Chu Lap Tai Sin (朱立大仙) to its left. Deities of Kwun Yam (觀音) and Pau Kung (包公) are on the altars of the side bays for worship.

reviews: Rating: 5 - The Guandi Temple, built in the 1970s next to Dawokou Village, contains inscriptions detailing its history. It was an important center of Chaozhou religious belief in the area. Times have changed. Now, it's not only worshipped by Chaozhou believers; locals also come to pay homage to Guandi. The Miaofa Hall on the left enshrines Guanyin Bodhisattva and the Three Jewels Buddha, as well as Ji Gong.

Rating: 5 - Tai Wo Hau Estate is located beside Tai Wo Hau Road in Tsuen Wan, New Territories, Hong Kong. Adjacent to the estate is a temple renovated in 2003. Flags flutter outside the temple, and incense burns brightly inside. It is the only Guan Yu temple in Tsuen Wan. Guan Yu was a figure from the Shu Han state during the Three Kingdoms period. His given name was Guan Yu, and his courtesy name was Yunchang. During his lifetime, he was enfeoffed as the "Marquis of Hanshou," and after his death, he was posthumously honored as "Guan Sheng Di Jun," enjoying imperial status. In Hong Kong, Guan Yu is considered a legendary deity. Whether police officers, business owners, restaurant owners, or triad members, both the legitimate and criminal worlds have shrines to Guan Yu, regarding him as a role model for loyalty and righteousness. This Guan Yu temple in Tsuen Wan is actually a temple where Guan Yu is worshipped alongside other deities. Incense smoke fills the air, and worshippers include various deities such as Zhang Laobo, Wong Tai Sin, Fu De Lao Ye (the Earth God), and Zhenzhu Niangniang.

Rating: 5 - When Han Yu, a renowned Tang Dynasty writer, was demoted to the position of prefect of Chaozhou, the area suffered severe flooding. The residents prayed to the mountain gods of these three mountains for rain to stop, and indeed, the rain ceased and the sky cleared. Han Yu then revered them as the "Gods of the Boundary Stones." Emperor Huizong of the Song Dynasty bestowed upon them the plaque "Mingkuang."  A folk legend tells of three sworn brothers who often played chess and drank wine on three mountains: Jinshan, Mingshan, and Dushan. One day, the three gathered in front of a cave on Dushan Mountain and performed magic on a dead maple tree, causing it to bloom. Villagers gathered to watch, and the three brothers then conjured a lotus flower several feet in diameter. The crowd believed the three brothers to be divine beings and immediately knelt in worship. A villager surnamed Chen said he wished to become their teacher. The three brothers smiled and then ascended into the clouds and disappeared. Not long after, a villager surnamed Chen passed away, and remarkably, he descended to the village spirit medium, claiming to have ascended to immortality. He revealed that his three brothers, Lianjie, Zhao Xuan, and Qiao Jun, were the gods of the three mountains: Jinshan, Mingshan, and Dushan. The villagers then built a temple on Jinshan to worship the gods of the three mountains and General Chen.  Also, some storytellers and legends say that Lianjie, Zhao Xuan, and Qiao Jun became sworn brothers who helped establish the Sui Dynasty. After their achievements, they retired from public life. Later, for protecting Emperor Taijun, they were all appointed Grand Generals. For protecting Prince You of Dai, they were granted the title of Duke Protector of the Nation. After the rise of the Tang Dynasty, they lived in seclusion on the three mountains. After their deaths, they manifested their divine power on the three mountains and were regarded as mountain gods. During the Northern Song Dynasty, Emperor Taizu of Song, Zhao Kuangyin, received divine assistance from three mountain gods to quell the Liu-Zhang Rebellion. He then bestowed upon them imperial edicts, ordered them to be worshipped with the highest sacrificial rites, and granted them royal titles: King of Jinshan, King of Mingshan, and King of Dushan. Emperor Taizong bestowed titles upon the three mountain gods: King of Mingshan was named King Qinghua Shengde Bao (Great King); King of Jinshan was named King Zhuzheng Mingsu Ning (Second King); and King of Dushan was named King Huiwei Hongying Feng (Third King).  Many temples enshrine King Dushan in the primary position among the three kings. There are various explanations for this. One theory is that when the imperial envoy, carrying the imperial edict and the imperial sword, traveled to Jinshan, Mingshan, and Dushan, he could not find any shrines to the mountain gods. He left the edict and sword on Dushan and committed suicide. Therefore, King Dushan possessed the greatest power among the three mountain gods and thus deserved the highest position. King Dushan is enshrined in the primary position at the Lintian Ancestral Temple and the Tainan Three Mountain Kings Temple. There are also theories that the three kings were enshrined in the main seat because they were the first to be conferred their titles.  One theory states that the King of Dushan was brave and had the most military achievements, thus he was conferred the title of "King of Dushan." Another theory says that when Emperor Bing of Song fled to Chaozhou, the three kings appeared to protect him, with the King of Dushan escorting him an extra mile, and Emperor Bing conferred the title of "King of Dushan." Yet another says that when Lu Xiufu prayed at the temple of the three kings, saying, "Heaven has ordained that barbarians cannot govern the Xia, and a casket cannot hold a pearl," the statues suddenly "swapped positions," with the statue of the King of Dushan moving to the center, representing a "reversal of cause and effect," signifying the impending demise of the Song Dynasty. From then on, most temples enshrined the King of Dushan in the main seat. Another legend states that the three kings were originally mountain bandits occupying three mountains within Chaozhou, but even thieves had their code of honor, robbing the rich to help the poor. The imperial court repeatedly sent troops to suppress them but failed each time, eventually having to persuade them to surrender and later confer upon them the title of king.  Another account states that at the end of the Song Dynasty, when the Mongols invaded the south, Emperor Bing of Song fled to the vicinity of Chaozhou. A large number of Yuan soldiers pursued and surrounded him. At the point of no return, three burly men suddenly appeared, leading countless warriors, blocking the Yuan army's advance. The soldiers believed that the Three Mountain Kings had appeared to protect Emperor Bing.  The following is a list of the Three Mountain Kings and their birthdays:  **King of Jinshan:** The eldest king, surnamed Lian, given name Jie, birthday is February 25th (lunar calendar). **King of Mingshan:** The second king, surnamed Zhao, given name Xuan, birthday is June 25th. **King of Dushan:** The third king, surnamed Qiao, given name Jun, birthday is September 25th.  The Three Mountain Kings Temple in Kwun Tong, Hong Kong, is located on Fukang Path, Pak Nai Shan, Shai Cao Wan, near Wai Fat Road. The Tin Hau Temple and Fuk Tak Ancient Temple are also located next to the temple.  The Kwun Tong Three Mountain Kings Temple existed in the 1950s and was originally located in the nearby Qiancao Wan wooden shantytown. Due to demolition, it was finally relocated and rebuilt at its current location in 1983.  Of the several Three Mountain Kings Temples in Hong Kong, only this one, with statues of the three kings, was newly built during the temple's 2006 renovation; the other Three Mountain Kings Temples each have only one.  Outside the temple is a couplet: "The temple, devoutly repaired, is magnificent and awe-inspiring, its power resounding overseas; Divine grace widely bestows blessings and longevity, its reputation spreading throughout Jiangnan."

reviews: Rating: 5 - Hung Hom Kwun Yum Temple is a quiet and spiritually meaningful temple located in the Hung Hom area of Kowloon, offering a peaceful retreat from the surrounding urban environment. Dedicated to Kwun Yum, the Goddess of Mercy, the temple is deeply respected by locals who visit to pray for compassion, protection, health, and emotional well-being. Compared to larger and more famous temples in Hong Kong, this temple feels more intimate and grounded in everyday local life.  The temple’s architecture is traditional and modest, featuring classic Chinese design elements such as red pillars, decorative roof details, and carved stone ornaments. Inside, the atmosphere is calm and reverent, filled with the soft glow of incense smoke and the quiet rhythm of worshippers offering prayers. Many visitors come alone or in small groups, creating a reflective and respectful environment that encourages slow, mindful observation.  Hung Hom Kwun Yum Temple is especially known among locals as a place to seek inner peace and guidance during difficult times. The presence of Kwun Yum symbolizes mercy and unconditional compassion, and this sense of spiritual comfort is strongly felt throughout the temple grounds. On special days of the lunar calendar and during festivals, the temple becomes livelier, yet it still maintains a sincere and humble character rather than a festive or commercial atmosphere.  The temple is well-maintained and easy to visit, making it accessible even for those who are not familiar with religious customs. Visitors are welcome to observe rituals respectfully, light incense, or simply take a moment of quiet reflection. Its location within a residential district gives it an authentic, local feel, offering insight into how spiritual practices are woven into daily life in Hong Kong.  Overall, Hung Hom Kwun Yum Temple is not just a place of worship but a gentle sanctuary of compassion and calm. It is an ideal stop for travelers interested in local culture, spiritual traditions, or those seeking a quieter, more personal temple experience away from the crowds. The temple leaves a lasting impression through its simplicity, sincerity, and sense of inner peace.

Inside, the atmosphere is calm and reverent, filled with the soft glow of incense smoke and the quiet rhythm of worshippers offering prayers. Many visitors come alone or in small groups, creating a reflective and respectful environment that encourages slow, mindful observation.  Hung Hom Kwun Yum Temple is especially known among locals as a place to seek inner peace and guidance during difficult times. The presence of Kwun Yum symbolizes mercy and unconditional compassion, and this sense of spiritual comfort is strongly felt throughout the temple grounds. On special days of the lunar calendar and during festivals, the temple becomes livelier, yet it still maintains a sincere and humble character rather than a festive or commercial atmosphere.  The temple is well-maintained and easy to visit, making it accessible even for those who are not familiar with religious customs. Visitors are welcome to observe rituals respectfully, light incense, or simply take a moment of quiet reflection. Its location within a residential district gives it an authentic, local feel, offering insight into how spiritual practices are woven into daily life in Hong Kong.  Overall, Hung Hom Kwun Yum Temple is not just a place of worship but a gentle sanctuary of compassion and calm. It is an ideal stop for travelers interested in local culture, spiritual traditions, or those seeking a quieter, more personal temple experience away from the crowds. The temple leaves a lasting impression through its simplicity, sincerity, and sense of inner peace.

Its cold, windy and hot at the same time, make sure to wear sunscreen when your here. There are also some nice gift and souvenir stall inside the statue itself. Rating: 5 - One ☝️of the key features of Lantau Island 🏝️ is the Big Buddha that sits on the very hill top of Lantau, which can be seen 👀 for many, many kilometres ♾️ away on the hiking 🥾trail.  Travel – There are many ways to travel up to the Big Buddha from Tung Chung 🗺️. The most convenient would be to take the cable car 🚠 or you can try a bus 🚎or taxi 🚕. Cable cars will have a queue, bus and taxi will take time ⏳but you can have a great view of the island as it drives up towards the top. After which, you can walk all the way up to the base of the Big Buddha. At the base level, you can walk a full circle 🔄 and take in the surrounding mountain ⛰️view.  Walking In – After all the photo taking, you can enter the inside of the Big Buddha via the base behind the main staircase. Inside, along the wall is a columbarium. Among those who are housed there, Anita Mui would be one of the most iconic Hong Kong 🇭🇰celebrities 💃. (🚫 pictures 📸) Inside, you then make your way up to the top 🔝whereby you can view the Tooth Relic of the Buddha. Along the inside walls, you will also find intricate wood 🪵carvings of the deities 🧚‍♀️ and buddha. Letters 📮from officials and construction details.  It is an impressive 😎 monument which you can only enjoy if you are fit 💪and are able to climb 🚶‍♀️the stairs to the top. So while you can do it, give it a go and with some blessings 🙏🏼, you will get good 👍weather 🌈 and clear skies 🌅 to enjoy the outing.

Rating: 5 - Traveling from TST to see the Tian Tan Buddha was a highlight of my trip.  Beyond the massive Tian Tan Buddha statue, make sure to visit the Po Lin Monastery. I was also impressed by the food variety; there are plenty of spots to eat, including great Indian options.  One big tip: The return queue for the cable car can be very long. Plan your timing carefully so you aren't stuck waiting for hours!

Rating: 5 - Tian Tan Buddha is one of Hong Kong’s most iconic landmarks and an unforgettable experience, both spiritually and visually. Located on Lantau Island, the massive bronze Buddha sits serenely atop a hill, offering breathtaking panoramic views of the surrounding mountains and sea.  Reaching the statue is part of the journey. After arriving in Ngong Ping (many visitors take the scenic cable car), you’ll climb over 200 steps to reach the base. The staircase can feel long, especially in warm weather, but the view becomes more impressive with each step. Once at the top, the scale of the Buddha is truly striking, calm, majestic, and incredibly detailed.  The atmosphere is peaceful despite the crowds. The nearby Po Lin Monastery adds to the cultural depth of the visit, with beautiful temple architecture, incense drifting through the air, and a sense of quiet reflection. It’s a place where sightseeing and spirituality blend naturally.  Whether you’re interested in history, photography, or simply soaking in panoramic views, Tian Tan Buddha is absolutely worth the trip. Try to go earlier in the day to avoid heavier crowds and to enjoy cooler temperatures during the climb.

Rating: 5 - Located on Lantau Island, this majestic bronze statue—often called the Big Buddha—stands tall at 34 meters, quietly overlooking the mountains and sea. The journey itself feels special. Climbing the 268 steps to reach the statue isn’t just physical; it feels symbolic, like you’re gradually leaving the noise of the world behind.  At the top, the view is breathtaking. Surrounded by lush greenery and open skies, the Buddha’s calm expression creates a powerful sense of peace. It’s not just a tourist attraction—it’s a spiritual landmark. The scale of the statue is impressive, but what truly stands out is the serenity you feel standing beneath it.  Right nearby is the beautiful Po Lin Monastery, where you can explore traditional temple architecture, light incense, and soak in the tranquil atmosphere. The blend of culture, history, and spirituality makes the entire visit meaningful.  Whether you’re religious or not, the Tian Tan Buddha offers something deeper—a quiet reminder to slow down, breathe, and reflect. If you’re in Hong Kong, this is absolutely a must-visit destination.

address: Lai Chi Chong, Hong Kong
reviews: Rating: 5 - To get here, there are two routes:  1) By Water: Take a ferry from Ma Liu Shiu (45-minute journey) or Wong Shek Pier (approximately 1 hour journey) to Lai Chi Chong Pier. Ma Liu Shiu has two ferry services on weekdays, at 8:30 AM and 3:00 PM, with an additional ferry at 12:30 PM on holidays. Wong Shek has two ferry services daily, on both weekdays and holidays, at 10:35 AM and 4:55 PM.  2) By Land: Take minibus route 7 (towards the sea) from the Sai Kung Pier minibus terminus and get off at Pak Sha O (approximately 30 minutes). From there, walk about 3 kilometers along the concrete path (approximately 45 minutes) to reach Lai Chi Chong.  If you are a geology enthusiast, Lai Chi Chong is a must-see. To the left of the pier is a site within the Chek Mun area of ​​the Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark, which showcases a variety of volcanic and sedimentary rocks formed approximately 146 million years ago. It was listed as a site of special scientific value in 1985.

reviews: Rating: 4 - Me and my family went for the Lake House (Le Vow) for celebrating the Chinese Lunar New Year. Not an easy place to reach if you don't have a car, so we went by Uber. It was a sunny, happy family day and this was my first time here.  There was a huge pink teddy bear bouquet outside greeting us. A great spot for taking pictures, ladies! (Many people were queuing for taking pics here 🤭)  The whole architecture of the Lake House is very grand and deluxe (I bet it will be stunning too at night when the lights put on🥰😍). As you can see from the pictures, they serve dim sum and chinese dining in here, most of the dishes tasted fantastic! (Not to mix up, beside the Le Vow, there's Billow for western fusion food😊both within the Lake House)  After lunch, we went to the backyard for family photos, it charged $20 HKD for entrance fee, but elderly aged 65 or above are free in charge.  This place was really a hidden gem in Hong Kong. Definitely worth a visit!

Rating: 5 - Finding The Lake House felt like stumbling upon a well-kept secret, a page torn from a storybook and gently placed in the midst of Hong Kong's relentless energy. This isn't just a hotel or a restaurant; it's a full-sensory experience, a deliberate step back into a more graceful, thoughtful era. Located in the unexpectedly tranquil setting of Tai Po, it offers a respite that is both profound and beautifully executed.  From the moment you approach the iconic red-brick facade, draped in lush ivy and standing proudly beside the placid waters of the Tai Po River (which, in this context, is affectionately referred to as the "lake"), you know you're somewhere special. The architecture is a loving homage to the old Tai Po Market Railway Station, and this heritage theme is woven seamlessly throughout the entire property. The check-in process, set in a room that feels more like a colonial-era study than a hotel lobby, is warm and welcoming, setting the tone for the stay.  We visited for a weekend staycation, and every detail felt curated. Our room was a masterpiece of design, blending nostalgic elements like wooden ceiling fans, four-poster beds, and classic tiled bathrooms with all the modern amenities one could need. The minibar was thoughtfully stocked with local treats, and the quality of the furnishings spoke of a property that cares deeply about comfort and authenticity. Waking up to the gentle sunlight filtering through the trees and the sound of birds rather than traffic was a luxury  Property itself is a destination. We spent hours exploring the "Art in the Lake" gallery, a series of charming red-brick buildings housing a fascinating collection of vintage posters, local art, and historical artefacts. It’s a quiet, reflective space that adds a layer of cultural depth to your visit. Walking along the riverfront promenade, watching families of ducks paddle by and seeing the local community enjoy the parkland, provides a wonderful glimpse into a slower, more residential side of Hong Kong life.  Getting There: It's surprisingly easy. The MTR to Tai Po Market Station is a direct line from Admiralty. From there, it's a pleasant 10-15 minute stroll through the Tai Po Waterfront Park, which is an lovely way to begin and end your experience. Taxis from the station are also readily available and very affordable. 2. Book in Advance: Whether for a staycation, a meal at one of their restaurants, or a weekend high tea, The Lake House is popular for a reason. Reservations are highly recommended. 3. Explore the Area: Don't just come and go. Allocate time to visit the nearby Tai Po Waterfront Park, the Hong Kong Railway Museum (which thematically complements The Lake House perfectly), and the old-town streets of Tai Po. 4. Ideal For: Couples seeking a romantic getaway, photographers looking for that perfect shot, families wanting a spacious outdoor area for kids, and any Hong Kong resident who needs a reminder of the city's diverse charm beyond the skyscrapers.  In a city that often equates luxury with glossy newness and dizzying heights, The Lake House offers a different, more soulful definition. Its luxury is in its tranquility, its character, and its deep connection to a forgotten Hong Kong. It’s a five-star experience not defined by thread count, but by the feeling of peace and wonder it instills. We left feeling not just relaxed, but genuinely enriched. I cannot recommend it highly enough.

I’d recommend going early in the day to avoid the biggest crowds and to enjoy the cool morning air. Rating: 3 - This is restored Hakka village house and declared monument in the Chai Wan area of the Hong Kong Island. Built in the mid-18th century and belonging to the Law Uk family, the property provides glimpse into the architecture and everyday life at what was once a major Hakka settlement. Now the building serves as a minor museum (free entry) for those who visit this area of the city and have interest in local history.  The grounds include the restored house which has five indoor rooms, several including displays of historic furnishing, farm equipment, ceremonial and other items from the past. There are information panels outside the museum in the small courtyard providing some history of the Hakka people, their village lives before and then during the British colonial period, customs and festive ceremonies, building architecture and details about the family who owned this particular house in the past.  There is also an annex property on the museum grounds as well, it is built in the same manner as the historic Law Uk house. It was closed when we passed by recently.  Overall, it is good that the government restores and protects historic properties and puts them to good use like what you will find with the Law Uk Folk Museum in Chai Wan. It makes for a good place to spend 20-30 minutes if you find yourself in the area. However, if you are real history buff, it is better to visit the Hong Kong Museum of History, where you will find similar displays and learning opportunity regarding the Hakka people and other Chinese ethnic groups that have roots here in Hong Kong.

Rating: 5 - Nice little museum located in Chai Wan.  Law Uk was a typical Hakka-style house in the Law Uk Village that was built at the beginning of the 18th century by the Law family. During the 1950s, Chai Wan began to develop and Law Uk Village was torn down, leaving just one house behind. In 1989, the Hong Kong Government took possession of the house and renamed it Law Uk Folk Museum.  The house contains a large living room in the center; on the right and left are rooms and mezzanines. In front of the living room are two small rooms used as the kitchen and a storage room.  Outside, there is an empty space used as a thrashing ground. Inside, It was decorated with traditional Hakka furniture and other household items.

Rating: 4 - The Tin Hau Temple located in Ma Wan Village, Lei Yue Mun was built in the 18th year of Qing Emperor Qianlong (1753 AD). The temple has once attracted large numbers of pilgrims but has been damaged several times, leaving behind an archway, a tablet, an inscription and an old clock at the scene. The temple was renovated in 1953 and 1986. Walking through the main path leading to the temple, people can see the beautiful scenery of Victoria Harbour. According to legend, Tin Hau (天后), the Heavenly Goddess, was born in the Sung Dynasty (960 - 1279 AD). Her native place was Fujian Province, and her mortal name was Lam Mak-leung (林默). Possessing supernatural power, she saved many people from disasters of the sea. Therefore, she is regarded by the seafaring folks as their Patron Saint.

Rating: 5 - Lee Cheng Uk Estate in Sham Shui Po, Kowloon, was Hong Kong's first government-run public housing estate for resettled low-rent residents. On Christmas Eve 1953, a fire broke out in the Pak Tin Tsuen shantytown and spread to the hillside of Lee Cheng Uk Estate, leaving many homeless and destitute. The government built dozens of seven-story resettlement buildings to house the affected victims, initiating a public housing program that expanded to include the grassroots. Today, more than half of the population, over three million people, are settled in the estate, with comprehensive community amenities benefiting residents' lives. During construction of Lee Cheng Uk Estate, an ancient tomb of an Eastern Han Dynasty noble was unearthed, proving that the area was already well-developed before the Common Era. The government built a museum on the site and a Han Garden next to it, designed in the style of ancient times. The garden features winding bridges, flowing water, pavilions, and long corridors, and is open to the public free of charge for rest and relaxation.
