reviews: Rating: 3 - Lik Wing Tong Study Hall (力榮堂書室) is one of the six study halls in the historic village of Shui Tau Tsuen (水頭村) of the Tang (鄧) clan in Kam Tin, Yuen Long. It was built by the descendents of Tang Lei-yuen (鄧履元) of the first branch (長房) of the clan in Kam Tin. The exact year of constriction of the study hall is not known. It was probably built before 1835 as a wooden board at the study hall has the 15th year of Daoguang reign of the Qing dynasty inscribed on it.  The study hall is at the right end of the village with six rows of village houses on its left. It is a Qing vernacular building having a two-hall-one-courtyard plan of three bays. The open courtyard is in-between the entrance and main halls. Side rooms and chambers are on either side of the halls and courtyard.  The forecourt in its front is slightly smaller than the width of the building with an entrance opened at its left end. The walls are retained with their fair-faced green bricks except the main hall with imitation brick lines. The black ridges are in boat shape with white curling pattern.
Rating: 5 - Tours are welcome. From what I read in the explanation, it seems to be a kind of school for the clan. Like this shrine, the nearby shrines seem to place an emphasis on studying.

Rating: 4 - Lik Wing Tong Study Room, also known as the Grand Study Room, is located in Shui Tau Village, Kam Tin, Yuen Long District, New Territories, Hong Kong. It was built by descendants of Tang Luk Yuen of the Kam Tin Tang clan, one of the five major clans in the New Territories, for the educational purposes of the clan's children. The study room was designated a Grade II historic building in 1994 and was further confirmed as a Grade I historic building on May 17, 2010.  Built around the Kangxi period of the Qing Dynasty, the Li Rong Tang Study is a two-courtyard, three-bay building with a recessed front. The main gate bears the couplet "Nanyang Family Legacy; Tax Bureau Family Reputation." The calligraphy on the gate is distinctive; the upper left is in standard calligraphy, while the upper right is written in reverse. The entrance leads to the front courtyard, where a screen wall bears the couplet "Exerting Human Sentiments Broadens the Horizon; Knowing Much of the World Pleasings the Mind." Between the two courtyards is a central courtyard with side rooms on either side. A moon gate on the left bears the couplet "How Convenient is it to pluck the laurel; Adorning oneself with flowers is commonplace." The main hall has a plaque inscribed "Excellent in Both Age and Virtue," written by scholar Deng Guangdou in the fifteenth year of the Daoguang reign.  Li Rong Tang originally provided education for the village clan and housing for teachers, but later lost its educational function and became a storage place for clan members' belongings. Due to long-term disrepair, the Hong Kong government funded its renovation with over HK$2 million, and it was opened to the public in September 2005.

However, it ceased to function as an educational institution around 50 years ago and is now used as a storage facility for the village.  The study was designated a Grade II historic building in 1994 and was subsequently designated a Grade I historic building on May 17, 2010.

Rating: 5 - The Lippo Centre, located in the Admiralty area of Hong Kong, stands out as one of the most iconic and visually distinctive structures in the city's skyline. Completed in 1988 and designed by American architect Paul Rudolph, this twin-tower complex is noted for its unique sculptural form and dynamic façade that set it apart from more conventional high-rise architecture.  The Lippo Centre’s exterior is characterized by its irregularly shaped “koala bear” design, a colloquial term inspired by its cantilevered blocks, which appear to cling to the building's sides. This bold geometric structure gives the building an energetic, almost organic appearance, as if it is reaching outwards rather than simply standing in place. The choice of dark reflective glass amplifies this effect, creating a play of light and reflections that shifts throughout the day and emphasizes the textured façade.  Standing at 186 meters, each of the two towers features a series of overhanging glass cuboids, breaking up the symmetry of a conventional skyscraper profile and giving the Lippo Centre a layered, almost modular look. This unique composition is both a tribute to Brutalist architecture, with its bold, expressive forms, and an innovative take on the more sleek and mirrored styles common in the 1980s. Rudolph’s vision here was deeply influenced by his study of modularity, and the Lippo Centre remains a compelling experiment in high-rise design that captures a sense of movement within the static form of a building.  Inside, the building provides a modern and flexible space for offices, equipped with large floor plans that allow for diverse layouts and excellent natural light due to the reflective glass and expansive windows. Despite the unconventional outer design, the interior spaces prioritize functionality and adaptability, meeting the demands of Hong Kong’s busy commercial environment.  The Lippo Centre’s design reflects Hong Kong’s eclectic architectural landscape—an ideal fusion of bold innovation and functional pragmatism. Its unusual form, which defies the rigidity of traditional skyscraper silhouettes, has secured it a place as a local landmark, and its resilience through changing architectural trends speaks to the vision of Paul Rudolph’s experimental approach to urban design. This structure is a symbol of Hong Kong’s progressive architecture, encapsulating the city’s balance of aesthetic daring and business-oriented practicality.

Rating: 5 - The Best Free View in Hong Kong – An Absolute Must-Do! ​If you are visiting Victoria Peak, don’t just stop at the shopping mall. You must take the walk along Lugard Road. It is, without a doubt, the highlight of any trip to Hong Kong. ​How to find it: ​Finding the start of the path is very easy. Once you exit the Peak Tram Upper Terminus (inside the Peak Tower), walk out onto the main square (Peak Piazza). With your back to the Peak Tower, turn right. The entrance to Lugard Road is located right next to the Peak Tower building and is clearly signposted as the "Peak Circle Walk." ​Why you should do it: ​Spectacular & Free: While the official observation decks charge an entry fee, this path is completely free of charge and offers even better, unobstructed panoramic views of the skyline and Victoria Harbour. ​Flat and Easy: The entire path is perfectly flat with no steep inclines or stairs. It is a paved, easy stroll that you can enjoy at a very peaceful and leisurely pace. ​60-Minute Loop: It is a beautiful 60-minute circular walk around the mountain. Lugard Road eventually turns into Harlech Road, which leads you right back to where you started at the Peak Tram station. ​Peaceful Atmosphere: It is much quieter than the crowded terrace. You walk through lush greenery and "jungle" sections before the view opens up to show the most famous skyline in the world.  ​This is an absolute must-do. Whether you are a photographer looking for the perfect shot or just want a relaxing walk with a "wow" factor, this is the place to be.

It was built in 1751 , Ching dynasty . I am so lucky that my good friend is the younger generation of the Liu's family, she lives in the Liu's Village and knows the family history very well . She took me walked around the village and told me all the history of all the 3 ancestral Halls. The hall is also newly renovated, everything is in such a good condition  and beautifully presented. It is as good as the Tang's  Ancestral Hall in Yuen Long.  Although it's surrounded by all the village houses, the road signs are rather clear, just follow the road signs or ask the locals. Rating: 4 - This is one of several heritage buildings and a Declared Monument (1985) situated in the historic area of Sheung Shui in the New Territories. It is an approximate 12-15 minute walk from the Sheung Shui MTR Station and is open from 9am to 1pm & 2pm to 5pm (Wed to Mon), closed on Tuesdays.  The Ancestral Hall is dedicated to the Liu Clan's prosperous ancestor and was originally constructed in 1751 during the Qing Dynasty. What you find is a three halls and two courtyard layout, one of the largest and finest examples of preserved and restored Lingnan architecture in Hong Kong. The Ancestral Hall has undergone several restorations since 1985 and is in very good condition, fronted by a small courtyard garden as well, it makes for a nice heritage attraction visit for anyone interested in exploring around Sheung Shui.

Rating: 5 - During the Song dynasty, the Lius lived in Fujian. In the middle of the Yuan dynasty (13th to 14th centuries), the ancestor Liu Chung-kit moved southward and settled down in this part of southern China. As the largest ancestral hall of all the Lius in Sheung Shui, the Liu Man Shek Tong Ancestral Hall celebrates a lineage that had exceptional beginnings. Many of the Liu ancestors were government officials and their learnedness is celebrated in the Liu Man Shek Tong Ancestral Hall.  The Liu Man Shek Tong Ancestral Hall was built in the 16th year of the Qianlong Reign during the Qing dynasty (1751). When the Lius have well-settled in Sheung Shui Heung for centuries, they began the construction of the Liu Man Shek Tong Ancestral Hall during the 18th century.  I could observe that the Liu Man Shek Tong Ancestral Hall is very special. There are many, many ancestral halls in the New Territories villages, and most of them come with a two-hall one-courtyard layout. The Liu Man Shek Tong Ancestral Hall is a three-court two-courtyard structure.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Lo Pan Temple in Kennedy Town is a fascinating piece of Hong Kong’s cultural and architectural heritage, dedicated to Lo Pan, the patron saint of builders and carpenters. Built in 1884, it’s one of the few temples in the city dedicated to a trade deity, making it a unique and historically significant site. The temple is known for its intricate architecture, colorful ceramic decorations, and detailed carvings that showcase traditional craftsmanship.  Unfortunately, when I visited, the temple was closed, so I wasn’t able to explore the interior or fully experience its rich history. However, even from the outside, the temple’s design and serene atmosphere were impressive. Despite being tucked away in a quiet residential area, its charm and cultural significance make it worth seeking out.  I’ll definitely plan to visit again next time when it’s open, as it seems like a peaceful retreat and a meaningful landmark for anyone interested in Hong Kong’s heritage. For those planning a visit, it might be a good idea to check the opening hours beforehand!

Rating: 3 - Lo Pan is traditional Chinese style temple located at the Ching Lin Terrace around half way between HKU and Kennedy Town Station. This is the only temple in Hong Kong dedicated to Lo Pan, the Chinese figure of builders and carpenters.  Constructed in 1884, this is a two-hall structure which follows the topography of the hillside, resulting in the front hall being a few steps lower than the rear hall. You will find an interesting exterior with side gable walls, which are unique amongst local temples in Hong Kong. The facade features impressive murals above the entrance as well as detailed plaster reliefs, which are unfortunately difficult to view as they are behind metal screens.  The interior features a rear hall with shrines, deity figures as well as more murals and plaster reliefs which you will see just above the doors to the right and left. Here you can view ceramic figurines up close. Do note that the interior is kept rather dimly lit so photography can be a bit of a challenge when little natural light is entering the temple from the front entrance.  In the end, Lo Pan is an interesting temple and something worth seeing if you are in the area around HKU and making your way to Kennedy Town. It is quite an uphill trek if starting from Kennedy Town and there is little else to see in the area for tourists. As such, unless you are in HK and actively seeking out temple visits, you may want to concentrate your efforts on temples nearby other sightseeing stops you have planned around the city.

reviews: Rating: 4 - This is a new heritage attraction which opened earlier this year in Fanling, making use of the reburbished 1950's era market building along Luen Wo Hui street in Fanling. Opening hours are 8am to 9pm daily and entry is free to the public.  Historically, this was an important food market building to foster food trade and basic commercial activity for the area residents, which was much needed during the immediate post WWII era after mass immigration from mainland saw population in this area swell. It was the largest market in the New Territories at that time and served the community for just over 50 years before closing down in 2002.  Now the old Luen Wo Market has been restored and revitalised into a local heritage attraction where you can visit and explore indoor and outdoor areas of the old market building. Within there are three main buildings, the centre is where you find stalls with local small businesses selling local foods, candies and other items. There is a small coffee kiosk here called Let It Be as well.  The left side building hosts a neat little restaurant called Wake Up Bistro selling affordable all day 'western' style breakfast dishes and coffee drinks. The right side building acts as a museum with displays and audio (barcodes) revealing much about the history of the Luen Wo Market and some neat facts about its purpose to the local community over the years.  Overall, this is a nice heritage preservation endeavour and something well worth making time to see if visiting Fanling. It is a very good add-on if you plan to see the nearby attractions that make up the Lung Yeuk Tau Heritage Trail.

Rating: 4 - Luen Wo Market was built in 1951 and is conserved, revitalised and reopened in 2024. We went there on a beautiful Saturday and it's now partially open. Less than half of the mini-stores are in operation though. Good thing is, about one third of the premises is rented by a canteen offering HK style meals. At around 5pm, this eatery was 70% full, and I believe I'll try it out myself next time when I come over. Btw, the renovated place is fully airconed and offers clean restrooms, albeit a bit small in size.

Rating: 5 - I came across this building by accident and what a treat. Such a beautiful and sensitive renovation job. It's a lovely space and I'm so glad it's been given a new lease of life.  There's a small but beautifully designed exhibition that tells the story of the market in a very visual way.  Within the building there are some market stalls and a very nice (and very clean), cafe/restaurant. The toilets are also very well designed and in-keeping with the art deco aesthetic.  Utterly beautiful and I hope the locals appreciate how good it is.

reviews: Rating: 5 - 🌊 My First Hike: Discovering the Hidden Gem of Sai Kung  I finally did it — my very first hike! Sai Kung was quite a distance from the city, but something about this place kept calling me. The journey was long and rough, but every step felt worth it once I reached Long Ke Wan Beach.  Tucked away between rolling green hills, this beach felt like a secret paradise. The moment I saw its white sand shimmering under the sun and the crystal-clear blue water, my tiredness disappeared. The waves were calm, the breeze was cool, and for the first time in a long while, my mind felt completely at peace.  It was also my first time seeing such a quiet, hidden campsite — simple, natural, and breathtaking. I stood there thinking how amazing it felt to be surrounded by nothing but the sound of waves and the scent of the sea.  The hike wasn’t easy, especially for a beginner like me. There were steep paths and rocky trails, but I kept going. And when I finally reached the beach, I felt proud — not just of finishing the hike, but of doing it alone.  It’s a moment I’ll never forget. Sometimes, the best adventures are the ones we take by ourselves — because that’s when we truly hear our own heart.  I may have gone alone, but I came back happy, fulfilled, and deeply connected to nature. Sai Kung, you’ve stolen a piece of my soul🤎🤎🤎

Rating: 5 - Long Ke Wan is hands down one of the most beautiful beaches in Hong Kong. The white sand, crystal-clear water, and peaceful surroundings make it feel like a hidden paradise. If you enjoy hiking, the trail from the MacLehose Trail is scenic and offers some amazing views along the way. If you’re short on time or prefer a more relaxed trip, hiring a speedboat from Sai Kung Pier is a good option.  There aren’t any shops or facilities on the beach, so it’s important to bring your own food, water, and any essentials you’ll need. The lack of commercialisation is what makes it so special. It’s completely unspoiled and incredibly peaceful.  If you love camping, this is an amazing place to stay overnight. The quiet surroundings and starlit sky make for an unforgettable experience.  Overall, Long Ke Wan is a must-visit for nature lovers, beachgoers, and anyone looking for a quiet, beautiful escape from city life. Just be prepared for the journey, and you’ll be rewarded with one of the most stunning beaches in Hong Kong!

Rating: 4 - The wetlands of Long Valley in Sheung Shui have finally opened to the public as a site of ecological tourism since November 2024. Wedged between the Sheung Yue River and Shek Sheung River in Sheung Shui, Long Valley had long been the freshwater marsh that gives home to water crops and many species of birds.  Due to its character as a wetland, Long Valley features quite a number of wet crops. Water chestnuts, arrowhead, rice, lotus, water lilies —all kinds of crops are grown in the soaked fields at Long Valley. The clumps of reeds add a touch of wholesomeness. There are also dry fields for regular crops, particularly green vegetables. I saw peanuts, Indian spinach, Indian lettuce, eggplants and more, including flowers. Finally, the fishponds are the “fields of choice” for the birds, as they seek food and rest there.  In my opinion, the Long Valley Nature Centre, which lies across the Long Valley Nature Park, over Sheung Yue River in Ho Sheung Heung Village, is not worth a visit. The exhibition is simply too small to be anything instructive. The public toilets are there, however, so that might be the only worthwhile reason to look there. There is a short video on site introducing the Long Valley Nature Park.  Although the signs on site suggest that there is an opening hour for the Long Valley Nature Park, the park area itself, namely the freshwater marsh fields, are actually open all day. Those visitor hours indicate the opening and closing hours for the Long Valley Nature Centre, or perhaps the parking facility as well.

There is the Biodiversity Zone in the eastern area.  Naturally waterways and wetlands are replaced by artificial waterways and ponds. Not as much birds as before were spotted. reviews: Rating: 5 - Tasting Menu for Two – $640  The Negitoro Tartare came mixed with chopped scallions, shredded egg, and ikura, giving it a nice mix of textures and layers of flavor. The tuna was fresh with no fishy taste, and the texture was really smooth — light and not greasy at all.  They also served it with crispy seaweed sheets so you could wrap your own bites. It felt a bit like eating mini hand rolls, which added a fun, interactive element. The seaweed added a nice crunch and worked really well with the tuna and ikura.  The Beef Tenderloin Chunks were presented in a glass jar, and as soon as you opened it, there was a gentle smoky aroma from the apple wood — not too strong, just a light, slightly sweet smokiness that was really pleasant. The beef was seared just right — a little crispy on the outside, juicy and tender inside. On top, there were some crispy garlic bits, which gave a nice crunch. The garlic flavor was subtle and didn’t overpower the beef or the smoke, just added a light touch that actually brought everything together.  The Japanese Seafood Paella was generous with the ingredients — razor clams, clams, Argentine red prawns, and halibut. Everything was fresh with no unpleasant smell. The prawns were firm and springy, while the clams and razor clams had a nice bite and weren’t overcooked.  The standout was definitely the grilled halibut. It was slightly charred for a bit of crispiness on the outside, but the inside was silky smooth. The fat from the fish was rich, almost like butter, and when eaten with the rice, it practically melted in your mouth. Really satisfying.  They also served a seafood and mushroom sauce on the side, and I’d strongly recommend pouring the whole thing over the rice. It took the flavor to another level — instantly more umami and intense, but still well-balanced and not overly salty. The rice soaked up all the goodness.

reviews: Rating: 4 - This is a new heritage attraction which opened earlier this year in Fanling, making use of the reburbished 1950's era market building along Luen Wo Hui street in Fanling. Opening hours are 8am to 9pm daily and entry is free to the public.  Historically, this was an important food market building to foster food trade and basic commercial activity for the area residents, which was much needed during the immediate post WWII era after mass immigration from mainland saw population in this area swell. It was the largest market in the New Territories at that time and served the community for just over 50 years before closing down in 2002.  Now the old Luen Wo Market has been restored and revitalised into a local heritage attraction where you can visit and explore indoor and outdoor areas of the old market building. Within there are three main buildings, the centre is where you find stalls with local small businesses selling local foods, candies and other items. There is a small coffee kiosk here called Let It Be as well. Rating: 5 - Quoting the original text: Founded in 1962.  Liuhe Xuangong is a branch of Liuhe Shengshi and is a government-registered temple. Both Liuhe Xuangong and Liuhe Shengshi belong to the same charitable organization, originating from the Guangzhou Xinshantan. Xinshantan first moved from Guangzhou to Macau, establishing its second branch. In 1962, several like-minded individuals, including Mr. Liang Peida, Mr. He Pei, Mr. Huo Minqiang, Mr. He Tuohuan, Mr. Huo Waicong, and Mr. Feng Qian, founded Liuhe Shengshi on Connaught Road West, Hong Kong Island. Two years later, they also founded Liuhe Xuangong on Lantau Island, providing another place of meditation for believers.  Liuhe Xuangong belongs to the Quanzhen School of Taoism, with the guiding principles of "respecting the Tao and upholding virtue, propagating Taoism, honoring deities, and helping the spirits of the dead." The temple enshrines the Three Pure Ones, Lü Zu, Donghua Dijun, and Fang Xiaode Zhenjun, with the annual birthday of Lü Zu being its main celebration.  Before 1981, Liuhe Xuangong held spirit writing activities, but these have been discontinued for many years due to the long distance and inconvenient transportation.  Liuhe Xuangong, along with Liuhe Shengshi and the Macau Xinshan branch altar, has maintained contact with Taoist temples in Beijing, Qingdao, and Huizhou in 1986 and 1989 respectively, to learn about the local Taoist culture.

reviews: Rating: 5 - We really enjoyed the Morning Trail to Victoria Peak. Getting there was super convenient—we just took a cab to the start point. The hike itself offers a good balance; it starts with a solid uphill climb that gives you a good workout, but there are flat sections nearer the top where you can catch your breath and enjoy the views. We spent about 3 hours in total. The highlight was definitely reaching the top and relaxing with an ice cream at the Peak Galleria before making the descent back down the same path. It's a much more active and rewarding alternative to taking the tram!

Rating: 5 - One of the best routes to ascend to the top of The Peak in Hong Kong. Showcasing some gorgeous views across the harbour on the way up the climb really is worth it. Best go early before it gets too hot as, whilst the ascent is well paved and maintained, the humidity and heat in the peak hours of sunlight make the journey much more challenging! Plenty of public loos along the route and rest stops too. Take the longer circuit once you reach the choice at the top. The rewards are well worth the extra few minutes! Taxis and buses will get you up to the starting point of the trail but the popular route starts off in town by taking the central/ mid town escalators up through the city and making your way up from there. It is much more fun!

reviews: Rating: 3 - The Lung Yeuk Tau Heritage Trail near Fanling is one of two self-guided walks you can find in the New Territories along with the Ping Shan Heritage Trail at Yuen Long. This trail is 2.6 km and winds through the the area of Lung Yeuk Tau which was settled by the Tang Clan from the Jiangxi Province in the late 13th century. It includes 12 heritage sites including a church, temple, ancestral hall and numerous walled village entrance towers, some of which are Declared Monuments of Hong Kong.  Of the heritage attractions along the Lung Yeuk Trau trail, the Lo Wai (stop 4) and San Wai (stop 11) walled villages are very impressive. Both have restored and preserved walls that remain intact and make for nice photography. Other notable attractions along the way include the historic Tin Hau Temple (stop 5) and the Tang Chung Ling Ancestral Hall (stop 6), both which you can enter to explore. Most do the trail from south to north.  Note: At the Tang Chung Ling Ancestral Hall, you will find a gallery area in the third hall that serves as a default Visitor Centre for the Trail. Within the three bays in this rear hall, there are panels setup for each of the 12 attractions along the trail, providing a historical account and other details for each. This is helpful to read up on and I recommend taking pictures of the respective panels as well as some of the attractions along the trail lack information signs. You can refer back to what you saw here to help understand what you are looking at.  Note: Quite a few of the stops along the trail are simply entrance gates and towers to the old walled villages. In order to avoid disturbing the residents, the villages themselves are not open to enter and explore. Just view the monument entrances and remaining village walls before continuing on your way to the next stop along the trail.  Note: Unfortunately the Lung Yeuk Heritage Trail is poorly signed and challenging to navigate without the use of maps. As such, best to download the trail map from the Antiquities and Monuments Leisure Office & Cultural Services Department website before setting off to begin this trail. The website trail pages are also a good resource for familiarising yourself a bit with the 12 different attractions ahead of time.  I also recommend using the Hiking Trail HK mobile app which includes the trail or Google Maps at the same time to help navigate specific small streets and alleys you will have to walk between some of attractions. Note that you can also pick up printed brochure material for the trail at the Hong Kong Discovery Centre in Kowloon Park.  Note: To access the Yung Yeuk Heritage Trail, you can actually walk from the Fanling MTR Station something I prefer to do during cooler months of the year. However, on hot days, you may prefer to save your time and energy and take public transportation to the starting point. In this regard, there is light green mini-bus service from the Fanling MTR Station (route 54K) that drops off just near the Tsung Kyam Church (stop 1) at the beginning of the trail if you are starting in the south. At the north end of the trail there is a similar service (route 56K) from Siu Hang Tsuen (stop 12) that can take return you to the Station.

Rating: 5 - I had a great time at the M+ cinema. I was there for an arts program, but it would be a good environment to watch all kinds of movies, including a blockbuster. This place is a little hard to find, but once you're there, it's worth it. Highly recommended for fans of art cinema, or movies in general.

You can also grab some snacks in between from either the cafes at M+ or the food trucks around 3 minute walk from M+. There are also restaurants at M+ to satiate your hunger.  I find the gift shops interesting as well. Don’t miss it, take time to browse through the uniquely curated books, cards, bags, albums, games, toys, and interesting knick knacks.  The most underwhelming display for me is the basement. That space could be better utilised with more interesting exhibits.  There is the pier right across M+ where you can take a ferry ride across to Central. This is a good way to take in the beautiful view of the harbour.

Rating: 5 - The architecture of the museum and the rooftop garden and its view alone make M+ worth the visit!  The art collection is stunning!  The Robert Rauschenberg and Zao Wou Ki exhibitions were serious highlights. We feel fortunate to have had the exposure to the Asian arts this museum provided.  A true must do for any trip to Hong Kong.  Highly recommended!

Rating: 5 - Beautiful museum by Herzog & de Meuron. Contempory exhibitions and nice restaurants. Promenade park with food trucks. Incredible sunset views on the skyline of Hong Kong Island from the rooftop terrace. Great rooftop terrace with opportunities to play, rest and enjoy the scenery, well executed planting plan. Worth a visit from noon to dusk.

Rating: 5 - This is a standout arts destination and really worth a visit if you’re into modern and contemporary art. The displays are engaging and often thought provoking, and there’s a good mix of local, regional, and international artists, which gives a broad perspective on contemporary creativity. The museum spaces are spacious and well organized, making it easy to explore at your own pace.

reviews: Rating: 5 - This is the highest peak in the Ma On Shan Country Park at 702 metres above sea level, overlooking the town of Ma On Shan and Tolo Harbour. It is one of the most dramatic peaks in Hong Kong as well as a challenging and rewarding hike.  You can approach Ma On Shan Peak most conveniently from the MacLehose Stage 4 trailhead along Sai Sha Road. Other popular routes start from Sai Kung, coming up along Ngong Ping and/or Pyramid Hill or be starting in the southwest, taking in the hunchbacks, a delightful ridge line and smaller series of peaks before approaching Ma On Shan peak.  The trails in Ma On Shan Country Park are easy to follow and you'll find plenty of other hikers making the trek. Much of the trail is exposed so be ready with hat and plenty of sunscreen if sunny. Bring sufficient water and snacks as well as there are no facilities after you leave the starting points.  Note: A really nice route is to take in the earlier mentioned Hunchbacks before or after hiking up Ma On Shan Peak. The views from each smaller peak is very impressive and the trail is fun to hike, lots of good and varied vegetation along the way and plenty of stops to take in the surrounding views in all directions.

reviews: Rating: 4 - The Ma On Shan Country Park includes a good network of trails of various distance and difficulty. One that is particularly interesting is the Ma On Shan Country Trail which weaves through the mountain range, linking Ma On Shan directly to the seaside village of Sai Kung.  This is a point-to-point trail, easier to start in Ma On Shan and finish in Sai Kung. The trail officially starts around 2.5 km away from the nearest MTR Stations (Ma On Shan and Heng On) to the Ma On Shan Country Park where the rural trail begins. From here, the official trail is 3.9 km in length with a moderate difficulty.  Most hikers take a taxi from the MTR stations or Ma On Shan town centre up to the Country Park before starting their hike. Otherwise, you can walk up the single lane road with few vehicles. Not much to see but its a fair bit of exercise going up the slow and steady inclined road if you want a longer overall hike.  The trail is nicely kept, lots of slow upward stone staircases that wind through the countryside, along streams and eventually reaching a grassland plateau, from which you will see excellent landscape and panoramic views of the Sai Kung village, coast and outlying islands. When sky conditions are favourable, this is a beautiful spot. Even with poor visibility, looking down to the village and sea is still really nice. From here, there are also nice views of the saddle shaped peak which you can also climb from this location if interested.  The walk from here towards Sai Kung is steeper so be ready to rest from time to time if you take the trail in reverse, starting in Sai Kung and ending in Ma On Shan. You eventually arrive at the upper village of Tai Shui Tseng, before winding your way down the streets towards Sai Kung village.  From Sai Kung you can grab lunch or drink at many of the restaurants scattered around the city. Sai Kung is well serviced by taxis and buses as well. So you can make your way back after the hike.

Rating: 5 - Article updated on 2024-02-09  Section 6 (M115-M124): Tai Po Road to Shing Mun - 4.6 km x 1.5 hours  Section 6 is the shortest and easiest route on the MacLehose Trail, perfect for families. This route is 4.6 km long and takes approximately 1.5 to 2 hours.  Section 6 can be considered a reservoir tour. The first part passes Kowloon Reservoir, the middle part is not far from Shek Lei Pui Reservoir, and the end is Shing Mun Reservoir. In terms of scenery, besides the reservoir views, there are also forest views. The trees along the route are mainly planted and well-maintained, with minimal vine and shrub obstructing the view, making the scenery quite open. Alternatively, starting from Tai Po Road, the road is vehicular from Section 6 to M121, then it goes up steps onto dirt roads. On the dirt roads, you can see a wide range of urban scenery in Tsuen Wan and Kwai Chung. The scenery is rather cluttered and may not appeal to those who love natural landscapes.

Rating: 3 - CAREFUL! Do not go unless you are experienced, the weather is good and there is a lot of sunshine hours left, and you have the right shoes and food/water. The hike is not as easy as it seemed!  We were staying in Tai O and were looking for daytime excursions and saw this one on Google Maps. We decided to walk from town up to Man Cheung Po campsite, and then reach the infinity pool by coming down from above. For this reason we did not see the warning signs that you would see if you were to reach this site from below. We did not know that this zone was closed off with a barrier (which you can go around by climbing, but clearly it’s preventing access given the accidents in the past). From the Man Cheung Po campsite, it’s a steep descent going down rocks, doable with good shoes and experience, but definitely not if you have a fear of heights as sometimes you would be next to a cliff.  There was no one else doing the route as we went during a quiet weekday in November, because of this it was difficult to know if we were on the right path or not, and where the path continued. Sometimes it was on the left and sometimes on the right of the stream. Google maps is not accurate so if you do go, we recommend to follow the maps from maps.me. From the infinity pool down the shore, the path is much easier but clearly abandoned.  In general if we were to do the path again from Man Cheung Po campsite, we would have approached it very differently. I recommend going in with the right expectations, very good shoes for climbing and descending rocks, and using maps.me to follow the right path, not google. Just know that access and swimming is prevented and there are cameras watching the infinity pool.  Also be careful as the rain prediction is not always accurate for Lantau and a cloudy day can turn to rain very quickly. In these situations, it’s very dangerous in this area for flooding.  The place is beautiful! but as we were uncertain about the path ahead given how abandoned it looked, and it started raining despite there being no rain forecast, we barely stayed longer than a few minutes to make sure we were able to get back before the sun went down. Overall the full loop from Tai O, to the campsite, down the stream, down to shore, and back to Tai O took around 5 hours.

And -follow- the ribbons which will lead to the pool. The part down/after the pool is quite overgrown, more than shown in the pictures (careful steps).

Rating: 5 - Man Mo Temple is a truly beautiful and serene place tucked away in the heart of Hong Kong. From the moment you step inside, you’re greeted with a calm and peaceful atmosphere that feels like a welcome escape from the busy city outside. The temple is very well maintained, clean, and thoughtfully preserved, which makes the entire experience even more pleasant.  The traditional architecture, intricate details, and hanging incense coils create a spiritual and tranquil vibe that allows you to slow down and really take in the surroundings. Despite being a popular spot for visitors, it never felt overcrowded or rushed, and there was a strong sense of respect and quiet throughout the temple.  It’s a wonderful place to pause, reflect, and appreciate Hong Kong’s cultural and spiritual heritage. Whether you’re visiting for prayer, cultural interest, or simply to experience a moment of peace, Man Mo Temple is definitely worth a visit. A calm, grounding, and memorable experience overall.

Rating: 4 - A Spiritual Oasis Right Off the Bus – A Must on the Red Route  ​If you are riding the Hop-on Hop-off bus (specifically the Red Route), the stop at Hollywood Road is arguably the most convenient cultural detour on the entire loop. The Man Mo Temple is located literally steps away from where the bus drops you off, making it the perfect place to "hop off" without worrying about navigating steep hills or getting lost in the winding streets. ​What makes this spot so special is the immediate contrast. One moment you are surrounded by the roar of traffic and towering skyscrapers; the next, you step over the high wooden threshold into a different world. The interior is dark, mystical, and surprisingly quiet. The city noise seems to bounce off the thick walls, replaced by a hushed, reverent silence. ​The atmosphere feels incredibly authentic. The ceiling is dominated by hundreds of large, spiral incense coils that burn for weeks, creating a hazy, cinematic lighting. It is also clearly a living site of worship—you will see many locals praying and making offerings, so it doesn't feel like a staged tourist trap. ​So, why 4 stars instead of 5? The temple is quite intimate and small. You can essentially see the entire complex in about 15 to 20 minutes, so it is a brief stop rather than a long excursion. Also, the incense smoke can be quite intense; if you have sensitive eyes or asthma, you might find the air a bit heavy after a few minutes inside. ​Verdict: A beautiful, soulful pause in a busy day. It is the ideal spot to catch your breath and soak in some culture before hopping back on the bus to rejoin the chaos of Central.

The memorial is one of two dedicated to early reservoirs built in Hong Kong to supply fresh water to residences before WWII.  What you find here is a memorial stone from the government of Hong Kong with a brief historical record of the establishment of the Shing Mun Reservoir in 1937. Rating: 4 - The largest WWII British war preparations and remains in Hong Kong, with actual attack by the Japanese troops happened in December 1941.  Mostly in intact, thanks to the clean up by some volunteers, and quite a section of these tunnels and trenches are walkable, best with a headlight or torch.  Interesting to find the tunnels are named after some famous shopping streets in London, and if one reads carefully from the information boards around one can easily figure out the approximation of the war event at that time, though the vegetation cover has been increased a lot, blurring the picture or viewing angle of those time.

Rating: 4 - Commenced in 1923, the construction of Shing Mun Reservoir took 14 years to complete. The massive scale of the project meant that water could be supplied to cater to the needs of the residents of Kowloon Peninsula, but also to relieve the pressure on demand on densely populated Hong Kong Island via the cross-harbour mains, and this made it the largest reservoir of the pre-war period to provide water for both sides of the harbour.  The memorial stones at Shing Mun Reservoir and Tai Tam Tuk Reservoir are the only two memorial stones that were erected to mark the completion of the two largest reservoirs in the New Territories and on Hong Kong Island respectively built before the Second World War. reviews: Rating: 5 - After watching a brief introduction to sights in Hong Kong, decided why no go actually take a look. As Mirror pool and Brides pool were just a short bus ride away, it seemed like a great chance to go look.  I headed put at 3ish, arrived at 3:30 and spent the next few hours enjoying the nature walk. It was great seeing the different sights and the fresh air.  Funny though that the hiking rating is considered easy, for all including elderly and children. I think they are think of very active elderly and very obedient children as the path even for me was quite a steep walk. Maybe just stick around the BBQ area if you decide to bring Grandma and the kids.

Rating: 5 - The Mirror’s Pool, with a 35 meters waterfall, is located in Shuen Wan Country Park. It is easily accessible (Difficulty 1/5), around 10mins from the main road, Bride’s Pool Road parking lot/gazebo. The walk was quite enjoyable, it’s mostly paved with mild ascend/descend through the woods. You’ll descend from the main road through some picnic/BBQ areas. Then pass by 2 bridges, if I remember correctly, until you reach a split end with a sign: ⬅️ to Bride’s Pool; ⬆️ to Mirror’s Pool. Take the right and continue. You’ll hear the waterfall as you get closer until it’s in your sight. Look below for the Mirror’s Pool. You can walk your way back to the main road or take the other direction and continue to the Bride’s Pool, which will take another 8-10 mins to reach.

Rating: 4 - The Mirror Pool Waterfall (照鏡潭) is a beautiful place to find while exploring the Bride's Pool nature area in the Plover Cove Country Park. This is one of Hong Kong's most attractive waterfalls found in a purely natural setting.  It is found at the end of a splinter trail that branches off the Bride's Pool Nature Trail just next to a historic bridge that crosses a lovely stream along the trail. After a few minutes walk, you'll find this a nearly 35 metre tall falls and a beautiful pool found in a ravine just below.  There are large boulders you can climb down to reach the falls from the end of the trail. During a recent visit we found a few turtles as well as a couple of Hong Kong Warty Newts in the pool as well. That made for a nice addition to seeing and taking pictures of the Mirror Pool Waterfall.  Note: The waterfalls are very popular for locals to visit during the warmer months of the year and on weekends. If you want unobscured photos, best to visit early in the morning before the day visitors begin to arrive.  Note: To visit the Bride's Pool and Nature Trail area you can take green mini-bus 20R or double-decker bus 275R (Sundays and public holidays) from the Tai Po Market Station. Both make drop offs at the Bride's Pool BBQ Site where the trail starts down to the falls nature area. Otherwise, you can also take mini-bus 20C which drops off in Tai Mei Tuk. From there you can hike up the reservoir up to Bride's Pool or take a short taxi ride.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Miu Fat (Miaohoji) Temple consists of two distinct and contrasting buildings. Standing in front of the temple gate, you will see the three-story Hall of Ten Thousand Buddhas: two giant golden dragons hovering on the gorgeous red exterior wall, as well as a pair of stone elephants and a pair of lions guarding the entrance. When you step into the Mahavira Hall inside, you will see three huge golden Buddha statues of Sakyamuni and countless Buddha statues decorated on the walls. The 21st-century Myohoji complex sits nearby, constructed of glass and concrete in stark contrast to the traditional Buddhist shrine next door. At the top of the building is a magnificent glass hall, shaped like a crystal lotus, which offers a panoramic view of Tuen Mun. Miu Fat Temple is a Buddhist monastery located in Lam Tei, Tuen Mun District, Hong Kong. Based on the principle of practising mercy, it has been actively organizing activities to promote Buddhism as well as education, culture, charity and welfare for years. The Miu Fat Buddhist Monastery was first constructed in 1950. Over the following two decades came the construction of the 3-storey Ten Thousand Buddhas Hall. It took six years to complete, with its consecration ceremony held in May 1980. A ceremony marking the completion of the 45-metre high and 7-storey main complex was held in mid-March 2010. The Mahavira Hall, located on the top storey of the Ten Thousand Buddhas Hall, has a floor height of about 20 metres. In the middle of the Hall, there are three gold-plated statues of the Buddha Sakyamuni, each of them is about 5-metre tall. Its interior walls are adorned with over 10 thousands of Buddha reliefs and a number of murals featuring a blend of Sino-Thai cultures. The monastery can be accessed via the LRT through Lam Tei stop. Three bus routes also serve the monastery that being Routes 53, 63X and 68A.

Rating: 4 - The Miu Fat Buddhist Monastery is located just north of Lam Tei Village in the Tuen Mun District. It is off Castle Peak Road and accessible by Light Rail (610, 614, 615 and 751) which stop at Lam Tei Village. What you find here are two main halls, one traditional and one modern.  There is a much taller, seven-storey concrete and glass building of modern architecture that is dominates the skyline. It was built in 1999 and is younger than the three-story tall Ten Thousand Buddha Hall with the deep red coloured and flamboyantly decorated facade featuring two elegant dragons coiling around two tall pillars. The building is fronted by guardian lions, stone elephants, tall incense burner as well as grotto and garden area.  This more traditional Buddhist monastery has a delightful interior as well. As you enter, make your way up the staircase to the third floor to the Mahavira Hall, which is ornately decorated with traditional shrine with three giant Buddha statues, walls covered with thousands of images of Buddha. You'll also see a giant hanging drum, bell as well 20-metre tall ceiling beautifully painted with mural scenes.

Rating: 4 - Interesting mix of old and new. The new temple is impressive in its own way, interesting architecture but pales alongside the existing old style temple. If the new temple was a standalone place it would be more impressive. The old temple is very impressive. Traditional style, impressive painted ceilings, lots of statues. Shame pictures of the inside aren't allowed but the place is well worth a visit.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Why do tourists actually want to visit this place? To feel something when they see the grungy looking, stacked-boxes-like density of the apartments? Sure, it does feel a bit claustrophobic when you look up and see just a rectangle of the sky. The buildings will seem like they close in above you.  But some reviews here go further and even write that they love the atmosphere but would they actually choose to live here themselves day in and day out? I observed many tourists spend only about 5 mins here; they quickly took pictures of themselves in wacky poses and left. It was like watching someone doing the busywork of ticking an unpalatable item off their to-do list. I guess some tourists will pose in front of a trash can too if someone told them it was a famous landmark.  Moreover, the building's residents must be really patient people to put up with the constant stream of tourists taking photos of the exteriors of their homes. I read that they are forced to keep their curtains closed at all times. 5 stars because I have nothing against the building nor its residents. But if you are short of time as a tourist in Hong Kong, you should give this location a very low priority.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Montane Mansion, also known as Monster Building, is one of Hong Kong’s most iconic urban landmarks—a place where architecture, density, and everyday life collide in the most cinematic way. Located in Quarry Bay, this massive residential complex is made up of five interconnected buildings that form a towering courtyard, creating a dramatic wall of pastel-colored apartments stacked endlessly upward.  What makes Montane Mansion so captivating is its raw authenticity. This is not a polished tourist attraction, but a real living space where thousands of residents go about their daily routines. Laundry hangs from windows, air conditioners hum constantly, and the narrow courtyard amplifies every sound, giving you a true sense of Hong Kong’s famously dense living environment. Standing in the middle and looking up, you feel both amazed and slightly overwhelmed—an unforgettable perspective on vertical city life.  Visually, the place is striking. The symmetry of windows, the aged textures of concrete, and the subtle color variations make it a favorite spot for photographers, filmmakers, and architecture lovers. Many scenes from movies and music videos have been filmed here, adding to its cult status. Even without a camera, simply observing the details—the balconies, window grilles, and signs of everyday life—feels like stepping into a living documentary.  That said, visitors should be respectful. This is a private residential area, and photography is best kept quick and discreet. Avoid blocking walkways or disturbing residents, and always be mindful of your surroundings.  Montane Mansion is more than just an Instagram spot. It represents the reality, resilience, and character of Hong Kong—beautiful, chaotic, and deeply human. If you want to understand the city beyond shopping malls and skylines, this place is a must-see.

Rating: 4 - Visiting Montane Mansion in Hong Kong was such a cool experience. I’d seen photos online before, but seeing it in person was something else. It’s this massive residential complex in Quarry Bay, with buildings stacked so close together it almost feels unreal. Getting there was super easy. I took the MTR to Tai Koo Station and walked about 10 minutes to reach it.  The place is really popular for photography, and it’s easy to see why. The way the buildings rise up around the narrow courtyard makes every angle look amazing. It’s also been used as a filming location for a bunch of movies, including Transformers, Age of Extinction, which is pretty awesome.  If you love taking photos or just want to see one of Hong Kong’s most unique spots, Montane Mansion is definitely worth a visit. Just remember people actually live there, so be respectful while exploring.

Rating: 4 - The Denglong Island Lighthouse, also known as the Kap Sing Lighthouse, was opened in 1912. The lighthouse is 11.8 metres tall, constructed from a cast steel frame with a white painted top. The steel frame and lighting equipment were both made in England. In the past, the lighthouse keeper lived in a brick building next to the lighthouse, which contained a bedroom, a kitchen, a toilet and a storage room. As there was no well water or drinking water supply on the island, rainwater was collected from the roof and then channeled into underground storage tanks for backup. Since the early 20th century, the Denglong Island Lighthouse has been providing navigation for countless ships entering Hong Kong from the west. The lighthouse is now managed by the Marine Department and is now automatically operated, eliminating the need for staff to be stationed there. (By AMO)

Rating: 3 - 燈籠洲燈塔位於香港島以西、馬灣以南的小島燈籠洲（原稱汲星燈塔），是香港現存其中一座戰前燈塔。  香港商貿發達，早在一八四一年前已是一個商港，一八六九年蘇彝士運河啟用後，香港的商業活動更趨頻繁。當時政府和商界人士均認為需要在港口沿岸設置輔航照明設施。  燈籠洲燈塔亦稱為汲星燈塔，於一九一二年啟用。該座燈塔高十一點八米、由鋼鑄骨架建成，塔頂髹上白色。鋼架及照明儀器均為英國製造。以往的燈塔管理員居於燈塔旁的磚構建築，內設睡房、廚房、廁所及儲物室各一。由於島上並沒有井水或食水供應，因此只能從屋頂收集雨水，再將雨水引入地下儲水箱備用。自二十世紀初以來，燈籠洲燈塔一直為無數由西面進入香港的船隻導航。燈塔現時由海事處管理，已改為自動操作，毋須派員駐守。  燈籠洲燈塔於二〇〇〇年列為古蹟。

reviews: Rating: 5 - Mount Austin Playground is a delightful Victorian-style garden perched along Mount Austin Road on Victoria Peak, offering a serene and peaceful escape from the bustling crowds at the nearby Peak Tower. This charming public park blends classic British garden aesthetics with Hong Kong's subtropical charm, featuring impeccably manicured lawns, elegant pavilions, winding shaded paths lined with lush greenery, and vibrant beds of blooming flowers in reds, pinks, and purples. Expansive open grassy areas invite picnics, relaxation, or play, while family-friendly elements like playground equipment, slides, and swings make it especially appealing for children and families.  What sets this spot apart is its breathtaking panoramic outlook from an elevated position around 400 meters above sea level. Visitors enjoy sweeping vistas over the western and southern sides of Hong Kong Island—lush green hills cascading dramatically toward the coastline, distant outlying islands such as Lamma shimmering on the horizon, and the sparkling expanse of the South China Sea stretching into the distance. On clear days, the natural coastal scenery unfolds unobstructed by dense skyscrapers, providing a refreshing contrast to the iconic urban harbor views found elsewhere on the Peak. Sunsets here are particularly magical, with golden light bathing the hills and sea.  Conveniently located halfway up the scenic Mount Austin Road walk (just a short stroll from The Peak Lookout), it serves as an ideal midway rest stop en route to the higher Victoria Peak Garden. Free to enter, quiet, and less crowded than main attractions, Mount Austin Playground delivers a perfect harmony of tranquil greenery, thoughtful landscaping, and high-elevation natural beauty—making it a hidden gem for anyone seeking respite and stunning views in the heart of Hong Kong.

Rating: 5 - Nan Lian Garden 南蓮園池is a beautiful, tranquil public park in Hong Kong, designed in the classical Tang Dynasty style. The garden is connected by a footbridge to the adjacent, equally impressive Chi Lin Nunnery志蓮淨苑, a large Buddhist temple complex that is also free to enter. The garden spans 3.5 hectares and features a one-way circular route that guides visitors through its key sights. The design follows classical Chinese landscape principles, incorporating artificial hills, ornamental rocks, water features, and manicured plants. The southern route, which ascends north from Luodingtian via the Back Path Road, reaches the summit. A loop trail also ascends and descends from Changli Village (where a 57K minibus connects Fanjin Highway and the entrance to Changli Village). The counterclockwise loop offers a gentle climb, and while some sections still require some use of hands and feet, the effort is relatively minimal. At approximately 300 meters, reaching the ridge, the view opens up. From the summit post, you can overlook the Deep Bay area, with Luodingtian and the North Blade visible from the mountain. The descent is a gravel path and quite steep, so exercise caution to avoid injury.

Its cold, windy and hot at the same time, make sure to wear sunscreen when your here. There are also some nice gift and souvenir stall inside the statue itself. Rating: 5 - One ☝️of the key features of Lantau Island 🏝️ is the Big Buddha that sits on the very hill top of Lantau, which can be seen 👀 for many, many kilometres ♾️ away on the hiking 🥾trail.  Travel – There are many ways to travel up to the Big Buddha from Tung Chung 🗺️. The most convenient would be to take the cable car 🚠 or you can try a bus 🚎or taxi 🚕. Cable cars will have a queue, bus and taxi will take time ⏳but you can have a great view of the island as it drives up towards the top. Note that the bus has a weekend price surge 📈(a lot! 😅)  Walking up - To get to the top of The Big Buddha, there is no 🚫 entrance fee (it is FREE 🎉🎊) but you are encouraged 🗣️to donate if you can. After which, you can walk all the way up to the base of the Big Buddha. At the base level, you can walk a full circle 🔄 and take in the surrounding mountain ⛰️view.  Walking In – After all the photo taking, you can enter the inside of the Big Buddha via the base behind the main staircase. Inside, along the wall is a columbarium. Among those who are housed there, Anita Mui would be one of the most iconic Hong Kong 🇭🇰celebrities 💃. (🚫 pictures 📸) Inside, you then make your way up to the top 🔝whereby you can view the Tooth Relic of the Buddha.  Faith 🪷 has it that if you have a potential relationship with Buddha, you will be able to see the Tooth Relic in different colours 🔴🔵🟡🟢⚫️while the rest of us will see it in just pure white ⚪️. Along the inside walls, you will also find intricate wood 🪵carvings of the deities 🧚‍♀️ and buddha. Letters 📮from officials and construction details.  It is an impressive 😎 monument which you can only enjoy if you are fit 💪and are able to climb 🚶‍♀️the stairs to the top. So while you can do it, give it a go and with some blessings 🙏🏼, you will get good 👍weather 🌈 and clear skies 🌅 to enjoy the outing.

Rating: 5 - Traveling from TST to see the Tian Tan Buddha was a highlight of my trip.  Beyond the massive Tian Tan Buddha statue, make sure to visit the Po Lin Monastery. It has a very traditional, serene vibe that feels worlds away from the hustle of TST. The architecture is stunning and full of intricate details.  I was also impressed by the food variety; there are plenty of spots to eat, including great Indian options.  One big tip: The return queue for the cable car can be very long. Plan your timing carefully so you aren't stuck waiting for hours!

Rating: 5 - Tian Tan Buddha is one of Hong Kong’s most iconic landmarks and an unforgettable experience, both spiritually and visually. Located on Lantau Island, the massive bronze Buddha sits serenely atop a hill, offering breathtaking panoramic views of the surrounding mountains and sea.  Reaching the statue is part of the journey. After arriving in Ngong Ping (many visitors take the scenic cable car), you’ll climb over 200 steps to reach the base. The staircase can feel long, especially in warm weather, but the view becomes more impressive with each step. Once at the top, the scale of the Buddha is truly striking, calm, majestic, and incredibly detailed.  The atmosphere is peaceful despite the crowds. The nearby Po Lin Monastery adds to the cultural depth of the visit, with beautiful temple architecture, incense drifting through the air, and a sense of quiet reflection. It’s a place where sightseeing and spirituality blend naturally.  Whether you’re interested in history, photography, or simply soaking in panoramic views, Tian Tan Buddha is absolutely worth the trip. Try to go earlier in the day to avoid heavier crowds and to enjoy cooler temperatures during the climb.

Rating: 5 - Located on Lantau Island, this majestic bronze statue—often called the Big Buddha—stands tall at 34 meters, quietly overlooking the mountains and sea. The journey itself feels special. Climbing the 268 steps to reach the statue isn’t just physical; it feels symbolic, like you’re gradually leaving the noise of the world behind.  At the top, the view is breathtaking. Surrounded by lush greenery and open skies, the Buddha’s calm expression creates a powerful sense of peace. It’s not just a tourist attraction—it’s a spiritual landmark. The scale of the statue is impressive, but what truly stands out is the serenity you feel standing beneath it.  Right nearby is the beautiful Po Lin Monastery, where you can explore traditional temple architecture, light incense, and soak in the tranquil atmosphere. The blend of culture, history, and spirituality makes the entire visit meaningful.  Whether you’re religious or not, the Tian Tan Buddha offers something deeper—a quiet reminder to slow down, breathe, and reflect. If you’re in Hong Kong, this is absolutely a must-visit destination.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Took Tuen Ma line MTR to Ma On Shan station, I forgot to exit B but went directly into MOStown. I requested the taxi to bring me to the trail head, not the Ma On Shan bbq site or village. It costs hkd $65. If you alight at the village it will probably take another hr of hike to reach the trail head. From trail head it took 45 mins for me to reach the campsite. There a lots of steps up but trail is well marked. You see dogs on leash hiking up too! And young children too. The view was absolutely  amazing from the camp! Many people not just camping, I even saw a bible study group! I decided to return by u turning cos I was not sure where is minibus stop n besides the bus schedule apparently infrequent. reviews: Rating: 5 - North and South Ninepin Islands, October 8, 2021. Took bus 92 from Diamond Hill to Sai Kung at 9:30 AM. Quickly bought bread for the afternoon, met up with friends, and boarded the speedboat. Soon after setting sail, a sudden downpour and we were soaked to the bone! 😅 Arriving at the North Ninepin Island pier, we could already see the imposing hexagonal basalt rock formations. Following the path to Lighthouse No. 200, we admired the rugged cliffs. Returning to the pier, we found the world-famous Silver Neck Bridge on the opposite shore, offering views of Moon Cliff, Cannon Rock, and other unique Hong Kong landscapes. We had visited Moon Cliff and Cannon Rock last November, and this time we aimed to see them. Be aware that climbing across is dangerous; assess your abilities and don't force it.  At 12:30 PM, we boarded the boat to South Ninepin Island. After disembarking, we found a place to eat. We continued taking photos at the Stone Arch, also known as the "Tiger's Mouth Cave," and then went to find the smallest Tin Hau Temple, which was already closed. With over an hour to spare before boarding, I sat down to enjoy the sea breeze and relax.  I was very happy and lucky; the weather was sunny and beautiful after we disembarked, resulting in many lovely photos.

reviews: Rating: 3 - One of the interesting landmarks to see when visiting Tai O is the North Lantau Obelisk which was erected just northeast of the village. The small obelisk monument is located up a hillside just north of the Yim Tim Mangrove Forrest. There are signs pointing the way and only a short ascent to climb.  The monument is now situated in front of a few trees with the sea in the background. On its base is a worn and difficult to read engraving. Research reveals that it is reference to the Convention between the British and Qing governments recognising the extension of the Hong Kong territory, whereby the New Territories including Lantau Island was be leased to Great Britain and full under British administration in 1898. The monument was erected here four years later in 1902 by the British Navy.  In the end, the obelisk monument is a minor attraction that is somewhat out of the way at Tai O. However, it is something that history buffs in particular will find interesting and worth making the time to see when visiting the village.

Although having quite a different appearance from the Old Tai Po Police Station, the two neighbouring structures do share a number of elements that are distinctly characteristic of that period of colonial buildings. First of all, a walk around of the whole building will reveal the veranda that does line all the extended area from the structure’s arched doors. reviews: Rating: 4 - This is a historic village house and a Declared Monument building (1986) situated within the Tak Wah Park in Tsuen Wan. In the past a Hakka mixed-lineage village was situated at this location. It included this village home built in 1904 by a village scholar, using traditional methods and consisting of rammed earth, grey and black brick and timber and represents a fine example of the traditional southern China architecture that was prevalent around the turn of the 20th century.  While the old Hoi Pa Village was eventually relocated to give way for the construction of the new town to Tsuen Wan, this Old House and two other buildings including the fellow Declared Monument, the Chan Yi Cheung Ancestral Hall, were preserved and formed part of the the Tak Wah Park which was constructed in the manner of the old Hakka village in the 1980's. Now it can be seen within the park in its preserved state.  At present, the Old House of the Former Hoi Pa Village isn't open to the public for visitation. However, you can walk around the building and view its exterior architecture from up close. Just follow the signs inside the Tak Wah Park to find this historic building.

reviews: Rating: 5 - I recently had the pleasure of hiking the Tung Chung to Mui Wo Olympic Trail, and I can confidently say it’s an excellent choice for beginner hikers! This trail offers a perfect blend of scenery, manageable terrain, and a welcoming atmosphere that makes it an ideal introduction to hiking.  Starting at Tung Chung, the trail kicks off with a gentle incline that allows newcomers to acclimatize without feeling overwhelmed. There’s a merchandise shop at the end of the exhibition where you will find Hong Kong-exclusive merchandise according to their website.  We spent about 1.5 hrs there including the merchandise shop. Overall we enjoy the exhibition. It brings back all the good memories of Studio Ghibli animation and a good way to end our holidays in HK.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Pacific Place is a really nice mall on Hong Kong Island and one of the more comfortable places to spend time in the city. The location is great — it’s directly connected to the Admiralty MTR and tied into several office towers and hotels, so everything flows together. You can walk between buildings, shops, restaurants, and even hotels without going outside, which makes it very convenient. One of the best things about Pacific Place is that it sits right next to Hong Kong Park. You can step out of the mall and suddenly you’re in a quiet green space with trees, water features, and walking paths. It’s a great contrast to the busy city around it. You can grab coffee or food in the mall and then walk over to the park to relax. The mall itself is modern, clean, and well organized. It leans toward the higher-end side with many international brands, but it still feels comfortable to walk around even if you’re just browsing. There are also a lot of good restaurants and cafes spread throughout the different levels. Overall Pacific Place is more than just a mall — it’s really a connected complex with offices, hotels, shopping, and the park right next door. Very convenient and a nice place to take a break while exploring Hong Kong Island.

The design is clean and modern, with spacious walkways and plenty of natural light.  Dining options are solid, ranging from casual bites to refined restaurants. However, do note that the eateries can get very crowded during weekday lunch hours due to the office crowd. Best to plan around the rush if you’re aiming for a relaxed meal.  Overall, it’s a convenient and stylish stop whether you’re shopping, grabbing lunch, or just looking to escape the heat in a refined environment.  Rating: ★★★★☆

reviews: Rating: 5 - Yuk Hau Kwong玉虛宮 (Pak Tai Temple北帝廟) is a historic and renowned temple in Cheung Chau長洲, Hong Kong, and is designated a Grade I historic building. It is located at the northern end of Pak She Street, Cheung Chau, Hong Kong. It is open daily from 7:00 AM to 5:00 PM. You can take a ferry from Central Pier 5 in Hong Kong Island to Cheung Chau and walk north along the Cheung Chau Ferry Pier Promenade for about 10 minutes to reach the temple. Long History: The temple was built in 1783 (the 48th year of the Qianlong Emperor's reign in the Qing Dynasty清朝乾隆皇帝四十八年), and has a history of over 200 years. Pak Tai Worship: The fishermen of Cheung Chau worship Pak Tai北帝 (also known as Xuanwu Emperor 玄天上帝or Zhenwu Dadi真武大帝), praying for safe voyages and protection from floods. Legend has it that before the temple was built, a plague struck Cheung Chau, and the plague subsided after residents welcomed a statue of Pak Tai, hence the temple's construction. The temple is the largest Pak Tai temple in Hong Kong, featuring exquisite brick, wood, and tile carvings, especially the two rare and precious dragon pillars.
Rating: 3 - A temple since 18th century.  A gathering place for gathering & praying safety and good wellbeing for the local people in Cheung Chau.

Rating: 4 - The most interesting and beautiful temple to visit on Cheung Chau is the Pak Tai (Yuk Hui) Temple on Pak She Street. The is a Grade I Historical Building built in 1783. Opening hours are 7am to 5pm daily.  The temple has Qing Dynasty characteristics including a beautiful facade with decorative murals. It is fronted by guardian lions. Within the are a separate halls connected by moon gate passageways. You will find expected shrines with deity figures, hanging incense coils, ancient drum and bell and nice wood carvings. You will also find beautifully carved dragon pillars and nice mosaic murals of a tiger and dragon in the two side halls.  In one of the side halls, there are two information panels describing the temple architecture in more detail and providing good description of the various temple highlights to look out for while exploring its grounds.  Note: The Pak Tai Temple is the scene of the annual Cheung Chau Bun Festival when worshippers come to seek blessings from Pak Tai. It can be very crowded at this time of the year.  Overall, if you are going to visit just one temple during your time on Cheung Chau, this is the one to find. The Pak Tai is the most impressive and interesting historic attraction on the island and a place well worth dedicating some time to visit.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Hung Hom Kwun Yum Temple is a quiet and spiritually meaningful temple located in the Hung Hom area of Kowloon, offering a peaceful retreat from the surrounding urban environment. Dedicated to Kwun Yum, the Goddess of Mercy, the temple is deeply respected by locals who visit to pray for compassion, protection, health, and emotional well-being. Compared to larger and more famous temples in Hong Kong, this temple feels more intimate and grounded in everyday local life.  The temple’s architecture is traditional and modest, featuring classic Chinese design elements such as red pillars, decorative roof details, and carved stone ornaments. Inside, the atmosphere is calm and reverent, filled with the soft glow of incense smoke and the quiet rhythm of worshippers offering prayers. Many visitors come alone or in small groups, creating a reflective and respectful environment that encourages slow, mindful observation.  Hung Hom Kwun Yum Temple is especially known among locals as a place to seek inner peace and guidance during difficult times. The presence of Kwun Yum symbolizes mercy and unconditional compassion, and this sense of spiritual comfort is strongly felt throughout the temple grounds. On special days of the lunar calendar and during festivals, the temple becomes livelier, yet it still maintains a sincere and humble character rather than a festive or commercial atmosphere.  The temple is well-maintained and easy to visit, making it accessible even for those who are not familiar with religious customs. Visitors are welcome to observe rituals respectfully, light incense, or simply take a moment of quiet reflection. Its location within a residential district gives it an authentic, local feel, offering insight into how spiritual practices are woven into daily life in Hong Kong.  Overall, Hung Hom Kwun Yum Temple is not just a place of worship but a gentle sanctuary of compassion and calm. It is an ideal stop for travelers interested in local culture, spiritual traditions, or those seeking a quieter, more personal temple experience away from the crowds. The temple leaves a lasting impression through its simplicity, sincerity, and sense of inner peace.

reviews: Rating: 3 - The main deity is Kwun Yam (觀音), the temple is also called Pat Heung Kwun Yam Temple (八鄉觀音廟). The temple was constructed before 1861 as a renovation tablet has the dating inscribed. It was built by the Pat Heung villagers with the land rent paid to the Kam Tin Tangs. The temple had a Chung Ching Tsz (忠精祠, hero shrine) to commemorate those villagers who died in inter-village battles, mainly those in Kam Tin in around the Qianlong (乾隆, A.D. 1736-1795) reign of the Qing dynasty. The temple is managed by a committee named Tung Yik Tong (同益堂).  The temple is a Qing vernacular building having a plan of three-bay-two-hall-one-courtyard in the middle and a side chamber of two-hall-one courtyard to the left and right. The Shiwan (石灣) figurines installed at the brackets are the most unique relic of the temple. (AMO)

Historically, Pat Kan Uk was built in the early 1930s to relocate families displaced during the construction of the Bluff Hill Battery. The compound is made entirely of red brick with green painted doors. It has traditional Chinese pan-and-roll tile roofing as well. reviews: Rating: 5 - The most rewarding hike in Hong Kong is the Pat Sin Leng ridge trail. It is a difficult hike, but offers you views of Tolo Harbor, both on the Hong Kong and Shenzhen sides of the mountain range. You can begin from either end of the trail. From the far Western side of the trail just before you descend (or as you ascend), you can also see Shenzhen quite clearly in the distance. The mountain ridge is called Pat Sin Leng because it has eight ("pat" or "bat") peaks named for eight Buddhist spirits ("sin") or immortals, and each of these peaks is marked with a sign on the trail.  As you work your way along the ridge, the views are great, but if you do this hike in hot weather (essentially May to October in Hong Kong), remember that you will have very little protection from the sun once you reach the ridge (the ascent and descent are largely protected by trees). Take plenty of water.  The Pat Sin Leng ridge trail is a roughly 23 km walk according to my steps when I walk it, and you can begin either from Tai Mei Tuk or from Hok Tau Wai. Fast walkers can complete the train in just over 3 hours and slow walkers might take more than double that amount of time.  Buses run to both points of entry, and if you want to begin from the Tai Mei Tuk side, some buses can take you to Plover Cove Country Park entrance, about 1 km Northeast of Tai Mei Tuk proper. If you begin from Hok Tau Wai, you will arrive at Tai Mei Tuk when you complete your hike, and that village has a number of restaurants offering plenty of refreshment, although not excellent food.

reviews: Rating: 3 - The final tick on Ros’ list was the trip to the Peak, the highest point in the city where the funicular railway takes you to the summit for panoramic views of this huge city landscape. Ros had purposely left this as the last attraction as it’s then possible to take in the view by day and night. The snag was, so had everyone else, and it took the best part of an hour in a long queue to get to the funicular to get to the top.  We’ve always said we shouldn’t go back to places, and the Peak showed us why, as it wasn’t a patch on what it used to be. Before, it was quaint, but now it’s like a theme park with throngs of people, bright lights, tacky gift shops, cafés and restaurants, called the SkyTerrace, definitely not a nice place. Before, there were no crowds, a large cobbled square, a small viewing area and a bar/restaurant selling drinks. Still, that’s progress. The funicular’s grown too. It used to hold 120 passengers; it now transports 210 camera phone snapping tourists at a time. Still, we joined in and enjoyed watching day turn to night and the panoramic array of buildings turn into a twinkling sea of Christmas lights.  Ros’ tour ended with no evening meal included, but fortunately, as we joined the queue to leave, we came upon an American diner offering deep fried seafood which looked delicious, so it was an easy decision to stop there to eat. Fortunately, they had a table for two by a window so we could enjoy our fisherman’s catch with a view over the brightly lit cityscape.  We queued again for three quarters of an hour for the funicular ride down, and a ten minute walk got us on the train home.

Rating: 5 - A great half day or full day get away from the Hong Kong island. Peng Chau island has some really nice swimming beaches and great nature trail that is easy for kids and pets.  Getting here: Take the ferry from Hong Kong central pier no. 6 , the hkkf ferry plues here; there are fast and slow ferries check the time.  At the island There is a huge supermarket (wellcome) There are few good restaurants and cafes (my recco is - the island table and the edible project) Did not notice pharmacies or dispensaries There is a hige public library (you can donate and pick up free books) There is a children’s park and playgrounds  Nature trail This goes all around the island and is a great way to explore the island, the map for this trail is only at the central ferry terminal (6) somehow but the google maps should help  We followed this route took us about 3 hrs including the swim break and lunch break  We first went to cafe to pick up food for the trail then we went to turtle island, from there made our way to fisherman’s rock ; on the way there are 2 beaches you can swim at we stopped at one of them. After fisherman’s rock we made our way to finger hill , on the way we stopped at tung wan barbeque area and ate pur lunch there. After finger hill we made our way to Ngan Chau Tsai view point and from here to edible project cafe and back to the ferry. If someone requires i can leave the coordinates of this route  Hope this review helps

Rating: 3 - Finger Hill is the highest peak on Peng Chau Island at 95 metres. You reach it as part of the Peng Chau Family Walk in the southern section of the island. Just follow the signs. It is no more than 5 minutes from the main village. Do expect a steady and steep climb up a long set of paved steps before reaching the peak.  At the Finger Hill peak you will find a pavilion with shaded seating where you can have a rest. Unfortunately the vegetation is thick and tall obscuring views pretty much in all directions from Finger Hill. If you stand on top of the concrete block at the peak you can see some very nice views of the village and as far as Lantau Island to the north as well as the open sea to the south.  In the end, you'll enjoy better views on the trail up to Finger Hill and from various lookout points throughout the Family Walk Trail than you will from the peak itself. If you want the exercise and don't mind the climb, its fine to include the walk up to Finger Hill. However, if it is really hot outside and you are feeling tired at this stage of your hike around Peng Chau, this is something you may want to skip.
