address: Sunset Peak, Lantau Island, Hong Kong
reviews: Rating: 5 - Hard to fault this hike really. The views are already stunning during the day, but every hongkonger needs to experience sunset at sunset peak once in their life. Absolutely breathtaking views, multiple ways to get up to the peak, we summated via Nam Shan (南山）and down via Pak Kung Au (伯公坳).  Honestly not a very technically challenging hike, but you’re rewarded with amazing scenery. Have to go a bit off trail to get to the peak. Definitely bring a headtorch for retracing steps in the dark.  Including breaks should take anywhere from 3-5 hours
Rating: 5 - Very nice view with silver grass all over the peak.  Good enough for a day trekking.

Rating: 5 - Sunset Peak is an absolute gem for nature enthusiasts seeking a breathtaking winter escape. You would be easily captivated by the ethereal beauty of the miscanthus fields that adorn the landscape, creating a truly enchanting experience.

Rating: 5 - Sunset peak is famous for its beautiful scenery and the little stone huts on top. Sure you won't be disappointed when you get there.  If you're to plan an expedition to your third tallest mountain in Hong Kong (869 meters), there are 3 major routes you can choose from.  Most do not recommend the Wong Lung Hang route as it's rather steep and there are flights after flights of stone stairs. However, if you think you are moderately fit and can handle those endless stone steps, you may actually consider going up this way for a few reasons.  1. It's shorter. According to the official sign, it takes only 1¾ hours to reach the peak (not the highest point though, but a place where you can enjoy breathtaking view and you won't even care the peak is still some distance, like 30 minutes or so away).  2. When you get to the end of this route, you've basically entered the area with lots of stone houses scattered all over the hill, whereas if you come from the most common Pak Kung Au route, you'll have to reach the peak first and then descend to these beautiful huts.  3. Most of the Wong Lung Hang route is well covered by trees. You won't be roasted by the sun as easily. And when the sun pierces through the leaves from above, it's a very beautiful scene indeed.  Then when you go down, I suggest taking the Pak Kung Au way. Three reasons.  1. You'll have the gorgeous sea view right in front of your eyes for at least half the way while you're descending.  2. The height of the steps is on average shorter than those in the Wong Lung Hang route, making it easier to walk down, especially when the climb before has taken a toll on your legs and your body.  3. Once you get to the end of the trail, the bus stop is right there. A 15- to 20-minute bus ride will take your weary body back to Tung Chung Town Centre or Tung Chung MTR Station.  Have fun!

Rating: 5 - Whether you are going to Phoenix Mountain or Dadongshan, Bogongao is a very important starting point. I climbed to the top of both mountains through this. I prefer Dadongshan. The rocky landscape on the top of the mountain attracts attention. It is definitely the best choice to shoot the sunset.  Young people are the main crowd at the top of the mountain. It coincides with Valentine's Day on February 14th. Couples will go together as the home court. They encourage and take care of each other to test the depths of the lover’s mutual feelings, and build deeper in the extreme hard journey.  Feelings.  Many climbers who like camping choose Dadong Mountain. The gentle terrain on the top of the mountain provides more opportunities to build street-sleeping tents. I admire these camping brave men the most, each carrying a huge bag and carrying food and water.  Since you are taking pictures of sunset, you must prepare lighting equipment when you go down the mountain, and be careful during night walks to avoid stepping on stone steps when you are tired.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Despite reading some negative reviews, I was still convinced by the photos of activities that this would be the right place to take my kids there in hot summer afternoon. And it was. It was the best indoor sport/play ground that we’ve ever visited. Across Europe and Asia. But this view can vary a lot depends on what your kids like. My kids enjoy almost all kinds of ball sports, plus jumping, the place is really catered for that, and that’s why we had a really fantastic time, almost no queuing time. The information online was however completely lacking, no website link, no price and timing info, and there was not even a phone number to call. If we weren’t staying in the neighborhood I wouldn’t be bothered to check it out in person. They have different entry price depends on the day and time. During a weekday, it would be $200 in the morning, and $240 in the afternoon. Weekends will be even more expensive. If your kid is under 8 years old, you are obliged to also buy a ticket for yourself to enter. On top of that you need to wear jump socks, cost $30 a pair of you don’t have one. Which very expensive and very environmental unfriendly; seeing most socks are thrown away afterwards. Further than that, it was really amazing. They played 4 hours non-stop, added some videos.

Rating: 4 - The Kwan Tai in Tai O is believed to be the oldest temple in Lantau Island. It is also a Grade II historic building in Hong Kong. Originally constructed between 1488-1505, Kwan Tai was restored around 1741 giving it the appearance of typical architecture found in temples of the Qing Dynasty.  The temple is dedicated to the God of War - Kwan Tai and is shares wall and building space with the Tin Hau temple found adjacent to the building. These two temples more or less represent a single building.  Here you will see a building of traditional grey brick construction. Above the entrance are colourful plaster murals and decorative roofing. Within, you'll find historic leather drum, copper bell and shrine setup with deity statues and offerings. The red faced centre figure of Kwan Tai is particularly interesting, as are his horseman figures which flank the entrance into the temple.  You can give both the Kwan Tai and adjacent Tin Hau temples a quick look-see while exploring this backstreet of the Tai O. Both can be conveniently viewed in 5-10 minutes. Then you can continue onward with other intended sightseeing you have around Tai O.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Club Captain Bear  Located along the secluded bay of Tai She Wan, Club Captain Bear is easily one of Hong Kong’s most surreal locations. The bungled resort project, which opened in 2006, was the miscarried dream child of a Wan Chai bar owner. Picking a location way out in the middle of nowhere on a bay in Sai Kung, he had envisaged the place to be a secluded retreat that people would flock to on weekends to get away from the city. Like some kind of twist on The Island of Doctor Moreau, animatronic animals were bought and shipped in from the now-closed Rainforest Café in Festival Walk, and a swimming pool was built along with a bar.  With no car access and limited pathways, private boats were set up to transport guests, and the place operated momentarily. However, it was a little too far off the beaten track, and the project ultimately failed, closing only a couple of years later. The owner abandoned the premises and left it to rot and to become the apocalyptical wonderland it is today. It currently somewhat resembles a theme park from a horror movie, with festering carcasses of fibreglass animals strewn across the property amid battered buildings and broken glass.

You'll see a couple of viewpoints overlooking the Tai Tam reservoirs with nice views over the Tai Tam reservoir which is furthest north of the four found in the valley. The trail takes no more than 20+ minutes to complete. There are public toilets near the midway point where the trail crosses the main road. Afterwards, you can circle back or make way down the enjoyable 5km Waterworks Heritage Trail where you can spend time close to the reservoirs and see interesting Declared Monuments situated around some of Hong Kong's earliest reservoir projects.

The Tai Wong Ancient Temple in Yuen Long Old Market is a Grade I historic building. On October 21, 2024, at approximately 6:48 AM, a fire broke out, with explosions heard from inside the temple. Firefighters used two hoses and two teams of smoke-wearing personnel to extinguish the fire, which was put out at approximately 7:57 PM. Over 60 people evacuated, either independently or with fire department assistance.  According to the Antiquities Advisory Committee, the Tai Wong Ancient Temple was designated a Grade I historic building on December 18, 2009. The temple primarily enshrines Hung Shing Tai Wong and Yeung Hau Tai Wong, and is believed to have been built during the Kangxi era (1662-1722). It is a two-courtyard, three-bay building with walls made of blue bricks, and is the main temple in Nam Ping Wai and Yuen Long Old Market. The temple follows the divination customs of the Tai Ping Ching Chiu festival. It once served as a government office and official residence. The ancient temple fair uses the funds raised through religious ceremonies to renovate the temple every ten years.
Rating: 3 - It's a small temple. It doesn't take long to explore. Personally, I found the surrounding densely packed houses more interesting than the temple itself.

Rating: 4 - The Great King Temple, also known as the Great King Ancient Temple, is located on Cheung Shing Street within the old Yuen Long market in the New Territories of Hong Kong. In the eighth year of the reign of Emperor Kangxi (1669), Deng Wenwei "moved the market from Daqiaodun to Yuen Long and built the Great King Ancient Temple." Major renovations were subsequently carried out in the 17th year of the reign of Emperor Daoguang (1838). The Great King Temple enshrines Hong Sheng Wang and Yang Hou Gong.  During the reign of Emperor Kangxi, the "sea migration" policy was implemented, and Yuen Long Market was relocated to Maozhou. After the market was later restored, the residents invited the South Sea Great King Hong Sheng from Maozhou to Yuen Long. Locals call the South Sea God Guangli Hong Sheng Da Wang, and the birthday of the South Sea God is celebrated on the 13th day of the second lunar month each year. Five steles within the temple record the establishment and evolution of Yuen Long Market. The Great King Temple is a traditional building with one entrance and two halls. Inside, there is a drum, the skin of which has been torn to reduce the sound and prevent it from frightening children. The Great King Temple is managed by Nam Pin Wai.  The Tai Wong Temple was the political and religious centre of the Yuen Long Old Town in the past. To this day, the Yuen Long Jianjiao (a festival held every ten years) still holds worship ceremonies in the temple.

It features some modern building exterior in Chinese temple appearance with more traditional interior with some interesting things to see. You'll find an archway entrance, hanging incense, lanterns, incense cauldrons, shrine with deity figures and a very large wooden sampan boat. There are interesting historical pictures of the Tai Po area from the early 20th century.  Walk past the main shrine to a small garden area and you'll find a small statue of the goddess Kun Iam. There is an attractive large stone mural worth seeing here. You'll find another on the exterior of the temple that is worth a look-see as well.  Overall, this is a neat temple that is worth the 5-10 minute stop if you are making the cycling journey along Tolo Harbour between the Shatin area and Tai Mei Tuk.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Tai Yuen Street in Wan Chai, Hong Kong, is a bustling market lane that feels like a bridge between generations, where old Hong Kong traditions meet modern-day charm. Known affectionately as "Toy Street," it's a favorite destination for families, collectors, and nostalgia-seekers alike.  Brightly colored stalls line the narrow street, packed with an eclectic assortment of toys that range from the latest anime figurines to vintage finds that hark back to the mid-20th century. You'll find everything from classic action figures, and dolls, to educational toys and trinkets that spark joy across all ages. Some vendors have been here for decades, selling beloved toys that evoke childhood memories. Wandering the rows, you can find rare collectibles that are hard to find elsewhere in the city, like limited-edition action figures, imported Japanese gashapon, and unique Hong Kong-made toys that showcase local culture and craftsmanship.  Besides toys, Tai Yuen Street also has small shops that sell practical goods and everyday essentials. You’ll find hardware stores, shops with traditional Chinese knickknacks, and vendors offering everything from inexpensive household items to brightly colored phone accessories. The energy is vibrant and communal, with shop owners cheerfully greeting regular customers and tourists alike.  Over the years, Tai Yuen Street has managed to retain its retro, mom-and-pop feel despite the changing cityscape around it. It's a unique experience where the charm of old Hong Kong mingles with the city’s modern-day influences, creating a delightful shopping destination for those looking for a bit of everything Hong Kong has to offer.

Rating: 5 - The oldest, longest running comedy club in all of Asia, TakeOut Comedy has been going at its current location in a basement in SoHo for 19 years.  The owner, Jami Gong, brought the idea for the club from New York, where he made lots of connections that pay off to this day.  Be sure to check their schedule online to see who is in town--the club hosts visiting comedians and locals, with most shows (almost every show, really) in English.  Jami has been a fixture of the Hong Kong comedy scene for almost two decades--before his club the only English comedy in HK was visiting Commonwealth comedians doing a weekend every month or so at an Indian restaurant.  Without him there would quite possibly be no English standup scene in HK, but now it seems like every other bar has an open mic some weekday--almost all performers have come out of TakeOut Comedy or performed there at one time or another.  The club itself isn't glamorous, a basement down some perilous steps with a low ceiling and only a single bathroom.  Unlike most comedy clubs, there is no bar and no food service.  While that may seem surprising, it helps keep an evening out affordable, because you can bring your own drinks!

reviews: Rating: 3 - The Tam Kung Tin Hau Temple on Blue Pool Road is an interesting temple ground to visit in the Happy Valley area of the city. Opening hours are 8am to 5pm daily.  The temple was originally located near the Hong Kong Sanatorium but was relocated here as part of urban development works at the turn of the 20th century. In 1901 it was rebuilt by the Hakka people upon the large perch over what is now Blue Pool Road. Entrance is at street level, you have to walk up a short staircase before arriving at two separate temples, the first and larger being dedicated to Tam Kung (Sea God - Lord Tam) and another smaller temple up another short set of steps to Tin Hau (Goddess of the Sea).  The temple terraces are nicely decorated with manicured plants, porcelain guardian lions, vases and other items one might associate with Chinese temples. Within you will find hanging lanterns, ancient drum and bell and shrines setup with deity figures. There is an English panel within the larger Tam Kung chamber with historic information related to this temple. Tam Kung becomes very busy with worshippers during the Tam Kung Festival held on the 8th day of the fourth lunar month each year.  Overall, this is a nice temple ground to see if you plan to spend time in Happy Valley. Give it 5-10 minutes of your time when passing by and then continue on with other intended sightseeing you may have in this area of the city.

Rating: 4 - The Tang Chung Ancestral Hall is Declared Monument building in Hong Kong (1997) and stop 6 along the Lung Yeuk Tau Heritage Trail. It is situated just next to the historic Tin Hau Temple (stop 5) and just past the walled village of Lo Wai (stop 4) if you are starting the trail from the south. What you see today is a well-preserved, three hall building which honours the memory of the founding ancestors of the Tang Chung-ling Clan who settled this area of Hong Kong as early as the late 13th century. The Ancestral Hall is open for visitation from 9am to 1pm (morning) and 2pm-5pm (afternoon) daily but is closed on Tuesdays.  Historically, the Tang Chung Ancestral Hall was built in the early 16th Century. The exterior is attractive with grey-brick construction, plaster, motifs, fascia boards, auspicious animal decorations and tiled roofing. It is similar to Chinese temple architecture and appearance you may have come across when sightseeing temples around Hong Kong.  The interior offers several interesting things to see including the large screen (dong chung) which separate the front and centre hall, the delicately carved wooden beams and a peculiar stone plaque of the Nam Him Study Hall which no longer exists. In the Rear hall, there are three bays with shrines dedicated to past members of the Tang Clan. The Centre Bay shrine includes the Soul Tablets including the Imperial relative, the Song Dynasty Princess and her husband Tang Wai-kap. The information panels will help you identify this particular Tablet amongst the others.  Of further interest and note, the Rear Hall serves as a default information centre for the entire Lung Yeuk Tau Heritage Trail and makes for an important source of information and details about the various attractions found along the trail. What you will find are large panels for the various respective heritage sight with historical accounts for each. It is very much worth spending some time here to read up and learn about the various places. I'd also recommend taking pictures of the panels as well. These come in handy later on, particularly when coming across the attractions which don't have posted information nearby.  In the end, a 10-15 minute visit to admire the architecture and craftsmanship work of the Tang Chung Ancestral Hall is warranted. Another 15 minutes reading up and reviewing the heritage sights information panels is advisable as well. Then continue onward to the somewhat isolated Tung Kok Wai (stop 7) which is the next call on the heritage trail.

reviews: Rating: 4 - This is a Christian Centre founded and built upon a ridge above Sha Tin between 1930 and 38 by Norwegian missionary Karl Ludvig Reichelt. The Eentre grounds are open to the public, allowing all to explore the unique Grade II historic buildings, seeing unique examples of Chinese architecture with western Christian elements.  The trail leading up to Tao Fung Shan start just outside the Sha Tin MTR Station and require a 20-25 minute uphill walk, partly along a paved path through mountainside forest and then up the To Fung Shan Road until you recent the Centre.  Within the Centre, visitors will find plenty of signage and basic history information explaining what you are looking at and when various building structures were constructed. There are courtyards with moon gate entrance, a delightful octagonal pavilion like 'Christ Temple'. Other highlights include a 12 metre tall cross facing the township of Sha Tin and a stone labyrinth and lotus pond.  Note: There are public toilets near the Entrance Archway as well as a small Art Shop and Information Centre in the building beside the Christ Temple.  Overall, the Tao Fung Shan Christian Centre is a peaceful location and an interesting historic place that you probably won't find in tourism information or tour guidebooks for Hong Kong. Thus, not likely a place many first time visitors to the city will make or have time to see. However, for expats or regular visitors wanting to check out new and different places, the Tao Fung Shan Christian Centre might be a place with making effort to visit.

reviews: Rating: 4 - This is a Christian Centre founded and built upon a ridge above Sha Tin between 1930 and 38 by Norwegian missionary Karl Ludvig Reichelt. The Eentre grounds are open to the public, allowing all to explore the unique Grade II historic buildings, seeing unique examples of Chinese architecture with western Christian elements.  The trail leading up to Tao Fung Shan start just outside the Sha Tin MTR Station and require a 20-25 minute uphill walk, partly along a paved path through mountainside forest and then up the To Fung Shan Road until you recent the Centre.  Within the Centre, visitors will find plenty of signage and basic history information explaining what you are looking at and when various building structures were constructed. There are courtyards with moon gate entrance, a delightful octagonal pavilion like 'Christ Temple'. Other highlights include a 12 metre tall cross facing the township of Sha Tin and a stone labyrinth and lotus pond.  Note: There are public toilets near the Entrance Archway as well as a small Art Shop and Information Centre in the building beside the Christ Temple.  Overall, the Tao Fung Shan Christian Centre is a peaceful location and an interesting historic place that you probably won't find in tourism information or tour guidebooks for Hong Kong. Thus, not likely a place many first time visitors to the city will make or have time to see. However, for expats or regular visitors wanting to check out new and different places, the Tao Fung Shan Christian Centre might be a place with making effort to visit.

Rating: 4 - Tap Mun (Grass Island) is an island located just north of the Sai Kung West Country Park that makes for a popular day trip and overnight wild camping location for Hongkongers. It is relatively small at 1.7 square kilometres and is known for its grassy hilltop (hence the name) and numerous ferrel cows that share the island with visitors and those who reside here.  Historically, the island has been habited since at least the mid 16th century. At its height there were likely 2000 residents, mostly tanka fisherfolks. Like most remote villages on the outlying islands of Hong Kong, those numbers dwindled to a spartan few towards the end of the 20th century, as youth opted to move to the city or abroad in search of better living conditions. Today it is estimated that around 100 people continue to reside here at Tap Mun.  To visit Tap Mun, most take daily ferries from the Ma Liu Shui ferry terminus at Science Park (1.5 hour one way) or the nearby Wong Shek Pier (15 minutes one way). Check the schedule online for exact sailing times before setting off to visit Tap Mun.  Upon arrival at the main ferry pier at Tap Mun, visitors will find public toilets and a few casual eateries and restaurants at the Old Fisherman's Village. Just to the south is a New Fisherman's Village where there are a few more places to eat. Otherwise, few options for food and drink provisions on Tap Mun so best to pack what you need prior to making your trip to the island.  Sightseeing around Tap Mun includes a roughly 1 hour long loop trail which circles the southern tip of the island. It passes by the 400 year old Tin Hau Temple at the Old Fisherman's Village, the grassy hilltops and gentle sloops that overlook the the western and southern coast. This is a very popular area for wild camping, particularly on weekends and public holidays.  There are a few pavilion rest stops along or near the main trail as well as a few interesting geological features for visitors to enjoy. These include the Balanced Rock and the Tap Mun Cave both accessible along the boulder and pebble beach just below the main trail.  Another popular geological land formation to find is Long Keng Kan (Neck of the Dragon) found at the end of the informal trail north of the Hilltop Pavilion. This beautiful natural landmark is accessible by way of rope repelling down the step wooded hillside. There are rewarding views of the sea and other outlying islands to the north and east from this location and along the trail. They rival the very good views found along the main loop trail to the south.  Overall, Tap Mun is a neat place to visit if you've done the rounds of island trips around Hong Kong and are looking for somewhere different to spend half a day. There is a nice mix of heritage, history, geology and natural beauty to enjoy and while time consuming to visit from the city, everything is pretty straightforward and easy to experience once you are there.

Rating: 4 - Tap Mun (Grass Island) is an island located just north of the Sai Kung West Country Park that makes for a popular day trip and overnight wild camping location for Hongkongers. It is relatively small at 1.7 square kilometres and is known for its grassy hilltop (hence the name) and numerous ferrel cows that share the island with visitors and those who reside here.  Historically, the island has been habited since at least the mid 16th century. At its height there were likely 2000 residents, mostly tanka fisherfolks. Like most remote villages on the outlying islands of Hong Kong, those numbers dwindled to a spartan few towards the end of the 20th century, as youth opted to move to the city or abroad in search of better living conditions. Today it is estimated that around 100 people continue to reside here at Tap Mun.  To visit Tap Mun, most take daily ferries from the Ma Liu Shui ferry terminus at Science Park (1.5 hour one way) or the nearby Wong Shek Pier (15 minutes one way). Check the schedule online for exact sailing times before setting off to visit Tap Mun.  Upon arrival at the main ferry pier at Tap Mun, visitors will find public toilets and a few casual eateries and restaurants at the Old Fisherman's Village. Just to the south is a New Fisherman's Village where there are a few more places to eat. Otherwise, few options for food and drink provisions on Tap Mun so best to pack what you need prior to making your trip to the island.  Sightseeing around Tap Mun includes a roughly 1 hour long loop trail which circles the southern tip of the island. It passes by the 400 year old Tin Hau Temple at the Old Fisherman's Village, the grassy hilltops and gentle sloops that overlook the the western and southern coast. This is a very popular area for wild camping, particularly on weekends and public holidays.  There are a few pavilion rest stops along or near the main trail as well as a few interesting geological features for visitors to enjoy. These include the Balanced Rock and the Tap Mun Cave both accessible along the boulder and pebble beach just below the main trail.  Another popular geological land formation to find is Long Keng Kan (Neck of the Dragon) found at the end of the informal trail north of the Hilltop Pavilion. This beautiful natural landmark is accessible by way of rope repelling down the step wooded hillside. There are rewarding views of the sea and other outlying islands to the north and east from this location and along the trail. They rival the very good views found along the main loop trail to the south.  Overall, Tap Mun is a neat place to visit if you've done the rounds of island trips around Hong Kong and are looking for somewhere different to spend half a day. There is a nice mix of heritage, history, geology and natural beauty to enjoy and while time consuming to visit from the city, everything is pretty straightforward and easy to experience once you are there.

Rating: 4 - Tat Tak Communal Hall was built by Tang Fan-yau (鄧勳猷, 1812-1874) and his clansmen in the Xianfeng (咸豐) reign of the Qing dynasty as a meeting place of local merchants and an assembling place of gengliantuan (更練團).The communal hall was the centre of resistance forces fight against the takeover of the New Territories by the British in 1899. During the war with the British, a number of villagers were killed and a tablet to commemorate them was erected at the hall. Chambers of the hall were named Wai Zik Tsz (慰寂祠) and Ying Yung Tsz (英勇祠) to honour their bravery death.  Ping Shan Shi had its business declined in the early 1940s. Its neighbouring areas have been reclaimed for development. It has been left vacated for years.

Rating: 5 - A temple that got expanded in the last few decades for selling out columbarium places. Locked in a 70's to 80's vibe of colours and style, it is not a place only for worshipping ancestors. Tourists can enjoy life-size statues of many Chinese deities, and a sacred cow that lived on the premise in the 80's and passed away telling worshippers it was the cow that accompanied apsaras in heaven. Also there are panels of porcelain arts telling stories of deities and filial piety. In a artificial cave there are statues showing scenes of punishment in hell. Note that entrance is up a flight of stairs and there is no wheelchair access. All signs and description of displays are in Chinese only.

Rating: 4 - Tao temple with folk leaning? Hard to characterize for me, I'm no expert.  No monkeys seen today. Very, very quiet on a Sunday afternoon, so probably even quieter during the week. Another area with many lessons about appropriate family behavoir, laid out in pictoral form (no English.) Decent views, much more relaxing than Wan Tai Sin (much less fancy/ creations not so well maintained) The entrance to a steep, paved hiking trail into the jungle is just a few steps down the road. You will need a way to translate the Chinese characters (google lens, or a Chinese guide) to understand the many, many statues and pictures.

A walk through here is definitely worth it to experience the city's pulsating energy up close. ​The market reveals its true strength especially at night: when the typical neon signs and the fantastic lighting turn on, the street just looks amazing. It is the perfect backdrop for photos and for soaking up Hong Kong's nightlife. You can easily spend hours just walking through and observing the scene. ​However, regarding the shopping, you should manage your expectations. There are countless stalls with an incredible amount of things to buy, but you quickly notice that it is mostly very simple merchandise or typical tourist trinkets. If you are looking for high quality, you likely won't find it here. ​The same applies to the food. While it is an experience to sit down there, and the quality is perfectly okay and edible, it is nothing super special in culinary terms. Hong Kong often has much more refined options to offer in other corners of the city. ​ An exciting experience for the atmosphere and visuals, but shopping and food are rather average.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Ten Thousand Buddhas Monastery (Sha Tin, Hong Kong)  A must-visit for both tourists and locals! 🌿 Just a short 10-minute hike brings you to a truly lovely monastery. From the very start of the trail, you’re greeted by rows of Buddha statues lining the path—while we didn’t count them all, it really does feel like there are ten thousand of them.  The walk itself is easy and rewarding, with peaceful surroundings that make the climb enjoyable. Once you reach the monastery, the atmosphere is serene and inspiring, offering a perfect escape from the city’s hustle.  Getting there is simple: take the MTR to Sha Tin Station, exit B, turn left, and after about a 5-minute walk near the cemetery, you’ll find the start of the hike.  Highly recommended for anyone looking to experience a mix of culture, spirituality, and a touch of adventure in Hong Kong.

Rating: 5 - Such an incredible walk up the hill with all the golden Buddha’s looking at you.  They are all different in their ways and as you ascend you find yourself taken away at the beauty at the top. All the other sculptures and buildings to look at.  And the main building (no pictures allowed) is the reason for the name - it houses 10,000 Buddha’s.  Such a stunning display inside the building with the other large Golden Buddha.

Rating: 3 - If you’re debating the trek up to the Ten Thousand Buddhas Monastery, keep in mind it involves a steep climb of over 400 steps lined with golden statues. While the sight is unique, from my perspective, it’s not a must-visit. Unlike the refined peace of Chi Lin Nunnery, the climb can feel like a bit of a repetitive workout, and the atmosphere at the top doesn't quite deliver that same 'soul-soothing' magic. If you’re short on time, your energy is better spent elsewhere.

Rating: 5 - I visited this place twice because the first time was at a weekend and it was busy with people shouting and being disrespectful. It's a place of worship. When I visit the second time, on the Tuesday. It was so much better. A short, but steep walk up the hill to the top. The Buddhas are great and all individual. The temples at the top are beautiful. I would highly recommend visiting during the week. It's worth every moment you spend there.

Rating: 5 - A short but sloping hike up a pathway lined with the 1000 golden status of monks takes you to a beautiful, peaceful temple with a grand vista of the city and the smell of incense all around. It was a very pleasant experience visiting this monastery and temple and was one of the quieter moments in our tour of Hong Kong.  Note that they close at 5pm. So, plan ahead.

Not many people did so you can avoid the crowds and enjoy the view.  The park at the bottom of the team is also worth a visit as it has a free Avery with some lovely birds there.

Rating: 5 - I see lots of reviews saying to buy tickets online,  buy in advance, don't go on the weekend, and avoid the long lines. We arrived at 9:40am on a Sunday, waited a minute in line, bought our tickets with a credit card in person, and walked right through the turnstile with no issues.  When we boarded the tram, an aggressive woman tried pushing her way past me, and her attack was repulsed. Otherwise, the ride up the mountain was glorious, and a must do for visitors to this beautiful city. There are so many intricate views between buildings built into the mountainside. And it's wild to realize the pitch of your journey, as you are only halfway vertical, while the parking garage alongside you is fully horizontal.  The views up at the peak are worth your wait and your tram fee. We did not pay anything additional for the highest viewing area, as all the other viewing areas provided more than enough vistas for us. There are several eateries, souvenir shops, bathrooms, and sitting areas for you to spend hours up here. And we went when the fog prevented us from seeing much past the initial mile or so of Kowloon's waterfront. It was still worth it.

Rating: 5 - The Peak Tram is one of those “classic” Hong Kong things that is actually worth doing.  The ride up is fun in a slightly strange way, with the buildings slowly tilting as you climb the mountain. Once you get to the top, the view over Victoria Harbour, Kowloon and the surrounding islands really puts the scale of the city into perspective.  Yes, it gets busy, but it is well organised and moves quickly. The ride itself is smooth and easy, and it is a great way to experience Hong Kong from above, especially later in the day as the city lights start to come on.

Rating: 5 - Riding the 6th-generation Peak Tram remains an essential Hong Kong experience, blending 130 years of history with a sleek, modern upgrade that features massive panoramic windows and increased capacity. The nearly 45-degree ascent provides a thrilling "optical illusion" where the city’s skyscrapers appear to lean into the mountainside, culminating in a breathtaking reveal of Victoria Harbour from the summit.  Ultimately, for the combination of nostalgic charm and those unbeatable, sky-high views of the skyline, it is absolutely worth the price on a clear day.  Best Time to Visit : Weekdays before 10:00 AM or after 8:00 PM to avoid crowds. For views, arrive 1 hour before sunset to see the city in both daylight and neon.  Seat Strategy: When going UP, sit on the right-hand side for the best views of the skyline.  Weather Check: Hong Kong can be misty in the spring (March/April).  Maintenance Alert: The tram is scheduled for a short maintenance break from March 9–12, 2026. If you're visiting then, you'll need to take Bus 15 or a taxi.

Rating: 5 - The Peak Tram ride was an excellent experience and one of the highlights of the visit. The tram itself is clean, smooth, and very well managed. The climb and descent feel unique because of the steep angle, and the city views keep getting better as you move along.  It’s really worth waiting a bit and getting a front row seat especially while going down because the view through the front glass is amazing and gives a thrilling perspective of the skyline and slope. Great photo opportunity and a memorable ride overall. Definitely a must-try attraction.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Pokfulam Farm is a fascinating place that offers a rare glimpse into Hong Kong’s agricultural history. It’s the site of the city’s first dairy farm, and walking around the space feels like stepping back in time. The old buildings and exhibits tell the story of how farming and milk production used to be a part of life here, which is something you don’t really think about in modern Hong Kong.  What I really enjoyed was the sense of calm—it’s surrounded by greenery and feels so different from the busy city. The guided tours are interesting, and there’s a lot to learn about sustainability and local history, but it’s also just a nice spot to explore on your own. It’s not a flashy attraction, but that’s what makes it special. If you’re curious about Hong Kong’s past or just want a quiet place to visit, Pokfulam Farm is worth checking out.

reviews: Rating: 5 - We took the iconic Star Ferry ⛴️from Tsim Sha Tsui Star Ferry Pier to Wan Chai Ferry Pier 🛟 and it was a beautiful night 🌌 to be sailing on the ferry.  The Star Ferry has been in operation since the 1920's and it is just amazing to be able to catch a ride on this big part of Hong Kong 🇭🇰history books 📚. So instead of taking a train 🚇 or bus 🚌, we diverted our route 🛣️ and decided to get on the ferry ⛴️.  Terminal – The Star 🌟 Ferry terminal is crowded. Although it has a high 📈 frequency of sail, (every 15 mins?) still lots of people rush 🏃🏃‍♀️🏃‍♂️ there. The cost 💵 for us was HKD$6.5 per person and we paid with an Octopus Card 💳. Use Google Maps 🌎 to determine exactly where you want to go 📍, locate the pier, double check with the staff 👮🏼‍♂️, then pay and board. An example would be me heading to Wan Chai, there are technically “2️⃣” piers at Wan Chai so read carefully.  Ferry - Once the Ferry comes alongside, the barrier ⛓️ will lift and the people can board. Do not need to rush, there should be ample seats 💺. The seats enable you to flip the backrest 2️⃣ ways so that you will “definitely face” the front / bow of the boat ⛴️ and will not end up sailing backwards. But if you are dying for the IG shoot 📸, you need to do your homework 📚and see exactly where the absolute front of the boat is.  It’s a short ⏱️ ride to cross the ocean 🌊 but the skyline was beautiful with all the buildings 🏢🏰🏯🏙️lighted up for Christmas 🎄and New Year 🎉🎊! (See my pics 📸 and videos 📹) as it sails across, the lights come nearer and nearer, brighter and brighter ... .It was cooling, charming and historic all at the same time. 😎  For less than USD$1, the question would be why would you not do it? 🤷‍♂️

Rating: 5 - I took the iconic Star ferry from this pier, crossing the Victoria Harbour from Tsim Sha Tsui to Central. The ferry runs pretty frequently and the crossing lasted about 10 minutes, offering wonderful views of the harbour and the city skyline.  Tickets are very affordable and I would absolutely recommend this as a practical means of getting from Kowloon to Hong Kong island, but also as an experience in and of itself.

Rating: 5 - The terminal is very old-school, like stepping into my auntie's old flat – mosaic tiles, rusty fans, the whole vibe. But it's clean and things move fast, no fuss.  The ferry itself also like from another time. Wooden benches, can open the windows, no air-con – just the natural sea breeze. Really simple, but honestly, quite shiok. For us used to everything so new and air-conditioned, it's a funny change.  The ride is the best part. Only a few minutes, but the view is power. You see the whole Hong Kong skyline, all the famous buildings, for just a few dollars.  Is it a must-do? One hundred percent. For the price of a coffee, you get the best photo spot and a nice breeze. #Visited Nov 2025.

Rating: 5 - This is one of those places where you don’t need a plan — just show up, walk, and let Hong Kong do the rest. We spent a wonderful evening strolling along the Tsim Sha Tsui Star Ferry Pier and promenade, and the scenery here is truly world-class. The best time to visit is right after sunset, when the sky is still blue and the city lights begin to shimmer and reflect across Victoria Harbour. The transition from day to night is beautiful and incredibly calming.  The views of Hong Kong Island’s skyline are expansive and iconic, with nonstop photo opportunities along the boardwalk, bridge areas, and waterfront railings. It’s the kind of place where you naturally slow down, take photos, and just enjoy being present.  Everything is also very conveniently located. The Star Ferry terminal is right there, making it easy to hop across the harbor or join a short cruise. For shopping and dining, K11 Musea is only a short walk away, and there are plenty of restaurants and cafés right along the harbor.  Whether you’re walking, sightseeing, or simply soaking in the atmosphere, this spot is a must-visit in Hong Kong.

reviews: Rating: 5 - The Wai (Chinese: 圍方; Jyutping: wai4fong1) is a shopping centre in Tai Wai, Hong Kong, which opened on 22 July 2023. The mall is managed by the MTR Corporation, and is the third largest shopping mall in eastern New Territories. The mall is located directly under private estate the Pavilia Farm, a property also managed by the MTR Corporation. It is connected to Tai Wai station. The shopping centre structure was designed by Ronald Lu and Partners, while P&T Group was responsible for interior design. The Wai has four storeys with a total floor area of 650,000 square feet (60,000 m2), including a 50,000-square-foot (4,600 m2) outdoor green area, an indoor car park with 390 parking spaces, and the largest bicycle parking lot in Hong Kong, with 330 bicycle parking spaces. Among the 150 shops in the mall, notable tenants include the largest of the 43 Market Place supermarkets in Hong Kong at the time of its opening, covering an area over 20,000 square feet (1,900 m2) and the Emperor Cinemas Plus+ cinema, the only cinema in Tai Wai, with six theatres and a total of 912 seats. There are eighteen electric vehicle charging stations and solar power facilities.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Visiting Tian Tan Buddha was one of the highlights of my trip to Hong Kong. The statue is massive and impressive up close, and climbing the 268 steps to the top is challenging but definitely worth it for the views and peaceful atmosphere. Its cold, windy and hot at the same time, make sure to wear sunscreen when your here. There are also some nice gift and souvenir stall inside the statue itself. They sell a variety of items like Buddha statues, prayer beads, keychains, and other small souvenirs that make great keepsakes from the visit. Overall, it’s a beautiful and memorable place to visit a mix of culture, scenery, and a peaceful spiritual atmosphere.

Rating: 5 - One ☝️of the key features of Lantau Island 🏝️ is the Big Buddha that sits on the very hill top of Lantau, which can be seen 👀 for many, many kilometres ♾️ away on the hiking 🥾trail.  Travel – There are many ways to travel up to the Big Buddha from Tung Chung 🗺️. The most convenient would be to take the cable car 🚠 or you can try a bus 🚎or taxi 🚕. Cable cars will have a queue, bus and taxi will take time ⏳but you can have a great view of the island as it drives up towards the top. Note that the bus has a weekend price surge 📈(a lot! 😅)  Walking up - To get to the top of The Big Buddha, there is no 🚫 entrance fee (it is FREE 🎉🎊) but you are encouraged 🗣️to donate if you can. After which, you can walk all the way up to the base of the Big Buddha. At the base level, you can walk a full circle 🔄 and take in the surrounding mountain ⛰️view.  Walking In – After all the photo taking, you can enter the inside of the Big Buddha via the base behind the main staircase. Inside, along the wall is a columbarium. Among those who are housed there, Anita Mui would be one of the most iconic Hong Kong 🇭🇰celebrities 💃. (🚫 pictures 📸) Inside, you then make your way up to the top 🔝whereby you can view the Tooth Relic of the Buddha.  Faith 🪷 has it that if you have a potential relationship with Buddha, you will be able to see the Tooth Relic in different colours 🔴🔵🟡🟢⚫️while the rest of us will see it in just pure white ⚪️. Along the inside walls, you will also find intricate wood 🪵carvings of the deities 🧚‍♀️ and buddha. Letters 📮from officials and construction details.  It is an impressive 😎 monument which you can only enjoy if you are fit 💪and are able to climb 🚶‍♀️the stairs to the top. So while you can do it, give it a go and with some blessings 🙏🏼, you will get good 👍weather 🌈 and clear skies 🌅 to enjoy the outing.

Rating: 5 - Traveling from TST to see the Tian Tan Buddha was a highlight of my trip.  Beyond the massive Tian Tan Buddha statue, make sure to visit the Po Lin Monastery. It has a very traditional, serene vibe that feels worlds away from the hustle of TST. The architecture is stunning and full of intricate details.  I was also impressed by the food variety; there are plenty of spots to eat, including great Indian options.  One big tip: The return queue for the cable car can be very long. Plan your timing carefully so you aren't stuck waiting for hours!

Rating: 5 - Tian Tan Buddha is one of Hong Kong’s most iconic landmarks and an unforgettable experience, both spiritually and visually. Located on Lantau Island, the massive bronze Buddha sits serenely atop a hill, offering breathtaking panoramic views of the surrounding mountains and sea.  Reaching the statue is part of the journey. After arriving in Ngong Ping (many visitors take the scenic cable car), you’ll climb over 200 steps to reach the base. The staircase can feel long, especially in warm weather, but the view becomes more impressive with each step. Once at the top, the scale of the Buddha is truly striking, calm, majestic, and incredibly detailed.  The atmosphere is peaceful despite the crowds. The nearby Po Lin Monastery adds to the cultural depth of the visit, with beautiful temple architecture, incense drifting through the air, and a sense of quiet reflection. It’s a place where sightseeing and spirituality blend naturally.  Whether you’re interested in history, photography, or simply soaking in panoramic views, Tian Tan Buddha is absolutely worth the trip. Try to go earlier in the day to avoid heavier crowds and to enjoy cooler temperatures during the climb.

Rating: 5 - Located on Lantau Island, this majestic bronze statue—often called the Big Buddha—stands tall at 34 meters, quietly overlooking the mountains and sea. The journey itself feels special. Climbing the 268 steps to reach the statue isn’t just physical; it feels symbolic, like you’re gradually leaving the noise of the world behind.  At the top, the view is breathtaking. Surrounded by lush greenery and open skies, the Buddha’s calm expression creates a powerful sense of peace. It’s not just a tourist attraction—it’s a spiritual landmark. The scale of the statue is impressive, but what truly stands out is the serenity you feel standing beneath it.  Right nearby is the beautiful Po Lin Monastery, where you can explore traditional temple architecture, light incense, and soak in the tranquil atmosphere. The blend of culture, history, and spirituality makes the entire visit meaningful.  Whether you’re religious or not, the Tian Tan Buddha offers something deeper—a quiet reminder to slow down, breathe, and reflect. If you’re in Hong Kong, this is absolutely a must-visit destination.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Visiting Tian Tan Buddha was one of the highlights of my trip to Hong Kong. The statue is massive and impressive up close, and climbing the 268 steps to the top is challenging but definitely worth it for the views and peaceful atmosphere. Its cold, windy and hot at the same time, make sure to wear sunscreen when your here. There are also some nice gift and souvenir stall inside the statue itself. They sell a variety of items like Buddha statues, prayer beads, keychains, and other small souvenirs that make great keepsakes from the visit. Overall, it’s a beautiful and memorable place to visit a mix of culture, scenery, and a peaceful spiritual atmosphere.

Rating: 5 - One ☝️of the key features of Lantau Island 🏝️ is the Big Buddha that sits on the very hill top of Lantau, which can be seen 👀 for many, many kilometres ♾️ away on the hiking 🥾trail.  Travel – There are many ways to travel up to the Big Buddha from Tung Chung 🗺️. The most convenient would be to take the cable car 🚠 or you can try a bus 🚎or taxi 🚕. Cable cars will have a queue, bus and taxi will take time ⏳but you can have a great view of the island as it drives up towards the top. Note that the bus has a weekend price surge 📈(a lot! 😅)  Walking up - To get to the top of The Big Buddha, there is no 🚫 entrance fee (it is FREE 🎉🎊) but you are encouraged 🗣️to donate if you can. After which, you can walk all the way up to the base of the Big Buddha. At the base level, you can walk a full circle 🔄 and take in the surrounding mountain ⛰️view.  Walking In – After all the photo taking, you can enter the inside of the Big Buddha via the base behind the main staircase. Inside, along the wall is a columbarium. Among those who are housed there, Anita Mui would be one of the most iconic Hong Kong 🇭🇰celebrities 💃. (🚫 pictures 📸) Inside, you then make your way up to the top 🔝whereby you can view the Tooth Relic of the Buddha.  Faith 🪷 has it that if you have a potential relationship with Buddha, you will be able to see the Tooth Relic in different colours 🔴🔵🟡🟢⚫️while the rest of us will see it in just pure white ⚪️. Along the inside walls, you will also find intricate wood 🪵carvings of the deities 🧚‍♀️ and buddha. Letters 📮from officials and construction details.  It is an impressive 😎 monument which you can only enjoy if you are fit 💪and are able to climb 🚶‍♀️the stairs to the top. So while you can do it, give it a go and with some blessings 🙏🏼, you will get good 👍weather 🌈 and clear skies 🌅 to enjoy the outing.

Rating: 5 - Traveling from TST to see the Tian Tan Buddha was a highlight of my trip.  Beyond the massive Tian Tan Buddha statue, make sure to visit the Po Lin Monastery. It has a very traditional, serene vibe that feels worlds away from the hustle of TST. The architecture is stunning and full of intricate details.  I was also impressed by the food variety; there are plenty of spots to eat, including great Indian options.  One big tip: The return queue for the cable car can be very long. Plan your timing carefully so you aren't stuck waiting for hours!

Rating: 5 - Tian Tan Buddha is one of Hong Kong’s most iconic landmarks and an unforgettable experience, both spiritually and visually. Located on Lantau Island, the massive bronze Buddha sits serenely atop a hill, offering breathtaking panoramic views of the surrounding mountains and sea.  Reaching the statue is part of the journey. After arriving in Ngong Ping (many visitors take the scenic cable car), you’ll climb over 200 steps to reach the base. The staircase can feel long, especially in warm weather, but the view becomes more impressive with each step. Once at the top, the scale of the Buddha is truly striking, calm, majestic, and incredibly detailed.  The atmosphere is peaceful despite the crowds. The nearby Po Lin Monastery adds to the cultural depth of the visit, with beautiful temple architecture, incense drifting through the air, and a sense of quiet reflection. It’s a place where sightseeing and spirituality blend naturally.  Whether you’re interested in history, photography, or simply soaking in panoramic views, Tian Tan Buddha is absolutely worth the trip. Try to go earlier in the day to avoid heavier crowds and to enjoy cooler temperatures during the climb.

Rating: 5 - Located on Lantau Island, this majestic bronze statue—often called the Big Buddha—stands tall at 34 meters, quietly overlooking the mountains and sea. The journey itself feels special. Climbing the 268 steps to reach the statue isn’t just physical; it feels symbolic, like you’re gradually leaving the noise of the world behind.  At the top, the view is breathtaking. Surrounded by lush greenery and open skies, the Buddha’s calm expression creates a powerful sense of peace. It’s not just a tourist attraction—it’s a spiritual landmark. The scale of the statue is impressive, but what truly stands out is the serenity you feel standing beneath it.  Right nearby is the beautiful Po Lin Monastery, where you can explore traditional temple architecture, light incense, and soak in the tranquil atmosphere. The blend of culture, history, and spirituality makes the entire visit meaningful.  Whether you’re religious or not, the Tian Tan Buddha offers something deeper—a quiet reminder to slow down, breathe, and reflect. If you’re in Hong Kong, this is absolutely a must-visit destination.

Rating: 3 - This particular Tin Hau Temple was built in the 1870s and is largely in its original form. The exterior is of a typical Tin Hau design with two dragon statue figures on the top of the roof and many figures carved into the wall which are worth inspecting. They are clearly showing their age and seem simpler in design compared to those found at more elaborate or recently restored Tin Hau Temples.  Inside we particularly liked the tiger and dragon wall murals as well as two large god statues. There are a couple of small rooms filled with various statues too and of course, burning traditional incense coils.  Around 4-5 minutes walk from the Tin Hau temple, there is another, lesser known temple called the Lin Ka Fung Temple. This temple is recessed along Tung Lo Wan Road. In contrast, Lin Ka Fung is a Kwun Yum temple and offers an architectural comparison, worth a quick look for those eager to see more of the Hong Kong temple scene.  Other Tin Hau temples of note that can be visited in Hong Kong include those in Stanley, Sai Kung and Ya Ma Tei among many other smaller temples spread around HK, dedicated to Tin Hau.

address: Tai Po, Hong Kong
reviews: Rating: 5 - Tin Hau Temple, Tai Po Old Market  I have a particular interest in historical sites.  Tin Hau Temple is one of the oldest temples in Hong Kong.  It's very popular, with incense smoke filling the air, creating a dimly lit atmosphere.  Tin Hau Temple was listed as a Grade II historic building in 1981, and later as a Grade III historic building.  Built in the 30th year of the Kangxi Emperor's reign (1691), it was built by the Li family. Originally located on the waterfront, it now stands in the heart of Tai Po town center due to land reclamation over the years.

Rating: 4 - Located in the Ancestral Hall Village of Tai Heng Township, Kowloon Hang, the Tin Hau Temple and the Wendi Ancient Temple were built in 1728 and 1884, respectively.  The Tin Hau Temple in Tai Heng Township, Tai Po, was completed in 1728 (the fifth year of the Yongzheng reign). Ancient bells and tripods cast during the Yongzheng reign are still preserved within the temple. The adjacent Wendi Ancient Temple was built in 1884 (the tenth year of the Guangxu reign). Beside the temple stand two slender-leaved banyan trees, their trunks intertwined, forming a chariot of love, said to be a century old.  The Tin Hau Temple and the Wendi Ancient Temple in Tai Heng Township are connected buildings.  The Tin Hau Ancient Temple is surrounded by mountains and forests behind it, and by a tranquil pastoral setting in front. During each Taiping Qingjiao festival, a grand stage is erected in front of the temple, creating a grand spectacle for both humans and gods to enjoy.  The Tianhou Temple in Taiheng Township was built in 1727, the fourth year of the Yongzheng reign of the Qing Dynasty, according to a cloud plaque still extant within the temple. Since then, the temple has undergone numerous renovations, and numerous plaques and inscriptions are preserved within the temple, including a plaque dedicated to the Tianhou Temple by a member of the Wen family in the 60th year of the Qianlong reign, a stele inscribed with the reconstruction of the Tianhou Temple in the 10th year of the Guangxu reign, and a stele inscribed with the reconstruction of the Tianhou and Wendi Temples in 1985.  A bell within the temple is inscribed with the words "Auspicious day of the spring month of Dingwei, the fifth year of the Yongzheng reign."  When the Tianhou Temple was rebuilt in 1884, Taiheng villagers added the Wendi Temple adjacent to it, enshrining the Wenchang Zitong Emperor, the Wenchang Jinjia Shenjun, and the Wenchang Kuidou Xingjun.  During the 2005 Taiheng Taiping Qingjiao Festival, the space between the two temples, formerly a kitchen, was converted into the Yuanchen Hall, dedicated to the sixty Tai Sui and offered to devotees.  Not far from the Tin Hau Temple are two slender-leaved banyan trees, known as the Century-Old Twin Trees. These ancient trees, with their lush roots and foliage, resemble the Wen clan, which has flourished into a major clan in the New Territories.  At the foot of the banyan trees stand the two immortals of harmony and unity.

Rating: 4 - This Tin Hau Temple along the Lung Yeuk Tau Heritage Trail is a Declared Monument in Hong Kong (2002). It is stop 5 on the trail and is located just beside the Tang Chung Ling Ancestral Hall (stop 6) if you are starting this self-guided walk from the southern end. What you will find is a small, two-hall structure that is built in traditional temple architecture of the Qing Dynasty. It is open from 9am to 5pm daily if you want to enter and have a look around.  Unfortunately, the original construction dates of this Tin Hau Temple are lost. However, history records that it was in here prior to the Tang Chung Ling Ancestral Hall being built in the early 16th century. The temple was given major restorations in 1913 and 1981.  From the outside, what you will see is a grey brick exterior with decorative plaster works below the the tiled roofing. There is additional decorative works on the roof. Do make sure to note the blue(ish) coloured board sign with the Chinese characters 'Tin Hau Kong situated just above the entrance.  The interior similarly resembles other Tin Hau Temples you may have seen and visited around Hong Kong. You'll see expected shrines with deity figures, guardian statues on both sides of main centre alter, hanging incense coils and lanterns. On the right side bay is a nice set of early 20th century style furnishing. Perhaps the most interesting are the two bronze cast bells located in the left side bay. These date back to 1695 and 1700 according to the history panel posted just outside the temple.  In the end, this is a nice historical Tin Hau Temple that is easy and quick to visit. You can conveniently do so in 5-6 minutes before your visit to the important Tang Chung Ling Ancestral Hall (stop 6) just next to the temple.

Rating: 5 - An interesting small temple that is next door to the Tang Chung Ling Ancestral Hall and a short distance from the walled village of Lo Wai. All are declared monuments and form key parts of the Lung Yeuk Tau Heritage Trail. Well worth a visit.

Rating: 4 - This Temple is a traditional two-hall building with a central courtyard. The facade of the temple is exquisitely decorated with plaster mouldings and murals of auspicious motifs. The main hall of the temple is devoted to the worship of Tin Hau and her guards, Chin Lei Ngan (who is believed to see things a thousand li [Chinese miles] away) and Shun Fung Yi (whose ears can hear sounds as far away as from heaven). The oldest relics surviving in the temple are two cast iron bells which are kept in the east chamber of the rear hall. One of the bells was cast in 1695 as a gift from the Tang clan to thank Tin Hau after having their sons adopted by her. The other bell was cast in 1700 as an offering to Tin Hau so that the young men of the clan could be blessed during their journey to the city for taking the provincial examinations. The temple was declared a monument on 15 November 2002. (By AMO)

address: Crooked Island, Hong Kong
reviews: Rating: 4 - There are numerous temples around Hong Kong dedicated to Tin Hau, the Goddess of the Sea, including this historic temple on Kat O (Crooked Island) in the Double Haven area of New Territories. Several small temples are scattered around Kat O, this being the largest and most impressive.  This is a traditional Qing Dynasty era temple with a two hall, three bay layout that was originally built in 1763. The exterior is grey brick with decorative entrance, facade and roofing. There are very attractive ceramic figurines on the exterior that are worth viewing before entering the temple.  The interior is very decorative with expected shrines and deity figures, large standing deities guarding the main centre chamber. You'll see nice wall murals, wood carvings as well as a large ceremonial drum and bronze bell with a gorgeous dragon handle in the side bays.  Overall, this is a nice Tin Hau Temple that is worth spending 10-15 minutes to enjoy while exploring Kat O island. Note, there is now a Kat O Story Room, a relatively new attraction (opened in Oct 2019) on the side of the Tin Hau Temple. This is a good opportunity to learn more about the history, heritage and culture of the island, a nice overall complement to a visit to Tin Hau Temple.

Rating: 4 - The Tin Hau Temple located in Ma Wan Village, Lei Yue Mun was built in the 18th year of Qing Emperor Qianlong (1753 AD). The temple has once attracted large numbers of pilgrims but has been damaged several times, leaving behind an archway, a tablet, an inscription and an old clock at the scene. The temple was renovated in 1953 and 1986. Walking through the main path leading to the temple, people can see the beautiful scenery of Victoria Harbour. According to legend, Tin Hau (天后), the Heavenly Goddess, was born in the Sung Dynasty (960 - 1279 AD). Her native place was Fujian Province, and her mortal name was Lam Mak-leung (林默). Possessing supernatural power, she saved many people from disasters of the sea. Therefore, she is regarded by the seafaring folks as their Patron Saint.

Rating: 5 - The Tin Hau Temple in Shui Wei Village is said to have been built during the reign of Emperor Kangxi of the Qing Dynasty (1662-1722), and has undergone reconstruction and repairs in the past. Among the temple's antiques is an ancient bell from the 60th year of the Qing Dynasty (1745), erected by Deng Chun-kui, a tribute scholar. The temple enshrines the Earth God, the Tin Hau Goddess, and the Golden Flower Goddess.  It will be open for a few days during the Lunar New Year.  The Tin Hau Temple once collapsed due to disrepair. It is said that a high-ranking monk named Fen Fu was instructed to assist the villagers of Kam Tin in its reconstruction. A wooden plaque from the 25th year of the Republic of China (1936) records the villagers' donations. In the list of donors for the reconstruction, High-ranking monk Fen Fu donated 280 silver dollars, followed by Kam Tin elders Deng Bo-qiu, Deng Wei-tang, and Deng Yong-shou, whose donations were all less than ten dollars. Other ancestral temples, Hung Shing Temple, and Ji Hing Wai also donated one or several silver dollars.  In Kam Tin's Shui Tou and Shui Wei villages, there are temples dedicated to Hung Shing and Tin Hau, both famous water deities in China. The villagers hope for their protection and good weather, as the Kam Tin plain is entirely dependent on water, with rivers and farmland everywhere. Worshiping the water deities is a way to ensure the rivers don't overflow and flood crops, and also to protect the villagers' safety.

Rating: 4 - There are numerous Tin Hau temples found throughout Hong Kong including this temple at the Old Fisherman's Village along Hoi Ping Street on Tap Mun (Grass Island). It is less than 5 minute walk north of the main ferry pier and the most interesting heritage attraction you will see on the island.  This Tin Hau Temple is a Grade I Historical building in Hong Kong that dates back nearly 400 years. It is beautifully situated above the shoreline, approached by a set of steps, through a monumental gateway entrance and offers fine exterior architecture and interior decor. There is a large traditional incense burner and two stone guardian lions in front of the entrance. You will nice mural and ceramic sculptures which line its facade.  The interior of the temple is very well maintained with decorative wood carvings, shrine with deity figures, guardian deity figures that guard both sides of the main altar, handing hanging lanterns, ceremonial decor and murals adorning its walls. There is an old wooden sampan boat and ancient drum and bell which dates back to 1737.  Within you will also find Chinese moon gate style side entrance to a separate annex temple to Kwan Tai. This temple space was added around 1788. Within the same complex there is another separated temple building to the south that is dedicated to Kun Iam. These are also worth a look-see while visiting the Tin Hau Temple here at Tap Mun.

Rating: 3 - There are many temples scattered around Hong Kong dedicated to Goddess of the Sea, Tin Hau, including several on Lamma Island. This Tin Hau Temple is located near the southern end of the Main Street in Yung Shue Wan village on the west side of the island. It is around a 5 minute walk from the main ferry pier and one of the first recommended stops to make for those hiking across Lamma to Sok Kwu Wan.  This is a typical Tin Hau style temple that is believed to be around 100 years old. It was reconstructed in the 1960s and has a subtly decorative facade and interior with expected shrine, deity figures, hanging lanterns and incense. There is an ancient bell and drum within as well. What makes this temple unique are the two stone lion figures guarding the temple entrance, they are uniquely western lions in style, considerably different to the classic Chinese lions that you see at almost all temples around Hong Kong. The lions sit horizontally, like the famous HSBC lions, Stitch and Stephen in Central District. This is also different to how Chinese lions are posted sitting straight forward and upward.

reviews: Rating: 3 - There are two temples on the small Tung Ping Chau Island. The larger of the two is the historic Tin Hau Temple located on the eastern side of the island facing the sea and mainland China.  Dedicated to the Goddess of the Sea, the Tin Ha Temple is believed to have been built around the middle of the 18th-century and is architecturally similar to those of the Qing Dynasty.  The exterior is cream colour and red with simple murals below the traditional green Chinese roofing. There are several porcelain figures of guardian lions in the flat front area of the temple. You will also see Chinese characters on both sides and directly above the entrance.  Within the Tin Hau Temple, there is a small entry area with red shrine on one side of the door and a ceremonial bell from the Qing Dynastay on the other. Proceed to the back chamber and you will find shrines with multiple deity figures, including the goddess Tin Hau on the centre altar. On the side altars, there are deity figures dedicated to Hung Shing and the Year God.  Note: Just outside the temple are two information panels. They are aged and quite faded from sun exposure over the years. However, you can still read them to learn about the history and architecture of this Tin Hau Temple.

address: Tai Po, Hong Kong
reviews: Rating: 5 - Tin Hau Temple, Tai Po Old Market  I have a particular interest in historical sites.  Tin Hau Temple is one of the oldest temples in Hong Kong.  It's very popular, with incense smoke filling the air, creating a dimly lit atmosphere.  Tin Hau Temple was listed as a Grade II historic building in 1981, and later as a Grade III historic building.  Built in the 30th year of the Kangxi Emperor's reign (1691), it was built by the Li family. Originally located on the waterfront, it now stands in the heart of Tai Po town center due to land reclamation over the years.

Rating: 4 - Located in the Ancestral Hall Village of Tai Heng Township, Kowloon Hang, the Tin Hau Temple and the Wendi Ancient Temple were built in 1728 and 1884, respectively.  The Tin Hau Temple in Tai Heng Township, Tai Po, was completed in 1728 (the fifth year of the Yongzheng reign). Ancient bells and tripods cast during the Yongzheng reign are still preserved within the temple. The adjacent Wendi Ancient Temple was built in 1884 (the tenth year of the Guangxu reign). Beside the temple stand two slender-leaved banyan trees, their trunks intertwined, forming a chariot of love, said to be a century old.  The Tin Hau Temple and the Wendi Ancient Temple in Tai Heng Township are connected buildings.  The Tin Hau Ancient Temple is surrounded by mountains and forests behind it, and by a tranquil pastoral setting in front. During each Taiping Qingjiao festival, a grand stage is erected in front of the temple, creating a grand spectacle for both humans and gods to enjoy.  The Tianhou Temple in Taiheng Township was built in 1727, the fourth year of the Yongzheng reign of the Qing Dynasty, according to a cloud plaque still extant within the temple. Since then, the temple has undergone numerous renovations, and numerous plaques and inscriptions are preserved within the temple, including a plaque dedicated to the Tianhou Temple by a member of the Wen family in the 60th year of the Qianlong reign, a stele inscribed with the reconstruction of the Tianhou Temple in the 10th year of the Guangxu reign, and a stele inscribed with the reconstruction of the Tianhou and Wendi Temples in 1985.  A bell within the temple is inscribed with the words "Auspicious day of the spring month of Dingwei, the fifth year of the Yongzheng reign."  When the Tianhou Temple was rebuilt in 1884, Taiheng villagers added the Wendi Temple adjacent to it, enshrining the Wenchang Zitong Emperor, the Wenchang Jinjia Shenjun, and the Wenchang Kuidou Xingjun.  During the 2005 Taiheng Taiping Qingjiao Festival, the space between the two temples, formerly a kitchen, was converted into the Yuanchen Hall, dedicated to the sixty Tai Sui and offered to devotees.  Not far from the Tin Hau Temple are two slender-leaved banyan trees, known as the Century-Old Twin Trees. These ancient trees, with their lush roots and foliage, resemble the Wen clan, which has flourished into a major clan in the New Territories.  At the foot of the banyan trees stand the two immortals of harmony and unity.

Rating: 5 - Poem Title: Jagged Rocks A sacred turtle ascends the mountain to see a monk, but the monk was once deserted. A bright lamp illuminates the way, and the Buddha's Hand Rock at the southern tip holds a unique charm.  This poem describes the scene I witnessed with my team while patrolling the Po Toi Country Trail on Po Toi Island. Po Toi Island is flat and appears as a floating platform at sea, hence its name. The highest point on the island is Tung Tau Ting (242 meters). Po Toi Island is the southernmost inhabited island in Hong Kong. Along the coast, one can see Ling Turtle Hill and Monk Rock. Twenty years ago, there weren't so many tourists here. Reaching the 126 Lighthouse and looking back, one can see the sacred turtle and the monk on opposite sides. This lighthouse is the southernmost navigation lighthouse in Hong Kong, used for ship navigation. Passing Nam Kok Tsui, one reaches Buddha's Hand Rock, a rock that strongly resembles a Buddha's hand, comparable to the Ghost Hand Rock in the sea at Wong Chuk Kok Tsui.

reviews: Rating: 5 - The Toy Soldiers Parachute Drop is a "parachute jump-style" drop tower attraction located in the Toy Story themed lands at Walt Disney Studios Park (Disneyland Paris) and Hong Kong Disneyland. Attraction Description The ride is themed around the green army men from the Toy Story films, specifically the scene where they parachute down the stair banisters to scout for Andy's birthday presents. Guests are enlisted as new recruits to "Sarge's" squadron for a high-flying training exercise. Riders board a 6-person vehicle that resembles a camouflage-canopied parachute. The vehicle is hoisted up an 82-foot (25-meter) tower, offering panoramic views of the surrounding area before "tumbling" back down to Earth in a sequence of gentle rises and falls. The ride is designed as a family-friendly drop experience, less intense than a typical freefall tower. The surrounding area is heavily themed to look like a giant toy army base, complete with oversized plastic accessories, a World War II jeep, and a large Playskool baby monitor that crackles with updates on "Andy's presence". Key Information Locations: Walt Disney Studios Park (Disneyland Paris) and Hong Kong Disneyland. Ride Type: A gentle "Paratower" or parachute jump-style drop ride. Height Requirement: Guests must be at least 81 cm (32 inches) tall to ride. Thrill Level: Moderate; it offers a fun, floating sensation rather than an intense, stomach-dropping freefall. Theming: Immersive, oversized toy army base setting as if guests have shrunk to toy size.

Rating: 3 - A historic walled village nested in Shatin with housing estates nearby. Close walk from train station and public parking at nearby estates. A long history below:  Tsang Tai Uk (Chinese: 曾大屋 or "Big House of the Tsangs"), also known as Shan Ha Wai ("Walled Village at the Mountain's Foot"), is a Hakka walled village in Hong Kong, and one of the best preserved. The complex is located in Sha Tin close to the south of Pok Hong Estate, near Lion Rock Tunnel Road.  The construction of Shan Ha Wai was begun in 1847 by the wealthy granite merchant and stonemason Tsang Koon-Man as a stronghold for the Tsang clan, and took around 20 years to complete. The original granite, bricks and solid timber are still preserved today. The complex is rectangular and consists of three rows of houses enclosed by grey brick walls. The four corners each feature a three-story guard tower with openings in the wall through which guns could be fired back in the early days of the complex's role as a defensive fortification.[1] All the houses are interlinked by passages and small courtyards. In the innermost row of houses is an ancestral hall where meetings and ceremonies took place. There are three arched entrances in the northern wall. The main or ceremonial entrance is in the middle and leads to the ancestral hall. In front of the main building is a massive courtyard, where villagers traditionally winnowed and dried their harvest. It also contained a study hall where the Tsang children were tutored before schools existed.  Shan Ha Wai gained its current name Tsang Tai Uk from locals when it housed displaced families after the Second World War.  During the 1970s development of the Sha Tin New Town, the surrounding area was developed significantly. During the course of new town development in Hong Kong, sometimes villages were relocated. However, Tsang Tai Uk was preserved due to its historical significance.  In 1979 the village had about 700 residents, of whom about 300 belonged to the Tsang clan.[3] Prince Charles, a former archaeology and history student, visited Tsang Tai Uk on 4 March 1979 during a royal tour.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Visited Tsing Shan Monastery for the first time yesterday. Lesser know of the monasteries in Hong Kong, it is more secluded and less frequented by the public. It is also known as Castle Peak Monastery, situated at the foot of Castle Peak, near Tuen Mun, Hong Kong. According to legend, an Indian monk who liked travelling in a wooden cup was believed to have lodged where the monastery now stands. Attracted by the natural wonders and the serene milieu, he built a chalet there for practicing meditation.Since then, the name of Reverend Pui To (杯渡禪師; 'travelling in a cup') has become widespread. It is a must visit if you enjoy the beautiful Hong Kong country side and observing traditions of Buddhism.

Rating: 4 - The Tsing Shan Monastery (Castle Peak Monastery) is situated along the Tsing Shan Monastery Path upon the lower slopes of Castle Peak mountain west of Tuen Mun. It can be visited on its own but given its isolation and distance from other sightseeing, it is best combined with hikes up to Castle Peak mountain.  Historically, it is believed that an early 5th-century Buddhist monk by the name of Master Pei arrived at Tuen Mun and lived out his days as a hermit at this location. Hence, Tsing Shan is considered the birthplace of Buddhism in Hong Kong.  The two main temples you can see here include Tsing Wan Kwan, a Taoist Temple designed in Qing Dynasty style architecture in 1829 (restored in 2009). It is just beside the Tsing Shan Monastery, which was build in more traditional Buddhist stye and manner between 1918-30. Both buildings are beautiful, well restored and maintained and worth a spending time to enjoy.  There are additional monuments, statues and other structures upon above the two main temples their are ornamental monastery grounds as well as information panels regarding the Bruce Lee film scenes from Enter The Dragon which took place here in 1973. This is a further reason some come to visit the Tsing Shan Monastery.  Quite a bit to see here so best to allow 30+ minutes if you are making a stopover here as part of a hike up to Castle Peak by way of the Tsing Shan Path.

Rating: 5 - Every year, a three-week winter Zen retreat is held, bringing together Zen practitioners from mainland China, Malaysia, Australia, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and other parts of the world to cultivate the supreme path, inherit the traditions of Weiyang Zen, and continue the wisdom of Buddhism.  【Transportation Guide】 1. From the airport: Take Airport Bus S1 or S64 to Tung Chung MTR Station, then transfer to Lantau Bus 11 to Lung Tsai Station. Walk into the Qiangshan Aqueduct, continue straight to the railway bridge, and then ascend the mountain. There are signs for Tse Hing Temple along the way. Follow the map and choose route two (as shown in the attached map, Gaode Map APP).  To build Tse Hing Zen Temple, Venerable Master Hsuan Hua worked tirelessly, even while ill, traveling far and wide, enduring wind and rain, and working day and night. He personally oversaw every aspect of the project, from hiring laborers and purchasing materials to preparing food for the statues. The Venerable Master wrote a verse:  Night falls on Linghui Mountain, I step out of Cixing Temple,  The lonely moon shines on the poor monk, A multitude of stars surround the North Pole.  Worldly affairs are like a dream, Few truly understand;  Do not be swayed by worldly dust, Grant yourself oneness of the six senses.  In 1962, Master Lun presided over the Cixing Temple, while the women's section was overseen by Masters Guoli and Guoren (also known as Hengyi and Hengqi).  Master Fazang, a Dharma heir of the eminent Tiantai master, Venerable Tan, renovated the temple over a year, completing the dormitories and guest rooms.
