Rating: 4 - Having spent a night here, I'm rewriting this travelogue here.  The western part of Lantau Island is remote and vast. Although I've been there before, I didn't climb all the peaks, so this time I split the trip into two days to explore properly. I chose Tsz Hing Temple halfway up the mountain as my midpoint.  Starting from Sham Wai Road, I ascended via the Lantau Trail, then took a smaller path to visit Kwun Yam Shan. At the summit, there's a tall marker pillar; looking down from the west, the Shek Bi Reservoir forms an angle with Sai Kau. Continuing down the Lantau Trail, there's a weather station by the roadside. There's a small hill to the left that's worth climbing. Further on, I crossed a valley and ascended several steps to Keung Shan. On the eastern slope, several large white rocks jut out above the Shek Bi Reservoir. The reservoir dam is curved like a barrel, with grassy slopes on the sides; cars drive along the edge of the barrel. Unfortunately, smog blew in, and the sunset weakened, so I quickly descended. At the valley, I turned right onto the Keung Shan Country Trail, then left onto the Lantau Trail for a short stretch of paved road. Afterwards, Phoenix Path leads away from the cement road, which goes straight up to Cixing Temple.  Passing the archway and a stream, I arrived at the temple. The iron gate was closed, but not locked. Entering, I found the temple quite large. There were several buildings in a row, and a large square. The main hall was lit, with only an old monk sitting on a stool, his head nodding as he dozed off. Not wanting to disturb him, I looked around. To the left of the main hall were the boys' dormitories, more than a dozen rooms on the second floor, each with several bunk beds and ceiling fans. A sign at the entrance said no food was allowed in the rooms. I ate my packed dinner in the square.  At nine o'clock, the alarm clock rang. The old monk got up, closed the door, turned off the lights, and went straight into the dormitory, seemingly not seeing me. I could have asked to borrow his bed for the night, but I was afraid of startling him. The room was stuffy, and wanting more outdoor experience, I went to the Western Three Saints Hall to the right of the main hall. I laid out a makeshift bed on the tiled floor in front of the door, above which were high eaves and half a starry sky.  The old monk went to bed early and got up early as well. I heard him pouring rice into the pot and checked my watch; it was only three o'clock. When it was light, I opened the door to leave. The old monk came out to greet me and asked if I needed water.

Rating: 5 - According to the original text from the same lineage: Originally built in 1930 by Master Fachuan, it was originally named Guoxing Temple. Unfortunately, it was burned down by the Japanese army during the Japanese occupation of Hong Kong, and Master Fachuan also perished. In the autumn of 1953, lay Buddhist Dong Guoqi, who was well-versed in Buddhist affairs, donated a two-story villa he had built next to Guoxing Temple to Master Dulun for Buddhist worship. Due to this special connection, the Master consulted with the relevant people of Guoxing Temple and, with their consent, decided to renovate the old temple and the villa together. The villa was renovated first and named: Cixing Temple Left Courtyard. The Three Jewels were enshrined in the courtyard, and it remains intact to this day. Later, Master Dulun raised more funds to build the current Mahavira Hall, and Yu Youren, a senior member of the Kuomintang, specially inscribed the plaque "Mahavira Hall" for Master Dulun. In 1962, Venerable Dulun served as acting presiding monk of Tse Hing Temple, while the women's quarters were presided over by Venerable Guoli and Venerable Guoren (also known as Hengyi and Hengqi). Venerable Fazang, a Dharma Master of the Tiantai School, wrote the Dharma inscription for the Venerable Master Tan. Venerable Fazang renovated the temple for over a year, completing the dormitories and guest rooms. The Venerable Master Tan personally inscribed the plaque "Jing Le Ju" (Pure and Joyful Abode), which still exists today. With the four major renovations, the main hall finally acquired its magnificent glazed tile roof and imposing grandeur.  Venerable Dulun accepted many Americans as disciples in the United States. In 1973, three of his American disciples came to Hong Kong to join Tse Hing Temple and began translating the Lotus Sutra into English. Tse Hing Temple thus became the first Buddhist temple in Hong Kong to accept foreign monks. Venerable Fazang left Cixing Temple in 1974, having made significant contributions to the temple community. After Venerable Dulun's cremation, he left behind thousands of relics, some of which were transported back to Cixing Temple for enshrinement. The temple is located at the source of Wanzhangbu, surrounded by interconnected streams, pools, and waterfalls, creating a magnificent spectacle that resembles a vast silver ribbon descending from the sky. Behind Cixing Temple, three rock formations are arranged. A layperson named Guosheng utilized the natural terrain to sculpt a reinforced concrete dragon. The dragon, about four feet long, is depicted with outstretched claws and vibrant colors, becoming a scenic wonder of western Yushu. Unfortunately, the mountain path is now overgrown with weeds, making it best viewed from afar. Behind the temple lies a spring that gushes forth from a rocky creek year-round, never drying up even in drought—an incredible phenomenon. Master Dulun refers to it as "Dragon's Mouth Water." A water geologist once analyzed the spring water and found it to be exceptionally pure and free of impurities. Cixing Temple is a relatively private Buddhist temple. Currently, the men's quarters are managed and practiced by Venerable Hengxing and monks sent by the Dharma Realm Buddhist Association. The temple still maintains the strict rule of not eating after noon.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Nina Fossil Garden is a truly unique and captivating attraction in Hong Kong. As the territory's only large-scale tree fossil garden, it offers a rare and profound experience 😍 The site is expansive, covering a beautifully landscaped 80,000 square feet, where visitors can stroll among dozens of incredible prehistoric relics.  The garden masterfully blends natural history with landscape design, presenting these ancient specimens some stretching an impressive 25 metres long as permanent open-air sculptures. Dating back hundreds of millions of years, the fossils are installed with great care, creating a powerful dialogue between the static, stone tree trunks and the vibrant, living plants that surround them.  This thoughtful presentation doesn't just showcase fossils; it immerses you in the narrative of our planet. It’s both an educational journey into deep time and an inspiring, peaceful escape. A visit here allows you to quietly contemplate the immense, dynamic forces of nature and geology, making it a must see for nature lovers, families, and anyone looking for a moment of reflection in Hong Kong 💯☺️

reviews: Rating: 4 - Tsuen Wan Plaza is basically a huge shopping mall in the New Territories that connects straight to the MTR, so it’s super easy to get to. Once you’re inside, it feels like a small city — you can shop, eat, watch a movie, and even let kids play, all without stepping outside. That’s especially nice in Hong Kong when it’s either really hot or pouring rain.  The mall has a big mix of shops: clothing stores, beauty counters, lifestyle brands, and plenty of local spots. You don’t need to go anywhere else because everything is under one roof. Food is a big highlight — there are casual cafés, bakeries, and proper restaurants serving Chinese, Japanese, and Western dishes. If you’re hungry late, you’ll still find something open.  Entertainment is built in too. There’s a modern cinema with 3D screens and a huge outdoor playground for kids, which makes it a family‑friendly place. The mall also changes decorations and hosts events during holidays, so it always feels lively.  Overall, Tsuen Wan Plaza is more than just a shopping mall — it’s a convenient hangout spot where you can spend hours without getting bored. Easy access, lots of variety, and a fun atmosphere make it a go‑to place in Tsuen Wan.

Rating: 4 - In the early 1990s, I used to visit the Plaza daily. On 31 Jan 2022, when I visited it again, I was surprised to find that it had uplifted itself. The ambience lured customers to shop or eat.  Postscript  On 19 March 2024, we came here again to park our car before watching a performance competition in the adjacent Tsuen Wan Town Hall. Parking here during week days was just $18/hour.

Rating: 3 - Tsuen Wan Plaza is one of the larger shopping malls near to the Tsuen Wan West MTR Station and is linked to other shopping venues in the area, like Citywalk, by way of covered bridges. This property originally opened in 1992 but was given a large scale renovation in 2009. The shopping space, particularly on the lower floors where there is a large atrium is well lit and rather nice.  Within Tsuen Wan Plaza, you'll find 6-7 floors filled with midrange retail brands and a recognisable group of restaurants and coffee shops found in better malls around the Hong Kong. You'll also find a Yata Department Store, cinema and children's playground area.  Overall, this is not a bad place, nicer than the cluster of lower end shopping centres and arcades around the Town Centre and Tseun Wan MTR Station. Instead, Tsuen Wan Plaza is more modern and similar to places like Citywalk, Nina Mall and Op Mall around Tsuen Wan West MTR Station.

Rating: 5 - Tsz Shan Monastery 慈山寺is a serene Buddhist temple in Tai Po, Hong Kong, known for its 76-meter-tall Guan Yin (Goddess of Mercy) statue and peaceful environment. Visits are free, but online registration in advance is required due to limited daily visitor numbers to maintain tranquility. Located at 88 Universal Gate Road, Tai Po, New Territories, Hong Kong. Admission is Free, but requires booking a spot via the official Tsz Shan Monastery website up to one month in advance. Key Attractions are the colossal 76-meter-tall bronze-cast Guan Yin statue, which is the focal point of the monastery. Beautifully manicured gardens, tranquil ponds, and various halls, including the Main Buddha Hall and Maitreya Hall.  Opportunities for spiritual practices like water offering and Zen calligraphy. To get to the temple, public transport is encouraged as visitor parking is not available. The best way is to take Minibus 20T: Operates directly between MTR Tai Po Market Station and the monastery entrance on weekdays (except public holidays).

Rating: 4 - Unique and unexpected canyon known locally as Hong Kong's mini Grand Canyon, located around 10 minute hike northeast of Por Lo Shan.  The Mini Grand Canyon wouldn't be particularly special in desert like destinations elsewhere but seems completely out of place here in Hong Kong. You can walk around the rim of the canyon and peer down into its shallow depths admiring the earth's layers and colour changes. In the distance, you will see more silty and grooved peaks that make up the Hinterland. To the west and north you can see Shenzhen in the distance as well.  Note: There are a few ways to hike up to Por Lo Shan and the mini-Grand Canyon. Probably the most convenient is to make way to San Wai Court by way of the Sui Hong MTR Station and Light Rail lines 505 or 615, getting off at San Wai and then walking through the estates until reaching the paved footpath that leads up to Por Lo Shan. The canyon is further northwest from there.  Alternatively, you can combine with a longer hike that takes in Castle Peak although I'd only recommend combining if you have good hiking fitness, sufficient water, sun protection and time on your hands.

Rating: 5 - I believe that Mui Dui Hai Village, located in Sai Kung, is another mysterious housing estate, after Sha Tau Kok Village, that many people want to explore but feel are unattainable—indeed, I had the same impression before visiting Mui Dui Hai Village. After all, the village isn't close to Sai Kung city center; you have to walk or take a minibus to get there, which isn't very convenient.  I remember the first time I heard the name Mui Dui Hai Village, I thought, "Is it on the other side of the sea?" I assumed Mui Dui Hai was on Hong Kong Island, separated by a harbor. Later I realized that "Mui Dui Hai" was actually a place within Sai Kung. (laughs)  However, even more memorable than the name is the first time I saw photos of Mui Dui Hai Village—my goodness, this isn't the public housing I usually imagine; it's a low-density residential area that's practically a luxury mansion!  Finally, on a whim, I decided to go to Sai Kung to relax and also visited the previously mentioned Tsui Tong Garden, as well as the protagonist of this article, which is also the easternmost housing estate in Hong Kong: Mui Dui Hai Village.  To explore the opposite seaside village was quite an ordeal, but it also allowed me to appreciate many sights I wouldn't normally notice. Although I knew there were minibuses running directly from Sai Kung town center to the village, having just visited Tsui Tong Garden earlier, I was still feeling a bit unsatisfied and thought: why not just walk to the opposite seaside village?  Even with the overcast skies, the beauty of the village's architecture remained undiminished. Entering the village once again shattered my usual expectations of public housing – the buildings, built into the hillside, were extremely sparsely populated, and even with stairs, the spaces between the buildings felt quite spacious. The entire village consists of only four buildings: Hoi Fu House, Hoi Tai House, Hoi Ning House, and Hoi Cheong House. Each building is only about four stories high, without elevators or gates, making entry and exit very convenient. To complement the surrounding rural environment, the village adopts a Chinese rural design style, with white walls and orange-brown tiled roofs, imitation dougong (bracket set) decorations on the exterior walls, round windows, and Chinese-style pavilions in public areas. Furthermore, upon closer inspection, I noticed that each building had a nameplate with calligraphy hanging high above its main entrance, adding to its antique charm.  The dripping sound grew more frequent, and coupled with the fresh, grassy scent, it truly seemed an impending downpour. It was then that I realized the housing estate had a memorial monument; shortly after the completion of the opposite seaside estate, Sir Edward Youde officiated at its opening ceremony in 1986.  Continuing to walk forward with my umbrella, I saw murals by illustrator Chocolate Rain, as well as a more modern one. A closer look revealed that the murals were created for the Housing Society's 75th anniversary this year, adding a touch of art to the otherwise unassuming rural housing estate.  Before leaving the estate, I thought: Hmm, looks like I'll have to come back to the opposite seaside estate again, this time when the weather is nice. Although I wanted to take more photos, the rain was getting heavier and heavier, so I couldn't. After researching, I learned that the village across the water was completed and occupied between 1984 and 1986. It was primarily built to relocate Sai Kung's indigenous residents affected by government-led demolitions. However, the village's appearance at the time didn't seem nearly as old as it is now; it had an otherworldly feel.  I was also curious to check the rent in the village, and I was stunned. What?! Monthly rents ranged from only $1,018 to $2,639, offering a tranquil natural environment and a view of a peaceful fishing harbor? Of course, there are always two sides to every coin. First, the village lacks shopping malls and convenience stores, and it's quite a distance from Sai Kung's city center. The most convenient way to get around is by minibus, so buying daily necessities isn't as easy as it usually is. And what's more! The village buildings don't have elevators, making it difficult for the elderly or those with mobility issues to get around.  So in the end, it all comes down to reality: Of course, I'd love to live in Sai Kung, away from the hustle and bustle, to breathe some fresh air, and to wake up to a view of blue skies, white clouds, and the ocean outside my window. But that's assuming I work in Sai Kung or am a freelancer who can work remotely. (bitter smile)

Rating: 4 - Tung Ping Chau, Hong Kong's "Jumanji Island". An island far from the City, a very quite and peaceful place. Island of Hong Kong that is formed entirely of sedimentary rocks with a variety of marine abrasion landforms along its coast. The shores of this island are decorated with colourful laminations of top rock forms and many other natural wonders. From MTR University Station Exit B, you can walk for about 15 minutes upto the Pier and board a ferry. The journey takes around 1.5 hours. This ferry service operates only on Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays.

Rating: 4 - Tung Ping Chau Marine Park was designated in 2001 and includes around 270 hectares of sea area that surrounds the small outlying island of Tung Ping Chau near mainland China's Mirs Bay.  The marine park protects the rich coastal ecosystem, particularly the coral communities around the island, which is amongst the finest in all of Hong Kong's territory. Additionally, you can see marine life in the rock pools and shallow waters that surround Tung Ping Chau. You'll find crabs, sea urchins, sea hares (slugs) and lots of small fish. The goby fish that hand out in the rock pools near Kang Lau Shek are really neat.  Another reason for visiting the Tung Ping Chau Marine Park is to view the outstanding geological features around the island, namely the sedimentary rock formations that offer splendid scenery and coastal areas to explore on foot. There are nice beachfronts and pebble beaches around the island as well. These contribute to the experience of visiting the Tung Ping Chau Marine Park.  Note: To visit the Tung Ping Chau Marine Park there are ferries that depart the Ma Lui Shui Pier near University MTR Station on Saturdays (9am, 3pm) and Sunday (9am). The ferry returns to Ma Lui Shui Pier (5.15pm). Note that there are no ferry service during weekdays.

reviews: Rating: 5 - The best geo park in Hong Kong, far better than the noisy high island hexagonal column rocks. Rating: 4 - Tung Ping Chau, Hong Kong's "Jumanji Island". An island far from the City, a very quite and peaceful place. Island of Hong Kong that is formed entirely of sedimentary rocks with a variety of marine abrasion landforms along its coast. The shores of this island are decorated with colourful laminations of top rock forms and many other natural wonders. From MTR University Station Exit B, you can walk for about 15 minutes upto the Pier and board a ferry. The journey takes around 1.5 hours. This ferry service operates only on Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays.

Rating: 4 - Tung Ping Chau Marine Park was designated in 2001 and includes around 270 hectares of sea area that surrounds the small outlying island of Tung Ping Chau near mainland China's Mirs Bay.  The marine park protects the rich coastal ecosystem, particularly the coral communities around the island, which is amongst the finest in all of Hong Kong's territory. Additionally, you can see marine life in the rock pools and shallow waters that surround Tung Ping Chau. You'll find crabs, sea urchins, sea hares (slugs) and lots of small fish. The goby fish that hand out in the rock pools near Kang Lau Shek are really neat.  Another reason for visiting the Tung Ping Chau Marine Park is to view the outstanding geological features around the island, namely the sedimentary rock formations that offer splendid scenery and coastal areas to explore on foot. There are nice beachfronts and pebble beaches around the island as well. These contribute to the experience of visiting the Tung Ping Chau Marine Park.  Note: To visit the Tung Ping Chau Marine Park there are ferries that depart the Ma Lui Shui Pier near University MTR Station on Saturdays (9am, 3pm) and Sunday (9am). The ferry returns to Ma Lui Shui Pier (5.15pm). Note that there are no ferry service during weekdays.

Rating: 5 - Lovely spot, especially late in the year when humidity and temperature are down. We did a full circuit of the reservoir clockwise from the pineapple dam side. 9K including the side trip to the viewing deck after half-way which is a proper view, unlike the viewing point just before it. The first 3k was nice and easy but it got tougher after that with quite a few ups and downs - tough on the calf muscles. We had a couple of 5-6 yr olds with us and they managed most of it without begging to be carried. I would not classify it as an easy family hike, rather a tough long family walk - but it is buggy friendly if you have a small one. For fit hikers, it is just a long trip which you could also run as a tough 9k if you are a runner. Very nice scenery and peaceful if you omit the annoying occasional monkeys who typically gather near the picnic areas. Don't rustle any plastic wrappers or show any food or wrapper - they will grab it. We got the 82 from Tsuen Wan since you can't get close any other way and exiting the shing mun bus interchange is not possible on foot. Very frequent and fast service on weekends. If I was to change anything, next time I would go anti-clockwise, main dam first to get the long road up from the bus out of the way along with the worst of the later ups and downs done early in the walk when I am fresher. Overall my whole party enjoyed the day immensely. Lovely spot - a slice of HK that everyone would enjoy.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Writing this review feels like visiting memorabilia from a past life. It was 2013 when we came here, it was unintentional, and we did not know what this palace was. Our host party took the lead, and they reimagine the tracks to a night story, which brought us to this underground facility. I tried to think, but then we got drinks, and the music was so damn good that the rhythm carried us away, and we lost it. I think we danced for hours before we realized it was time to go. A broken glass, somebody pushed my buddy, we got violent, and we made our way to the street level. Some things will never change; others will be different. But if I can travel back in time, I would make the same mistakes and revisit VOLAR.

Rating: 5 - Great music! One section of the club dedicated to rnb/hip hop with the other dedicated to house/edm. Great bar service and a very welcoming vibe from both locals and tourists. However, nearly got declined entry as my only form of id was an aus drivers license, so bring passports to be safe! Thought the reviews on the police raids were a lie but it actually happened. Other than that, great club!

Rating: 2 - I think I sensed a distinct racism towards Russians or east Europeans from this club staff behavior. Was it my feeling? The place has a good design and lighting atmosphere, the music is good. But bouncers and personnel are very low in professionalism, courtesy and respect.
Rating: 4 - Girls get re-entry stamp but guys don't. Make sure you have HKID or Passport as the Police often come in and check.

Rating: 3 - OK, so this place was a mixed bag for the Wednesday Halloween party;  Straight up the good stuff first: Oh my goodness those speakers. If you're on the dancefloor the sound is more or less everywhere, very bassy and very full sound. If you're like me, you're there to dance, the bass more than goes through you - very potent and yet the sound quality is good and full enough that you can hear the details and top ends and vocals. The décor is great, classy with a futuristic vibe, top marks on that front too. Great air conditioning provided it's not too overcrowded.  So the bad for me: Good décor and brilliant speakers a good club does not make. It was overcrowded, overcrowded, overcrowded. It didn't help that an entire section was booked off at the back, VIP was packed out too and yet they refused to open the spillover room. A friend said they felt it was '5% too crowded', I would have probably gone further to over 10%. That's just me though, I like to dance and that was *simply not possible* on the dancefloor and probably would have been a struggle even with 10% less people. The music was meh. It was mostly pretty safe remixes of pretty safe pop songs, which is fine, but not what I personally pay entry for, and to me, a waste of such great speakers. The drinks were expensive. I expected them to be expensive, but I asked the bar tender for the cheapest drinks, he asked what I wanted, I said double rum straight and I *think he understood*, keyed in the - customer facing - tills and I kid you not, HK$120. I would have said half that was expensive but not necessarily unexpected, that blew me away. I didn't buy a drink. The vibe was slightly off. This is very subjective, but the overcrowding, mediocre music, expensive drinks and costumes didn't really do it for me. I know people had fun, and I'm not saying I didn't; but even some of the group I was with were saying something was off. Security was incredibly tight with loads of bouncers everywhere and it didn't help the DJ was too vocal and always wanted us to 'put our hands in the air' and expected us to sit down and jump up at one point, in what little space we had...  Conclusion: No doubt the facilities - particularly the speakers - are top notch, probably the best in LKF though I haven't really experienced much at LKF itself so can't say for certain. If you don't mind the entry costs, you pre-drink, and choose the right night with the right music (check out the DJs before you go) you should have a great night. But if you're a dancer or like a slightly more underground feel, a different club might be for you!

The exhibition runs from Aug 3rd to Nov 3rd 2019. You can buy the tickets online which is slightly cheaper but otherwise you can walked in like we do (on our last day in HK) as buying online you will have to pick the available slot times and you can’t do that unless you bought the ticket first. There’s a merchandise shop at the end of the exhibition where you will find Hong Kong-exclusive merchandise according to their website.  We spent about 1.5 hrs there including the merchandise shop. Overall we enjoy the exhibition. It brings back all the good memories of Studio Ghibli animation and a good way to end our holidays in HK.

reviews: Rating: 3 - The final tick on Ros’ list was the trip to the Peak, the highest point in the city where the funicular railway takes you to the summit for panoramic views of this huge city landscape. Ros had purposely left this as the last attraction as it’s then possible to take in the view by day and night. The snag was, so had everyone else, and it took the best part of an hour in a long queue to get to the funicular to get to the top.  We’ve always said we shouldn’t go back to places, and the Peak showed us why, as it wasn’t a patch on what it used to be. Before, it was quaint, but now it’s like a theme park with throngs of people, bright lights, tacky gift shops, cafés and restaurants, called the SkyTerrace, definitely not a nice place. Before, there were no crowds, a large cobbled square, a small viewing area and a bar/restaurant selling drinks. Still, that’s progress. The funicular’s grown too. It used to hold 120 passengers; it now transports 210 camera phone snapping tourists at a time. Still, we joined in and enjoyed watching day turn to night and the panoramic array of buildings turn into a twinkling sea of Christmas lights.  Ros’ tour ended with no evening meal included, but fortunately, as we joined the queue to leave, we came upon an American diner offering deep fried seafood which looked delicious, so it was an easy decision to stop there to eat. Fortunately, they had a table for two by a window so we could enjoy our fisherman’s catch with a view over the brightly lit cityscape.  We queued again for three quarters of an hour for the funicular ride down, and a ten minute walk got us on the train home.

address: Victoria Peak, The Peak, Hong Kong
reviews: Rating: 5 - ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (Must-Visit) .  If you want the best views of Hong Kong without the "tourist trap" headaches, follow this specific loop: Bus 15 Up, Peak Tram Down.  The Peak Experience Once at the top, don't just stay in the mall (Peak Tower). • Lugard Road (Free): For the absolute best photos, walk 15 minutes along Lugard Road. It’s flat, shaded, and offers a panoramic "postcard" view of the harbor for free. • Sky Terrace 428: If you want the highest 360° platform, it’s worth the ticket, but the free trails often have better photography angles.  Most tourists rush to the Lower Tram Terminus and wait in lines that can exceed 60–90 minutes. By taking Bus 15 from Central (Exchange Square or the Ferry Piers), you get: • The Price: It only costs about HK$10–$13, compared to over HK$80 for a single tram ride. • The Views: If you sit on the upper deck, front row, the winding ride up Stubbs Road offers incredible "cliffside" views of the city that you can't see from the tram. • No Waiting: Buses run every 10–15 minutes, and you almost always get a seat if you board at the start of the line.  The return journey via the Peak Tram is the perfect way to finish.  Lines for the tram going down are almost always shorter than the lines going up. • The Experience: You still get to experience the 27° "gravity-defying" tilt and the historic funicular vibe without the morning rush.

Rating: 5 - I absolutely loved visiting Victorian Peak and think it is a must see when in Hong Kong. I not only really loved the views from the peak but also the numerous walks and shops. It is a tourist spot and does get busy however I enjoyed people watching and socialising with others. I also didn't find prices overly expensive here. Victoria Peak has the famous, spectacular view of the city and Victoria Harbour but if you take one of the other walking tracks, you can see the other side of Hong Kong Island which I also found really beautiful and serene. The houses and residence in the area are great to look at too. I found staff at the eateries and shops very friendly, courteous and helpful. In order to get to the peak, you can take the tram. Another option is to take the public bus which drives through the streets and roads snaking up. I feel that in doing this you get to see even more of the views and area. I would highly recommend visiting here.

Rating: 5 - When in Hong Kong….. it’s a must to go up Victoria Peak for the magnificent views over the city and Victoria Bay.  There are various ways to get up the Peak be it walk, taxi or the tram. Naturally it’s a personal choice but riding the tram up Victoria Peak is the fun thing to do.  Fares are reasonable and based upon where you want access to once at the top. Be prepared to queue in the ticket and boarding line down at the bottom but it does move pretty quickly.  The trams are in excellent condition and I believe they hold circa 150 or so people each tram which are made up of double carriages.  5 or so minutes and you are at the top and surrounded by a range of things to do. There are various outdoor spaces and footpath walks but inside there are shops, restaurants and more. Naturally, one of the main reasons people go up here is to go on the observation deck and see the sights of Hong Kong.  It was a sunny day for us but incredibly windy when stood in the wrong position. However, that didn’t matter as the panorama was spectacular.  Lots of people buzzing around observing the views but it all works seamlessly.  Plenty of photo opportunities to be had and even some professional photographers are there if you fancy paying for a special photo shoot.  Victoria Peak is an iconic landmark of Hong Kong and I would certainly recommend experiencing a trip up there if you’re in Hong Kong and never done it before.  Get Victoria Peak ticked off your Hong Kong list as you won’t be disappointed.

An absolute must visit for anyone visiting Hong Kong for the first time.

reviews: Rating: 3 - The Wan Chai Green Trail is a fairly steep 1.1 km trail between Kennedy Road and the Wan Chai Gap at the Peak Road and Stubbs Road intersection. It is a steady uphill climb that takes around 1 hour to complete and covers quite a bit of forested area of mountain slope.  Vegetation is fairly thick at times and views of the harbour are mostly obstructed by trees and growth so photographs are not easy. The Wan Chai Trail includes a host of interesting different historic buildings, temples and market places on or near Queen's Road East. These include The Green House (Burrow's street), Blue House, Yellow House, old Ruttonjee Hospital building, buildings Nos. 186-190 and the Old Wan Chai Market building.  Two temples, around Queen's Road are also included. These are Hung Shing Temple and Pak Tai Temple (Lung On Street) as well as several open market areas, Cross Street, Tai Yuen Street and Gresson Street.  Other trail inclusions are the historic Pawn and Ovologue buildings on Johnston Street, building No 18 and Nam Koo Terrace on Ship Street as well as the nearby Starstreet Precinct.  Overall, you can stroll the area and see each of these heritage buildings and sites in around 2-3 hours depending if you stop at any neighbourhood restaurants or bars. The Pawn is now a popular bar/restaurant and there are quite a few options on Ship Street and within the recently developed Star Street Precinct.

reviews: Rating: 5 - West Kowloon Art Park is a spacious and beautifully designed cultural park along Victoria Harbour, offering a refreshing contrast to Hong Kong’s dense urban landscape. The park blends open green spaces with contemporary architecture, making it a popular place for both locals and visitors to relax, walk, and enjoy the waterfront views.  One of the highlights of the park is its stunning harbour scenery, with wide promenades that are perfect for sunset walks and photography. The area is also home to major cultural venues such as M+ and the Hong Kong Palace Museum, adding artistic depth and creative energy to the surroundings. You’ll often find people picnicking, cycling, or simply sitting on the grass enjoying the sea breeze.  The atmosphere here is calm and open, especially compared to the busy districts nearby. It’s well-maintained, family-friendly, and easy to access by public transport. Overall, West Kowloon Art Park is an ideal spot to slow down, enjoy modern art and architecture, and experience a more relaxed, scenic side of Hong Kong.

Rating: 5 - It's an outdoor fun place to be. With open views of Hong Kong Island across the Victoria Bay and TST area this park office open area setting with lots of restaurants around it’s quite close to the M+ art museum. It’s easily accessible by local transport either the MTR or buses and taxis. Kids can run around and play in the park or you can also pitch in your small tent for picnics. The art park occasionally hosts some of the events for example recently there was Sun-Life big bouncy castle organised near the park. It’s quite popular in the evenings to catch a sunset across the bay.

From the trail, you can choose to ascend Lion Rock for panoramic views or descend into Wong Tai Sin district. For the more adventurous, continuing on to Kowloon Peak is also an option.

Rating: 5 - This (Wilson Trail Section 9) is the hardest thing I've (26F) done in my life. I teared up many times in this trail that took us 8 hours (with plenty of breaks that were not a choice but a voluntary bodily reaction) total. One might ask; why not just turn back? Well because I'm about to tell you 2 important points to note:  1. The first peak is the summit. Turning back meant that we would have to trek down the highest elevation in the trail. Pressing on, however, is just as bad so here's the next point to note should you choose to continue the trail:  2. It's not all downhill from the summit. It felt like a never-ending ascent and descent, where every new peak tested the strength of my calves and my mind. I still remember how it felt looking at the peak ahead of me when I had barely made it up (and down) the previous one.  Perhaps it was the unpreparedness and a whole lot of underestimation but hey, if an obese girly like myself can do it, you definitely can too. Mind over matter and all that but pack enough water and maybe consider going with someone who has mountaineering experience, just in case. We were lucky to have clear skies and insanely beautiful views at every turn, but I knew God understood how desperate I was for a small win up there.  Funnily enough, contrary to its name, this trail had only reminded me of - no, emphasised - my mortality. Glad I lived to tell the tale (that everyone around me will have to hear again and again until I'm over it). Stay safe!

Rating: 5 - Truly beautiful trail which is not difficult yet offers great scenery. The hike is quite safe with mostly well maintained path. The view from the top of Violet Hill is quite amazing. It took us around 2 hours to hike from Parkview to Tai Tam reservoir.

Rating: 5 - Highly recommended but take your time with this. Started at this point, went on to hike Violet Hill The Twins. The incline steps are no joke (1200 steps) and I struggled alot with it. Very beautiful view when you get to the various peaks throughout the path.

reviews: Rating: 5 - Wong Tai Sin Temple Square is the vibrant open plaza located at the entrance of the famous Wong Tai Sin Temple, one of Hong Kong’s most important and widely visited religious sites. The square serves as both a gathering space and a transition area between the busy city and the spiritual calm of the temple grounds, making it an essential part of the overall experience.  The atmosphere at the square is lively and full of energy, especially during weekends, festivals, and significant dates on the lunar calendar. Visitors from all walks of life gather here, including locals seeking blessings, tourists exploring Hong Kong’s spiritual culture, and worshippers preparing incense offerings before entering the temple. The movement of people, the scent of incense, and the surrounding sounds create a unique blend of urban life and spiritual devotion.  The open design of the square allows visitors to pause, observe, and appreciate the surroundings before entering the temple. From here, you can see the iconic architecture of Wong Tai Sin Temple, with its red pillars, golden roofs, and traditional Chinese decorative elements that symbolize Taoist, Buddhist, and Confucian influences. The space feels ceremonial yet welcoming, encouraging both reflection and curiosity.  Wong Tai Sin Temple Square is also closely associated with the practice of kau cim (fortune stick divination), as many visitors prepare themselves mentally and spiritually in the square before seeking guidance inside. During Chinese New Year and major festivals, the square becomes especially crowded and festive, filled with a strong sense of hope, renewal, and shared belief.  Overall, Wong Tai Sin Temple Square is more than just an entrance plaza — it is a cultural and spiritual threshold that reflects Hong Kong’s deep-rooted traditions. Whether you are visiting for worship, cultural exploration, or photography, the square offers an authentic glimpse into the city’s spiritual life and collective faith, making it a meaningful stop for any visitor.

Rating: 4 - The heritage site of Woodside lies on Mount Parker at the beginning of this trail. The Swire Group built it during the 1920s, originally intended to house the quarters for the European staff in the mid-management of the Swire Group.  The red brick building features two stories with an arched veranda. The foundation is built from granite, and the interiors were fitted with wooden floors and staircases and window frames. The original building had two separate sections.  The building has been restored and managed by the Hong Kong Government since 1976. Since 2012, it opened its doors for public visits as the Woodside Biodiversity Education Centre. The museum closes on Tuesdays except on public holidays.

Rating: 5 - This small and sweet nature center is truly a hidden gem and a peaceful retreat within the city. Built in the 1920's as a residence for Taikoo Sugar staff, the building was renovated in 2012 and Woodside Biodiversity Education Center was born.  Located a 20-minute walk uphill from Quarry Bay, Woodside's beautiful setting is well worth the climb. once you arrive and briefly explore the outdoor garden, head indoors! You will find three small but well-done galleries that introduce biodiversity in a fun, hands-on way.  Please note that there is no parking Woodside. If the walk up from King's Road is too daunting, take a taxi straight to Woodside, and enjoy the easy and shaded walk downhill when you leave. Along the way through the lush greenery, you will have nice views of the city and will pass hikers on their way to Quarry Bay Tree Walk and Hong Pak Country Trail.

Rating: 3 - Wu Kau Tang is a village just off the main Bride's Pool Road roughly half way between the northern and southern ends of the Plover Cove Country Park in the New Territories. It is also the starting point for numerous trails that explore stretches of the park taking hikers to various peaks, through thick wooded areas, along beautiful coastlines as well as some of the historic villages.  One of the short and easy trails is the Wu Kau Tang Country Trail which is around 3km in distance. It is a one way trail that starts at the Bride's Pool Road (north) and makes way east and south through the country park, passing through the Wu Kau Tang village before continuing south and back west towards Bride's Pool Road, passing nearby famous waterfalls and nature area at Mirror Pool and Bride's Pool.  The section between Wu Kau Tang and Bride's Pool is what is of interest to most hikers and can be combined with several other interesting hiking routes including the trek east over to Lai Chi Wo or south to the Plover Cove Reservoir and onward to Tei Mei Tuk. The trails are in very good condition, include some delightful sections of ancient road, stone paths constructed by local villages long ago. The trails are sign marked throughout and easy to follow. You just need to know where you intending to go.  Note: Best to research and do your homework before making your way to Plover Cove Country Park to enjoy the Wu Kau Tang Country Trail or others in the area. Be familiar with the estimated hike times as some of the trails are rather long and take most of the day to complete and transportation in and out of the park is a bit limited to buses that call upon Bride's Pool Road stops and the occasion weekend ferry departures from the historic village of Lai Chi Wo.  Note: While public toilet facilities can be found, there is almost nothing in the form of shops and restaurants throughout the country park so make sure to bring enough food and drink with you or be prepared to wait until the end of your hike to grab a bite in Tai Mei Tuk on your way out.

Rating: 4 - Wu Kau Tang is located in Plover Cove Country Park in the northeastern New Territories of Hong Kong. Wu Kau Tang is home to seven Hakka villages: San Uk Tsuen, San Uk Ha, Sam Ka Tsuen, Ho Pui, Ling Pui, Lo Wai, and Tin Sam Tsuen. Located within Sha Tau Kok, Wu Kau Tang boasts a history of approximately 400 years. During the Anti-Japanese War, Wu Kau Tang served as an important base for the Dongjiang Column and the Hong Kong and Kowloon Brigade. A monument commemorating the anti-Japanese martyrs of Wu Kau Tang Village still stands on Bride's Pool Road near Wu Kau Tang.  Wu Kau Tang is within Plover Cove Country Park and offers numerous hiking trails, including Sam A Chung, Lai Chi Wo, Lock Lo Pan, Yung Shue Au, Kuk Po, Fen Shui Au, Lai Chi Wo, Sam A Tsuen, Plowstone, and Kau Tam Tsu. In Tin Sam Tsuen, Wu Kau Tang, there's also a trail that leads to the fire lookout tower and then continues down to Bride's Pool Road in Lower Au. Due to the inconvenient transportation to Wujiaotang District, you can only take a public light bus, taxi or drive. Buses only run on weekends and public holidays, so there are very few tourists.

reviews: Rating: 3 - Yan Tun Kong Study Hall is one of the declared monuments of the Ping Shan Heritage Trail, situated a couple minutes north of Tang Ancestral Hall and Yu Kiu Ancestral Hall. There are red colour signs pointing the way to this recently restored attraction in the village of Hang Tau Tsuen at Yuen Long. Opening Hours are 9am to 1pm and 2-5pm daily (closed on Tuesdays)  The Yan Tun Kong Study Hall played an important role in village life in past centuries, being the location where children were educated and prepared for the Imperial Civil Service Exams. It also provided accommodation for visiting scholars. After the abolition of the Imperial Exams, the building was used to provide modern education per mandate of the Crown until it was replaced with the construction of the Tat Tak School in the early 1930s.  Historically, the building has undergone several restorations, the most recent just a few years ago, giving it a rather pleasant, restored appearance which you can enjoy. The exterior facade is of grey brick construction with plaster motifs and murals around the ridge of the roof.  Inside the study hall, you will find a two hall structure with a typical centre courtyard. The second chamber includes a shrine as well as panels providing historical accounts of the building as well as other information regarding the Ping Shan Heritage Trail.  In the end, this is one of several very interesting historical buildings that you can see along the Ping Shan Heritage Trail. It is not difficult to find if you are using a Heritage Trail map and simply follow the red signs. It can be conveniently visited between stops at the Yeung Hau Temple and the Tang Ancestral Hall.

Rating: 3 - This place is right within the maze of houses. It can be easily missed and lost. However, there are some signs (not big and seems to be put up by locals) that maybe able to help you get there. The place is not big. Keep in mind, they are closed at lunch time.
Rating: 4 - Enjoy some walk around this historical site and the peace.

Rating: 3 - The building was named after their three ancestors, namely, Yan-shaw (仁所), Tun-fuk (敦服) and Ming-kong (鳴岡). The hall was originally called Yen Yi Tong (燕翼堂).  The study hall was used to educate the village children preparing them for the Imperial Civil Service Examination so that they can gain position in the government. It then can enhance their power, wealth and status. Both Chinese classics and martial arts were taught in the hall.

Rating: 4 - The Yeung Hau Temple at Tai O is a Declared Monument building in Hong Kong and one of the most interesting temples to visit in the village. It is located a couple hundred metres north of the stilt houses at the end of the Kat Shing Back Street and is open from 7am to 5pm for public visitations.  Historically, this is one of the oldest temples in Tai O, dating back to around 1699 and is dedicated to the General Hau Wong. It is noted for the Hau Wong Festival which is held here on the 6th day of the 6th lunar month each year and for its associated with the annual Tai O Dragon Boat Water Parade.  What you find is a traditional Qing Dynasty temple of grey brick exterior and a two hall, three bay layout. The facade, entrance and roofing are very decorative, particularly the delightful ceramic folk figures. There is an attractive incense cauldron in front of the temple as well.  What you find within is equally impressive. The interior is highly decorative with shrines, deity figures, hanging lanterns, wooden carvings. You'll also find old whale bones, found by area fisherman in the past, a historic leather drum and an iron cast bell dating back to 1699. Other traditional temple items of worship fill in the space, providing much to see during visits to the Yeung Hau Temple.  Overall, it is well worth making the time to venture north past the stilt houses in Tai O to see the historic Yeung Hau Temple. It is found in a lovely setting where the sea meets the mouth of small canal leading into the village and makes for a rewarding place to visit for those who enjoy historic buildings and/or Chinese temples.

reviews: Rating: 3 - One of the interesting old buildings to see in Tai O is the pre-war shophouse at 60 Kat Hing Street. This property was constructed in 1933 and is recognised as a Grade 2 historic building by the Hong Kong Antiquities and Monuments Office of Hong Kong.  What you see is a two-storey shophouse with a rounded balcony and canopy, nice hints of European exterior which complement well the more traditional Chinese interior. In the past, the ground floor was used as a grocery store, while the owners would have lived upstairs.  Today the property is operated by Yi O Farm House, a business selling farm and seafood based speciality foods. You can also learn a bit about the history of the house and the 3 generations of the Chan family who have lived here since the house was built.  Give the old shophouse a brief look-see when walking down Kat Hing Street if you are interested in architecture or if you want to learn more about this protected heritage building in Tai O. reviews: Rating: 4 - The petite exhibition on site shows various aspects of Kam Tin’s history, its land, its people and its development.  The name “Yi Tai” means the “study hall of the two immortals.”  It refers to the two gods, the literary and the martial gods, that guarded a pagoda built exclusively to bring good feng-shui to the villagers who sat for the Imperial Civil Service Examinations of the Qing Dynasty.
Rating: 5 - An old study hall built almost two hundred years ago in the Qing Dynasty.

Rating: 5 - Yi Tai Study Hall (also known as Yi Tai Shu Yuen) is situated in Shui Tau Village, Kam Tin, Yuen Long. It was erected by a group of 16 local scholar-gentry from Tang Yi Tai Wui during the Daoguang reign (1821-1850) of the Qing dynasty to accommodate the statues of Man Cheong (God of Literature) and Kwan Tai (God of Martial Arts), which were originally worshipped in the nearby Man Cheong Pagoda. Hence, the study hall was named after them. The hall became an important academy, with prominent seholars from around the region giving lecturers there.  With the introduction of modern education in the early 20th century, Yi Tai Study Hall was subsequently used as a primary school for about 30 students. The school was discontinued after the Second World War.  The study hall is a two-hall rectangular building, made of grey bricks and rammed earth. The building is enclosed by a wall with entrances at both ends. Probably for fung shui reasons, the main entrance opens on the side between the two halls, unlike similar buildings. The forecourt of the study hall is paved with white stones, so it is commonly known as “Pak Shek Hong” (White Stone Lane). Full restoration works on Yi Tai Study Hall were completed in 1994. (By AMO)

reviews: Rating: 5 - Yuk Hau Kwong玉虛宮 (Pak Tai Temple北帝廟) is a historic and renowned temple in Cheung Chau長洲, Hong Kong, and is designated a Grade I historic building. It is located at the northern end of Pak She Street, Cheung Chau, Hong Kong. It is open daily from 7:00 AM to 5:00 PM. You can take a ferry from Central Pier 5 in Hong Kong Island to Cheung Chau and walk north along the Cheung Chau Ferry Pier Promenade for about 10 minutes to reach the temple. Long History: The temple was built in 1783 (the 48th year of the Qianlong Emperor's reign in the Qing Dynasty清朝乾隆皇帝四十八年), and has a history of over 200 years. Pak Tai Worship: The fishermen of Cheung Chau worship Pak Tai北帝 (also known as Xuanwu Emperor 玄天上帝or Zhenwu Dadi真武大帝), praying for safe voyages and protection from floods. Legend has it that before the temple was built, a plague struck Cheung Chau, and the plague subsided after residents welcomed a statue of Pak Tai, hence the temple's construction. The temple is the largest Pak Tai temple in Hong Kong, featuring exquisite brick, wood, and tile carvings, especially the two rare and precious dragon pillars.
Rating: 3 - A temple since 18th century.  A gathering place for gathering & praying safety and good wellbeing for the local people in Cheung Chau.

Rating: 4 - The most interesting and beautiful temple to visit on Cheung Chau is the Pak Tai (Yuk Hui) Temple on Pak She Street. The is a Grade I Historical Building built in 1783. Opening hours are 7am to 5pm daily.  The temple has Qing Dynasty characteristics including a beautiful facade with decorative murals. It is fronted by guardian lions. Within the are a separate halls connected by moon gate passageways. You will find expected shrines with deity figures, hanging incense coils, ancient drum and bell and nice wood carvings. You will also find beautifully carved dragon pillars and nice mosaic murals of a tiger and dragon in the two side halls.  In one of the side halls, there are two information panels describing the temple architecture in more detail and providing good description of the various temple highlights to look out for while exploring its grounds.  Note: The Pak Tai Temple is the scene of the annual Cheung Chau Bun Festival when worshippers come to seek blessings from Pak Tai. It can be very crowded at this time of the year.  Overall, if you are going to visit just one temple during your time on Cheung Chau, this is the one to find. The Pak Tai is the most impressive and interesting historic attraction on the island and a place well worth dedicating some time to visit.
Rating: 5 - A wonderful and beautiful historical temple worthy of its conservation status. Intricately decorated with nuggets of history retold.

Rating: 3 - This particular Tin Hau Temple was built in the 1870s and is largely in its original form. The exterior is of a typical Tin Hau design with two dragon statue figures on the top of the roof and many figures carved into the wall which are worth inspecting. They are clearly showing their age and seem simpler in design compared to those found at more elaborate or recently restored Tin Hau Temples.  Inside we particularly liked the tiger and dragon wall murals as well as two large god statues. There are a couple of small rooms filled with various statues too and of course, burning traditional incense coils.  Around 4-5 minutes walk from the Tin Hau temple, there is another, lesser known temple called the Lin Ka Fung Temple. This temple is recessed along Tung Lo Wan Road. In contrast, Lin Ka Fung is a Kwun Yum temple and offers an architectural comparison, worth a quick look for those eager to see more of the Hong Kong temple scene.  Other Tin Hau temples of note that can be visited in Hong Kong include those in Stanley, Sai Kung and Ya Ma Tei among many other smaller temples spread around HK, dedicated to Tin Hau.

Rating: 3 - This particular Tin Hau Temple was built in the 1870s and is largely in its original form. The exterior is of a typical Tin Hau design with two dragon statue figures on the top of the roof and many figures carved into the wall which are worth inspecting. They are clearly showing their age and seem simpler in design compared to those found at more elaborate or recently restored Tin Hau Temples.  Inside we particularly liked the tiger and dragon wall murals as well as two large god statues. There are a couple of small rooms filled with various statues too and of course, burning traditional incense coils.  Around 4-5 minutes walk from the Tin Hau temple, there is another, lesser known temple called the Lin Ka Fung Temple. This temple is recessed along Tung Lo Wan Road. In contrast, Lin Ka Fung is a Kwun Yum temple and offers an architectural comparison, worth a quick look for those eager to see more of the Hong Kong temple scene.  Other Tin Hau temples of note that can be visited in Hong Kong include those in Stanley, Sai Kung and Ya Ma Tei among many other smaller temples spread around HK, dedicated to Tin Hau.
